# shaderlib catalog

Every WGSL file in `warp_sdk/shaderlib/`, one line each. Pick by tag, then
compose by path:

```rust
let wgsl = warp_sdk::shaderlib::compose(&["material/stone.wgsl"]);
```

Format of a line: `path` — what it gives — `fn` names — tags.

## core

- `core/material.wgsl` — the `MaterialSample` surface record — `material_default` — surface, pbr

## noise

- `noise/hash.wgsl` — PCG integer hashes as floats in [0,1); seeded lattice hashes, cell wrap, quintic fade, random unit gradients — `noise_pcg`, `noise_pcg3d`, `noise_u2f`, `noise_hash11/21/22/31/33`, `noise_hash2i`, `noise_lattice2/3`, `noise_wrap2/3`, `noise_fade2/3`, `noise_dfade2/3`, `noise_grad2/3` — hash, random, seed, lattice
- `noise/value.wgsl` — value noise 2D/3D in [0,1] with analytic derivative, tileable — `noise_value2/3`, `noise_value2d/3d`, `noise_value2d_tiled`, `noise_value3d_tiled` — value, lattice, derivative, normal, tileable
- `noise/gradient.wgsl` — Perlin gradient noise 2D/3D in [-1,1] with analytic derivative, tileable — `noise_perlin2/3`, `noise_perlin2d/3d`, `noise_perlin2_tiled`, `noise_perlin2d_tiled`, `noise_perlin3_tiled`, `noise_perlin3d_tiled` — perlin, gradient, derivative, normal, tileable, terrain
- `noise/simplex.wgsl` — simplex noise 2D/3D in [-1,1] with analytic derivative, seeded, no repeat — `noise_simplex2/3`, `noise_simplex2d/3d` — simplex, derivative, normal, animated
- `noise/cellular.wgsl` — Worley F1, F2, F2-F1, cell id in 2D/3D; exact cell border distance; smooth F1; tileable — `noise_worley2`, `noise_worley2_tiled`, `noise_worley2_border`, `noise_worley2_smooth`, `noise_worley3`, `noise_worley3_tiled` — worley, voronoi, cellular, cracks, scales, pebbles, clouds

items.name: asset_root
items.doc:
Resolve the asset root directory. Cached after first call.

Checks four locations in order, then falls back:
1. `STELLA_NOVA_ASSETS` environment variable
2. `src/assets/` relative to the working directory (dev mode)
3. `assets/` alongside the executable
4. `Contents/Resources/assets/` inside a macOS `.app` bundle
5. `src/assets/` again, unchecked, when none of the four exist

items.name: asset_path
load_ship_atlas
items.sig: pub fn load_ship_atlas( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, layout: &wgpu::BindGroupLayout, ) -> ImageAtlas
items.doc: Load the primary single-directory atlas declared by the application.

items.name: ship_image_names
items.doc:
Returns sorted, leaked (&'static str) filename stems from the primary
image atlas directory. Returns an empty vec when nothing is declared or
the directory is missing.

items.name: MegaAtlasSet
items.doc:
The loaded mega-atlases, one per slot, always MAX_ATLAS_SLOTS long.

The Vec is private so every reader goes through `get` or `mapping` and
gets the clamp. Slot numbers are the indices the application gave its
atlases in the descriptor.

items.name: load
items.sig: pub fn load( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, layout: &wgpu::BindGroupLayout, ) -> Self

items.name: placeholder
items.sig: pub fn placeholder( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, layout: &wgpu::BindGroupLayout, ) -> Self
items.doc:
One placeholder per slot. SharedGpu builds this before the real
textures exist, so the first frame has a bind group to draw with.

items.name: len
items.doc: How many slots this set holds. Always MAX_ATLAS_SLOTS.

items.name: get
items.doc:
Atlas by slot number. Slots past the last one answer with the last
one, which is a placeholder in every set that declares fewer atlases
than the render path addresses. The clamp keeps a wrong slot number a
wrong sprite rather than a panic on the render thread.

items.name: mapping
items.doc: Texture mapping by slot number.

items.name: mappings
items.doc:
Every mapping, in slot order. RenderContext takes the whole list, so
the callers that used to build a fixed-size array now call this.

items.name: BUS_SAMPLE_RATE
items.doc:
The rate every lane runs at, in Hz.

Chosen rather than discovered, for the reason in the header. 44.1 kHz is
also the rate the game's own assets are at, so the common case does no
resampling before the tap and the monitor sees the file's own samples.

items.name: BUS_CHANNELS
items.doc:
The channel count every lane runs at.

The tap folds these to one mono sample per frame before the scope. A
spectrogram of a stereo pair is two spectrograms, and nobody reading this
panel is asking a question that needs the second one.

items.name: reset
items.doc:
Forget everything the monitor is holding: samples, peaks and events.

For the transport's Stop edge, where the game has stopped its own sinks and
every voice the board still believes in has in fact ended. Without it the
panel holds the last frame of a game that is no longer running, which reads
as a game still running.

items.name: Bus
items.doc:
The lanes the game plays into.

Holds only the controller half of each lane. The mixer half went to rodio
inside a `Tap` when the bus was built, and lives on the audio thread from
then on.

items.name: new
items.doc:
Build every lane and hand each one's tap to the output stream.

Every lane is registered in one pass, before any of them can carry
sound. rodio defers a pending source until its channel count divides
the samples it has produced, so lanes offered together are accepted
together and begin at one offset. Offering them at different times
would risk starting one a sample later than the other, and the scope
sums the lanes by index on the promise that this does not happen.

items.name: sink
items.sig: pub fn sink(&self, lane: Lane) -> Sink
items.doc:
A sink on one lane.

Replaces `Sink::try_new(&stream_handle)` at a call site and changes
nothing else about it. The returned sink is stopped by dropping it,
reports `empty` when its queue drains, and takes volume and pause the
way it always did.

items.name: play_raw
items.sig: pub fn play_raw<S>(&self, lane: Lane, source: S) where S: Source<Item = f32> + Send + 'static,
items.doc:
Play a source on one lane with no handle to control it.

For sound that is over before anything could want to stop it, and for
the silent primer a device wants at open. Everything else should take
a sink, because a sound with no handle cannot be silenced when the
transport stops.

items.name: Chord
items.doc: A named chord and how well the profile matched it.

items.name: name
items.doc: The chord symbol: `C`, `Am`, `F♯m7`.

items.name: tones
items.doc:
Which pitch classes this chord contains, as a mask over the wheel.

A mask rather than a list because every caller is asking "is this
wedge in the chord" once per wedge, and a twelve-entry linear search
per wedge is the shape that invites an inner loop nobody notices.

items.name: is_chord
items.doc: True for anything that is really a chord, as opposed to one note.

items.name: now
items.doc: The chord sounding right now, or None while nothing is.

items.name: dominant
items.doc:
The chord carrying the passage, or None before there is enough
agreement to name one.

items.name: chroma
items.doc:
The twelve-wedge profile, smoothed for display. Normalised so the
loudest class is 1.0.

items.name: level
items.doc:
How much signal the last frame had, 0..1. The panel's own idea of
loudness — the meters answer that question properly.

items.name: tuning_cents
items.doc: How far the input sits from A440, in cents. Positive is sharp.

items.name: notes
items.doc: How many separate notes the last frame resolved.

items.name: reset
items.doc:
Forget the passage and the profile. For a cleared capture, or a
source that has just been switched out from under the panel.

items.name: feed
items.sig: pub fn feed(&mut self, mono: &[f32], rate: u32)
items.doc:
One analysis frame over the most recent sound.

`mono` is read from the END, so a caller handing over a ring longer
than the window gets the newest sound analysed rather than the oldest.
Shorter input is zero-padded at the front, which is what a capture that
has just started actually is.

items.name: Quality
items.doc: What kind of chord, independent of what it is rooted on.
items.body:
Major,
Minor,
Dom7,
Maj7,
Min7,
Sus2,
Sus4,
Dim,
/// One note, sounding alone. Not a chord, and the panel says so rather
/// than guessing a triad from a third of one.
Single,

items.name: CHORDS
items.sig: pub const CHORDS: [Quality; 8] = [ Quality::Major, Quality::Minor, Quality::Dom7, Quality::Maj7, Quality::Min7, Quality::Sus2, Quality::Sus4, Quality::Dim, ]
items.doc:
Everything the template table is built from. `Single` is deliberately
absent: it is what the detector falls back to when there is only one
pitch class alive, not something a profile is matched against.

items.name: intervals
items.doc:
Semitones above the root. The first is always the root itself, which
is what the root weighting keys off.

items.name: suffix
items.doc:
What goes after the root in a chord symbol. Major is the empty string,
as it is written.

items.name: label
items.doc: The same thing said in words, for the line under the symbol.

items.name: SoundEvent
items.doc:
One sound, at the moment the game started it.

Everything here is what the game knew at that instant. Nothing is filled in
later, because the sink is gone by then and the game would be guessing.

items.name: sfx
items.sig: pub fn sfx(name: impl Into<String>) -> SoundEvent
items.doc:
A sound effect on the effects lane, with everything else defaulted.

The builders below fill in what the call site knows. A call site that
knows nothing but the name still produces a useful row, which is what
keeps instrumenting a new sound down to one line.

items.name: music
items.sig: pub fn music(name: impl Into<String>) -> SoundEvent
items.doc: A track on the music lane. Exclusive, because there is one music sink.

items.name: Lane
items.doc:
Which of the game's two kinds of sound a block of samples belongs to.

The two are separated at the bus and stay separated all the way to the
display, because the question the monitor exists to answer is usually
about one of them: whether the music is ducking, or whether a sound effect
fired. A single mixed lane can be summed out of these two, and two lanes
cannot be recovered from one mixed one.

A third kind — ambient beds, dialogue — is one variant here, one row in
`ALL`, and one arm in `label`. Nothing else counts lanes.

items.name: ALL
items.doc: Every lane, in display order.

items.name: index
items.doc: Its index into the ring array.

items.name: label
items.doc: The name the panel puts on it.

items.name: from_index
items.doc: The lane at `i`, or none when `i` names no lane.

items.name: LANE_COUNT
items.doc: How many lanes there are. Derived from `Lane::ALL` so the two cannot drift.

items.name: Analyzer
items.doc:
Turns a block of mono samples into one spectrogram column.

It holds every buffer the transform needs, sized once, so a column costs a
window multiply, a transform per lane and a fold, and no trip to the
allocator. A free function taking the scratch by argument was the first
shape and made every caller carry six buffers it had no opinion about.

items.name: new
items.doc:
`bins` is the number of output bins (spectrogram rows). Typically
128..256.

Everything is allocated here and nothing after. Zero bins is allowed
and yields an analyzer that produces an empty column; rejecting it
with a panic was considered and lost, because the caller sizes bins
from a panel height that is legitimately zero while a dock animates.

items.name: multi
items.sig: pub fn multi(bins: usize, windows: &[usize], hop: usize) -> Self
items.doc:
One analyzer reading `windows` window lengths, emitting a column every
`hop` samples.

`windows` is a set of powers of two; anything else in it is dropped
rather than refused, because the alternative is a panic in a display
path over a constant somebody mistyped. An empty set — or one that is
empty after the filter — falls back to a single `FFT_SIZE` lane, which
is the behaviour of `new`.

`hop` matters only to lanes shorter than it: those are placed as many
times as fit, so no part of the interval between two columns escapes
being looked at.

items.name: set_sharpen
items.sig: pub fn set_sharpen(&mut self, amount: f32)
items.doc:
How much of the window's own smear is taken off the picture, 0..=1.

Zero is the plain fold. One leaves only the reassigned partials, on a
floor of black. The default is most of the way up, because the smear
is an artefact of the window and not a property of the sound.

items.name: bins
items.doc: Number of output bins.

items.name: window_len
items.doc:
Samples the longest lane reads, which is how much recent sound a
caller has to keep in order to feed a full column.

items.name: bin_window
items.sig: pub fn bin_window(&self, k: usize) -> usize
items.doc:
The window length band `k` was measured with, for a panel that wants
to say what the time resolution is where the pointer is.

Out of range reads as the longest lane, because a band that does not
exist has no measurement and the coarsest answer is the safe lie.

items.name: bin_hz
items.doc:
The centre frequency in Hz of each bin, for axis labels. Length ==
bins().

The centre is the geometric mean of the band's edges, which is the
midpoint of the band as drawn, since the axis is logarithmic. The
arithmetic mean was used at first and put every label above the middle
of its own row.

items.name: set_rate
items.sig: pub fn set_rate(&mut self, rate: u32)
items.doc:
Point the axis at a sample rate without analyzing anything.

For a caller that holds an analyzer only to ask it where the rows are
— `bin_hz`, `bin_window` — and never feeds it samples. Calling
`analyze` on a buffer of zeros was the alternative and runs the whole
ladder to answer a question about labels.

items.name: db_range
items.doc:
Floor and ceiling of the dB mapping, so the UI can label the colour
scale.

items.name: set_db_range
items.sig: pub fn set_db_range(&mut self, floor_db: f32, ceil_db: f32)
items.doc:
Move the floor and ceiling of the dB mapping.

The two are sorted, and a range with no width is opened by a hair, so
a slider dragged past its partner cannot divide the normalisation by
zero. Rejecting an inverted range was the alternative and it makes the
caller carry state it has no reason to.

items.name: analyze
items.sig: pub fn analyze(&mut self, mono: &[f32], sample_rate: u32) -> &[f32]
items.doc:
Analyze the most recent sound at `sample_rate`.

`mono` should hold at least `window_len()` samples, newest last;
shorter input is zero-padded at the front and longer input uses the
tail, so a caller feeding a growing ring buffer always sees the most
recent sound. Returns `bins` magnitudes, each already mapped to
0.0..=1.0 for display.

items.name: Bus
items.doc:
The lanes the game plays into.

Holds only the controller half of each lane. The mixer half went to rodio
inside a `Tap` when the bus was built, and lives on the audio thread from
then on.

items.name: new
items.doc:
Build every lane and hand each one's tap to the output stream.

Every lane is registered in one pass, before any of them can carry
sound. rodio defers a pending source until its channel count divides
the samples it has produced, so lanes offered together are accepted
together and begin at one offset. Offering them at different times
would risk starting one a sample later than the other, and the scope
sums the lanes by index on the promise that this does not happen.

items.name: sink
items.sig: pub fn sink(&self, lane: Lane) -> Sink
items.doc:
A sink on one lane.

Replaces `Sink::try_new(&stream_handle)` at a call site and changes
nothing else about it. The returned sink is stopped by dropping it,
reports `empty` when its queue drains, and takes volume and pause the
way it always did.

items.name: play_raw
items.sig: pub fn play_raw<S>(&self, lane: Lane, source: S) where S: Source<Item = f32> + Send + 'static,
items.doc:
Play a source on one lane with no handle to control it.

For sound that is over before anything could want to stop it, and for
the silent primer a device wants at open. Everything else should take
a sink, because a sound with no handle cannot be silenced when the
transport stops.

items.name: WINDOW
items.doc:
Samples one analysis frame reads.

341 ms at 48 kHz, 2.9 Hz a bin. See the header for why this is four times
the longest window the spectrogram will use.

items.name: NOTE_NAMES
items.doc:
The twelve pitch classes, sharp-spelled.

Sharps and not flats because the wheel is a circle of twelve and the
spelling would have to come from a key this does not estimate. Naming
A♯ where a score would say B♭ is a spelling error; naming the wrong pitch
class would be a measurement error, and only one of those is here.

items.name: CHORDS
items.sig: pub const CHORDS: [Quality; 8] = [ Quality::Major, Quality::Minor, Quality::Dom7, Quality::Maj7, Quality::Min7, Quality::Sus2, Quality::Sus4, Quality::Dim, ]

Everything the template table is built from. `Single` is deliberately

A mask rather than a list because every caller is asking "is this

items.sig: pub fn feed(&mut self, mono: &[f32], rate: u32)
items.doc:
One analysis frame over the most recent sound.

`mono` is read from the END, so a caller handing over a ring longer
than the window gets the newest sound analysed rather than the oldest.
Shorter input is zero-padded at the front, which is what a capture that
has just started actually is.

items.name: QUEUE_LIMIT
items.doc:

A busy combat frame pushes perhaps a dozen. This is several seconds of the
worst case, which is more than an editor drawing at sixty hertz can fall
behind by without something else being wrong.

items.name: MAX_DRAIN_PER_FRAME
items.doc:
Events the editor takes in one frame.

The same bargain `build.rs` strikes with its log: a burst is spread over a
few frames rather than spending one frame draining all of it.

items.doc:
How long a voice with no declared duration is held on screen.

Long enough to read, short enough that a mistake clears itself. Voices
retired this way are flagged, and the panel says so.

items.name: HELD_VOICE_LIFE

How long an exclusive voice with no declared duration is held.

Long, because what ends such a voice is the next one taking its lane, not
a clock. The bound exists only so that a lane whose owner stopped without
saying so eventually clears rather than showing a track that finished half
an hour ago.

Stella Nova's library holds a few hundred, so the cap only bites on a root

tree and useless about the editor, which has to hold the result in memory

descent runs for minutes and the panel has nothing to show for the wait.

items.sig: pub const CAPACITY: usize = 1 << 15;  const MASK: usize = CAPACITY - 1;  /// Which of the game's two kinds of sound a block of samples belongs to. /// /// The two are separated at the bus and stay separated all the way to the /// display, because the question the monitor exists to answer is usually /// about one of them: whether the music is ducking, or whether a sound effect /// fired. A single mixed lane can be summed out of these two, and two lanes /// cannot be recovered from one mixed one. ///
items.doc:
Samples held per lane. A power of two, so the index wraps with a mask.

At 44.1 kHz this is 0.74 s of history. The spectrogram reads a window of
about two thousand samples per frame, so the ring holds far more than one
read needs; the surplus is what lets a frame the editor missed still be
there when it draws the next one.

items.name: Lane
items.doc:
Which of the game's two kinds of sound a block of samples belongs to.

The two are separated at the bus and stay separated all the way to the
display, because the question the monitor exists to answer is usually
about one of them: whether the music is ducking, or whether a sound effect
fired. A single mixed lane can be summed out of these two, and two lanes
cannot be recovered from one mixed one.

A third kind — ambient beds, dialogue — is one variant here, one row in
`ALL`, and one arm in `label`. Nothing else counts lanes.

items.doc: How many lanes there are. Derived from `Lane::ALL` so the two cannot drift.

items.name: ALL
items.doc: Every lane, in display order.

items.name: Ring
items.doc:
One lane's samples, its cursor, and its peak since the last read.

`#[repr(C)]` and a fixed-length array rather than a `Vec`, because this is
one of the things two processes map. A `Vec` here would be a pointer into
the writer's heap, which in the reader's address space is not a ring — it
is whatever happens to be at that address.

items.name: Block
items.doc:
Every lane's ring, the format they were captured at, and a header that says
so — the whole of what the monitor reads.

WHY THIS IS A STRUCT AND NOT A HANDFUL OF STATICS
------------------------------------------------
It was a handful of statics, and that was correct while the game was linked
into the editor: one process, one set of rings, the audio callback writing
them and the panel reading them.

The game is now a child process. Its callback fills ITS copy of these
statics, in an address space the editor cannot see, and the editor's copy
stays at zero for ever — the panel reads a rate of zero, calls itself
silent, and draws "waiting for audio" over a game that is playing. Gathering
the state into one `#[repr(C)]` block is what lets a second process map the
same bytes and read the sound where it is actually being made.


Nothing about the single-process case changes: with no block adopted the
accessors work against a process-local one and behave exactly as before.

items.name: BLOCK_BYTES
items.doc: How many bytes a block occupies. What a shared mapping must be sized to.

items.name: init
items.doc:
Stamp a freshly zeroed region as a block.

Zero is the correct initial value for every other field — an empty
ring, a cursor at nothing, no peak, no format — so there is nothing to
write but the header, and a caller that hands over a region which is
NOT zeroed hands over a ring full of somebody else's bytes.

The magic goes last, with a release. Everything a reader validates
against was written before it, so an attacher that sees the magic sees
a finished header.

# Safety
`self` must point at `BLOCK_BYTES` of zeroed, writable, aligned memory.

items.name: is_valid
items.doc: Whether this region is a block this build can read.

items.name: adopt
items.sig: pub unsafe fn adopt(ptr: *mut Block) -> bool
items.doc:
Read and write a block somebody else is holding, instead of this process's
own.

Both ends of the host link call this: the game, over a region it created
and published, and the editor, over the same region attached by name. From
then on `write` in one process and `latest` in the other are the same ring.

# Safety
`ptr` must point at a valid, initialised `Block` that stays mapped and
writable until `release` is called or the process ends. A block unmapped
while adopted is a use-after-free on the audio thread.

items.name: release
items.doc:
Go back to this process's own block.

The editor calls this when the game it was reading exits. The local block
is empty, so the panel reads a rate of zero and says silent — which is the
truth once there is no game, and is better than holding the last second of
sound a dead process made.

items.name: is_adopted
items.doc: Whether a block other than this process's own is in use.

items.name: set_format
items.sig: pub fn set_format(sample_rate: u32, channels: u16)
items.doc:
Record the format the bus opened, once, at device open.

The spectrogram cannot label a frequency axis without the rate, and the
rate is not known until cpal has picked a device. Hardcoding 44100 would
be right on most machines and silently wrong on the rest, which is the
worst of the options: an axis that is off by a factor nobody can see.

items.name: sample_rate
items.doc: The device sample rate in Hz, or zero when no device is open.

items.name: channels
items.doc: How many channels the tap folds into each mono sample, or zero.

items.name: is_live
items.doc: Whether a bus has opened a device and named its format.

items.name: write
items.doc:
Append a block of mono samples to one lane. Audio thread.

Takes a block rather than a sample so the cursor is published once per
callback instead of once per sample. A per-sample release store would be
correct and would also put a fence in the innermost loop of the mixer, for
no reader that could use the extra resolution.

items.name: cursor
items.doc:
Total samples ever written to a lane.

Two calls a frame apart say how much sound passed between them, which is
how the panel tells a lane that is playing silence from a lane that has
stopped being pulled at all.

items.name: mixed_cursor
items.doc:
The cursor of the lane that has advanced least.

`latest_mixed` anchors on this rather than on any one lane, so it never
reads a lane past what that lane has actually written.

items.name: mixed_head
items.doc:
The cursor of the lane that has advanced MOST.

The game feed's summed source anchors on this, not on `mixed_cursor`. A
lane the running game never plays — a title screen with music and no
effects — is pulled by the mixer and advances in step, so in the common
case the two agree. But a lane that is never WRITTEN sits at zero, and the
minimum would then pin the summed capture at zero and record nothing while
the other lane is plainly sounding. The maximum records what played and
reads the silent lane as the silence it is.

items.name: window_at
items.sig: pub fn window_at(lane: Lane, end: u64, out: &mut [f32])
items.doc:
Read one lane's window of `out.len()` samples ending at `end`.

For a reader stepping through history at its own pace rather than taking
whatever is newest. A spectrogram wants this: its columns have to advance
by a fixed number of samples each, or the time axis stretches and squeezes
with the editor's frame rate and a steady tone draws as a wobble.

`end` further back than `CAPACITY` reads samples the writer has since
overwritten. The caller is the one that knows how far behind it is, so it
is the caller that decides to snap forward; this reports no error.

items.name: mixed_window_at
items.doc:
Read every lane summed, over the window of `out.len()` samples ending at
`end`.

items.name: latest
items.sig: pub fn latest(lane: Lane, out: &mut [f32]) -> u64
items.doc:
Read one lane's `out.len()` newest samples, oldest first. Returns the
cursor the window ends at.

A lane with fewer samples than asked for is zero-padded at the front, so
the caller always gets a full buffer and a spectrogram opens on silence
rather than on whatever the ring was initialised to.

items.name: latest_mixed
items.doc:
Read the newest samples of every lane summed, oldest first.

This is the mix as the device hears it, not an approximation of it: the
lanes are pulled in step by one mixer, so the sample at a given index in
one lane and the sample at that index in the other were emitted together.

items.name: take_peak
items.doc:
The largest magnitude a lane carried since this was last called, then zero.

Taking rather than peeking is what makes the reading independent of the
draw rate. A peeked peak decays on whatever schedule the panel happens to
run at; a taken one is the true peak of the interval the panel is drawing,
whatever length that interval turned out to be.

items.name: reset
items.doc:
Zero every lane's samples, peaks and cursors.

For the transport's Stop edge. The play gate suppresses calls and releases
nothing, so without this the monitor holds the last frame of a game that
has stopped and reads as a game still playing it.

items.name: FFT_SIZE
items.doc:
Default window size in samples, for `Analyzer::new`. Power of two.

A thousand points at 44100 Hz is 23 ms of sound and 43 Hz of resolution,
which is the usual compromise: long enough to separate two notes, short
enough that a drum hit stays one column. A longer window was tried and
smears the attack across the width of the display.

It is the single-lane default and not a limit. `Analyzer::multi` takes a
ladder of lengths and spends the long ones on the bass, where this is far
too coarse to resolve a band.

items.name: F_LO
items.doc:
Bottom of the frequency axis, in Hz.

Below this the log axis spends rows on rumble and DC offset. Starting at
zero was the obvious first choice and cannot be done at all, because the
axis is geometric and zero has no logarithm.

items.name: axis_range
items.doc:
The lowest and highest frequency the axis covers at `rate`, in Hz.

The same two numbers `retune` builds the band edges from, so a panel
drawing gridlines puts them where the rows actually are. Working it out a
second time in the UI was the previous arrangement and drifted the moment
the capture arrived at a rate the axis had assumed nothing about.

items.name: DEFAULT_FLOOR_DB
items.doc:
Default floor and ceiling of the dB map, in dBFS.

Public because a panel storing a column as bytes has to know what a byte
MEANS in order to label a colour scale with it, and working it out a
second time in the UI is how the two drift apart.

items.name: DEFAULT_SHARPEN
items.doc:
How much of the window's smear to take off a PICTURE.

A recommendation and not the default. An analyzer starts at zero, because
reassignment moves energy and a fresh Analyzer has to mean "the largest
linear bin inside this band" for whoever is reading it as a measurement.
The thing that wants a picture asks for it, and the capture that feeds the
spectrogram is the thing that asks.

Not one. At full strength the bed goes to black and a picture of anything
broadband — a cymbal, a snare, room noise — is empty, because none of it
is a partial. Three quarters keeps that bed visible while pulling the
tonal content into lines.

items.name: Analyzer
items.doc:
Turns a block of mono samples into one spectrogram column.

It holds every buffer the transform needs, sized once, so a column costs a
window multiply, a transform per lane and a fold, and no trip to the
allocator. A free function taking the scratch by argument was the first
shape and made every caller carry six buffers it had no opinion about.

items.name: new
items.doc:
`bins` is the number of output bins (spectrogram rows). Typically
128..256.

Everything is allocated here and nothing after. Zero bins is allowed
and yields an analyzer that produces an empty column; rejecting it
with a panic was considered and lost, because the caller sizes bins
from a panel height that is legitimately zero while a dock animates.

items.name: multi
items.sig: pub fn multi(bins: usize, windows: &[usize], hop: usize) -> Self
items.doc:
One analyzer reading `windows` window lengths, emitting a column every
`hop` samples.

`windows` is a set of powers of two; anything else in it is dropped
rather than refused, because the alternative is a panic in a display
path over a constant somebody mistyped. An empty set — or one that is
empty after the filter — falls back to a single `FFT_SIZE` lane, which
is the behaviour of `new`.

`hop` matters only to lanes shorter than it: those are placed as many
times as fit, so no part of the interval between two columns escapes
being looked at.

items.name: set_sharpen
items.sig: pub fn set_sharpen(&mut self, amount: f32)
items.doc:
How much of the window's own smear is taken off the picture, 0..=1.

Zero is the plain fold. One leaves only the reassigned partials, on a
floor of black. The default is most of the way up, because the smear
is an artefact of the window and not a property of the sound.

items.name: bins
items.doc: Number of output bins.

items.name: window_len
items.doc:
Samples the longest lane reads, which is how much recent sound a
caller has to keep in order to feed a full column.

items.name: bin_window
items.sig: pub fn bin_window(&self, k: usize) -> usize
items.doc:
The window length band `k` was measured with, for a panel that wants
to say what the time resolution is where the pointer is.

Out of range reads as the longest lane, because a band that does not
exist has no measurement and the coarsest answer is the safe lie.

items.name: bin_hz
items.doc:
The centre frequency in Hz of each bin, for axis labels. Length ==
bins().

The centre is the geometric mean of the band's edges, which is the
midpoint of the band as drawn, since the axis is logarithmic. The
arithmetic mean was used at first and put every label above the middle
of its own row.

items.name: set_rate
items.sig: pub fn set_rate(&mut self, rate: u32)
items.doc:
Point the axis at a sample rate without analyzing anything.

For a caller that holds an analyzer only to ask it where the rows are
— `bin_hz`, `bin_window` — and never feeds it samples. Calling
`analyze` on a buffer of zeros was the alternative and runs the whole
ladder to answer a question about labels.

items.name: db_range
items.doc:
Floor and ceiling of the dB mapping, so the UI can label the colour
scale.

items.name: set_db_range
items.sig: pub fn set_db_range(&mut self, floor_db: f32, ceil_db: f32)
items.doc:
Move the floor and ceiling of the dB mapping.

The two are sorted, and a range with no width is opened by a hair, so
a slider dragged past its partner cannot divide the normalisation by
zero. Rejecting an inverted range was the alternative and it makes the
caller carry state it has no reason to.

items.name: analyze
items.sig: pub fn analyze(&mut self, mono: &[f32], sample_rate: u32) -> &[f32]
items.doc:
Analyze the most recent sound at `sample_rate`.

`mono` should hold at least `window_len()` samples, newest last;
shorter input is zero-padded at the front and longer input uses the
tail, so a caller feeding a growing ring buffer always sees the most
recent sound. Returns `bins` magnitudes, each already mapped to
0.0..=1.0 for display.

items.name: fft_in_place
items.doc:
Radix-2 in-place complex FFT. `re` and `im` must be the same length and a
power of two.

Decimation in time: the input is permuted into bit-reversed order and then
combined in log2(n) passes of butterflies. Nothing is scaled on the way
out, so a forward transform of n points multiplies amplitude by n and the
caller divides. A recursive formulation reads better and was rejected
because it allocates a pair of half-length buffers per level, and this
runs every frame.

A length that is not a power of two, or halves of unequal length, leave
the buffers untouched rather than panicking; the display can survive a
blank column and a panic in the UI thread takes the editor with it.

items.name: hann
items.doc:
A Hann window of `n` points, cached by the caller.

The periodic form, `0.5 - 0.5*cos(2*pi*i/n)`, whose coherent gain is
exactly one half. The symmetric form with `n - 1` in the denominator is
the right one for filter design and the wrong one here, because it is not
periodic in the block it is applied to and leaks a little at the seam.

items.name: Action
items.doc:
One thing a person can do, and what it is on by default.

Every field is `'static`: an action catalog is written down in the source
of the application, not built at run time. That is what keeps `Action`
`Copy` and the whole table cheap to hand around.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub const fn new( id: &'static str, name: &'static str, group: &'static str, defaults: &'static [Chord], ) -> Action
items.doc: A declaration with no hint and no context, which is most of them.

items.name: hinted
items.sig: pub const fn hinted( id: &'static str, name: &'static str, group: &'static str, hint: &'static str, defaults: &'static [Chord], ) -> Action
items.doc: The same, with the line of explanation.

items.name: in_context
items.sig: pub const fn in_context( id: &'static str, name: &'static str, group: &'static str, context: &'static str, defaults: &'static [Chord], ) -> Action
items.doc: The same, live only in a named context.

items.name: full
items.sig: pub const fn full( id: &'static str, name: &'static str, group: &'static str, context: &'static str, hint: &'static str, defaults: &'static [Chord], ) -> Action
items.doc: Everything at once.

items.name: ActionWire
items.doc:
One action, with its text owned rather than `'static`.

`Action` is `Copy` because a catalog is source code, and that is worth
keeping — every query in this file copies one. It is also exactly what
stops an `Action` being deserialised, because there is no `&'static str`
on the far end of a socket. So the wire carries this and `install` puts
the `'static` back by interning.
items.body:
pub id: String,
pub name: String,
pub group: String,
pub context: String,
pub hint: String,
pub defaults: Vec<Chord>,

items.name: Snapshot
items.doc:
A whole binding table as the process that owns it sees it.

The overrides ride with the catalog and are not left to the viewer's own
store. Both processes read the same file, but only one of them has the
catalog that says which lines in it are live — a viewer loading the file
itself would be guessing at a table it cannot see, and would disagree with
the owner the moment the owner wrote to it.

items.name: Edit
items.doc:
A rebind made in a process that does not own the table.

Three variants and not one, because `reset` is not `set` to the defaults:
it REMOVES the override, so a later build that moves a default reaches
somebody who pressed Reset. Collapsing them here would quietly convert
every reset into a pin at whatever the default was on the day.
items.body:
Set { id: String, chords: Vec<Chord> },
Reset { id: String },
ResetAll,

items.name: ActionId
items.doc:
Anything that names an action.

Implemented for the string types so a caller can pass an id directly, and
meant to be implemented by an application's own action enum so the call
sites read as `held(A::CameraUp, input)` and a typo is a compile error
rather than a control that silently does nothing.

The return is `&str` and not `&'static str` on purpose. A panel editing
this table holds the id it is working on as a `String` — it came from a
click, not from source — and a `'static` return would force that caller to
leak it to say the same thing.

items.name: register
items.doc:
Declare the catalog and load whatever the person has overridden.

Replaces any earlier catalog. Overrides naming an action that is not in the
new catalog are kept in memory and written back out unchanged, so a panel
opened by a build with a smaller catalog — a tool window, say — does not
erase the bindings of the actions it cannot see.

items.name: catalog
items.doc: Every action, in declaration order.

items.name: groups
items.doc: The groups present in the catalog, in the order they first appear.

items.name: action
items.sig: pub fn action(id: impl ActionId) -> Option<Action>
items.doc: The action with this id, if the catalog has one.

items.name: chords
items.sig: pub fn chords(id: impl ActionId) -> Vec<Chord>
items.doc:
What is bound to this action now: the override if there is one, the
declared defaults otherwise.

items.name: defaults
items.sig: pub fn defaults(id: impl ActionId) -> Vec<Chord>
items.doc: What the application declared for this action.

items.name: is_default
items.sig: pub fn is_default(id: impl ActionId) -> bool
items.doc:
True when nothing overrides this action, or the override happens to match
the default. The panel shows a reset affordance on the negation of this.

items.name: set
items.sig: pub fn set(id: impl ActionId, new: Vec<Chord>)
items.doc: Rebind an action. An empty list is a deliberate unbind, not a reset.

items.name: reset
items.doc: Put one action back on its declared default.

items.name: reset_all
items.doc:
Put every action back on its declared default.

Only actions this build knows about are cleared. An override belonging to a
catalog this process does not carry is left alone, for the same reason
`register` keeps it: a tool window must not be able to wipe the game's
bindings by pressing Reset on a panel that lists none of them.

items.name: revision
items.doc:
Bumped by anything that changes the catalog or the overrides.

What a publisher compares against what it last sent. It is compared for
equality only: a viewer's copy is somebody else's counter and interpreting
it as an ordering would be reading meaning into a number minted elsewhere.

items.name: is_viewing
items.doc: Whether this process is drawing a table it did not declare.

items.name: snapshot
items.doc: The whole table, in a form that can go on a socket.

items.name: install
items.doc:
Draw somebody else's table.

Replaces whatever is here and turns on viewing, which is what stops the
mutators writing a store this process does not own. Idempotent: the owner
republishes on every change of its own revision, and installing the same
snapshot twice leaves the same table.

items.name: detach_viewer
items.doc:
The game whose table this was is gone.

Puts back whatever this process had declared for itself, which for a build
that hosts and does not link is nothing — the panel goes back to its empty
state, correctly, because there is again no application to have controls.

The outbox is dropped rather than held. An edit queued for a process that
has exited has nowhere to go, and delivering it to the NEXT game would
apply a rebind aimed at a catalog that game may not have.

items.name: drain_edits
items.doc: Rebinds made here, for whoever owns the table. Empties the queue.

items.name: apply_edit
items.doc:
Perform one, on the side that owns the table.

Routed through the ordinary mutators, so an edit that arrived over a socket
takes the same path as one made in this process: it lands in the table and
it lands in the store. There is nothing here that knows it came from
elsewhere, which is what keeps the two paths from diverging.

items.name: actions_on
items.sig: pub fn actions_on(input: Input) -> Vec<(Action, Chord)>
items.doc:
Every action bound to one physical input, with the chord that does it.

The panel colours a keycap from this: no entries is unbound, one entry
takes that action's group colour, more than one is a stack.

items.name: conflicts
items.doc:
Chords carrying more than one action that can fire at the same time.

Identical chords only. Two actions on one key with different modifiers are
resolved by specificity and are not listed here, and two in different
contexts are not a conflict at all.

items.name: is_conflicted
items.doc: True when this exact chord carries more than one action in one context.

items.name: bound_keys
items.doc:
Every key any action is bound to.

For `set_raw_key_watch`, so the focus-immune press path follows a rebind
instead of watching whatever the application hardcoded at startup.

items.name: live_mods
items.doc:
The modifiers down right now.

Command and the Windows key are one bit. An application binding `Logo+S`
gets Cmd+S on a Mac and Win+S elsewhere from one declaration, which is what
the author of that binding meant.

items.name: held
items.sig: pub fn held(id: impl ActionId, input: &WinitInputHelper) -> bool
items.doc: Is this action's input down right now?

items.name: pressed
items.sig: pub fn pressed(id: impl ActionId, input: &WinitInputHelper) -> bool
items.doc: Did this action's input go down this frame?

items.name: released
items.sig: pub fn released(id: impl ActionId, input: &WinitInputHelper) -> bool
items.doc: Did this action's input come up this frame?

items.name: is_modifier_key
items.doc:
True for a key that only ever acts as a modifier.

A binding whose whole content is Shift cannot be told from the modifier
half of every chord that uses Shift, so capture refuses one. The keys are
still in the table above because the board draws them.

items.name: key_label
items.doc:
What the panel draws on the cap. Falls back to the winit spelling, so an
exotic key still reads as something rather than as a blank cap.

items.name: key_token
items.sig: pub fn key_token(k: RawKey) -> Option<&'static str>
items.doc: The token the config file holds for a key, if this build can name it.

items.name: modifier_bit
items.doc: The modifier bit a modifier key contributes, if it is one.

items.name: mods_label
items.doc:
How a modifier set is drawn in the panel.

The platform's command modifier is drawn as it is printed on the keyboard
in front of the person, which is not the same string the file holds.

items.name: parse_chord
items.doc: Read a chord back from its token. None when any part is unknown.

items.name: Chord
items.doc: An input and the modifiers held with it.

pub input: Input,
pub mods: Mods,

items.sig: pub const fn key(k: RawKey) -> Chord
items.doc: A key with no modifiers. `const`, so action tables can be `static`.

items.name: keyed
items.sig: pub const fn keyed(k: RawKey, mods: Mods) -> Chord
items.doc: A key with modifiers.

items.name: moused

items.doc: A mouse zone with modifiers.

items.name: token
items.doc:
How the config file spells it: `Ctrl+Shift+W`.

None for an input with no token, which cannot be persisted and is
therefore dropped on save rather than written as something that will
not read back.

items.name: label
items.doc: How the panel draws it on a chip.

items.doc: One physical thing that can be pressed.

Key(RawKey),
Mouse(MouseZone),

items.name: Mods
items.doc:
The modifier keys held with an input, as a bit set.

A set and not four bools, because the panel ranks chords by how many
modifiers they name and `count()` is the whole of that comparison.
Serde is derived here, and on the three types below, because a catalog
crosses the hostlink socket: the process that declares the controls is not
always the process that draws them.

It is derived rather than routed through `token()`/`parse_chord` on
purpose. That pair is lossy by design — `token` returns None for an input
the config file cannot spell — and a lossy wire form would drop exactly
those bindings out of the panel with nothing on screen to say why. The
file may be allowed to lose them; the picture of the scheme may not.

`VirtualKeyCode` already crosses this socket inside an `InputEvent`, so
this adds a derive and not a dependency.

items.doc: True when `self` names everything `other` does and at least one more.

One parameter set to one value, and the census the row was drawn from.

Not `Copy`, because `Value` holds a String. That is why this is a queue of
its own rather than a variant of `Action`: `Request` is a small Copy struct
that a whole file's worth of code passes by value, and widening it to carry
a String would cost every click a clone to serve the one case that needs

items.name: EDIT_LIMIT
items.doc:
How many DISTINCT parameters can be mid-edit before the oldest is dropped.

Higher than the request limit and it barely matters, because coalescing
means the queue grows with the number of parameters touched and not with
the length of the drag. A person cannot have two hundred and fifty six
knobs in flight; a publisher that has stopped draining can.

items.name: set_param
items.doc:
Panel: set a parameter.

COALESCES on `(id, param)`. A slider dragged for a second is sixty calls
naming one parameter, and every one of them but the last describes a value
the person has already moved past. Queuing them makes the publisher apply
a recording of the drag, one frame per frame, and the knob keeps moving
after the mouse has stopped.

The id is enough to key on WITHOUT the generation, and it has to be: an
edit made against generation 12 and a correction made against 13 are the
same knob, and keeping both would apply the older one second.

items.name: inspect
items.doc:
Panel: this row is what the Inspector is about, and show the Inspector.

Both, because there is one caller and it means both — a click on a row in
the tree. A caller that means only the first writes `set_reveal`.

items.name: inspecting
items.doc: Panel: the row to draw, if anything has named one.

items.name: set_inspect
items.doc:
Publisher: the subject is now THIS row. `ROOT` for "it is gone".

AN ID IS NOT A HANDLE, AND THIS IS WHERE THAT BITES. A publisher whose ids
are indices into a table it rebuilds — which is the arrangement this
channel was designed around — hands out an id that names a different thing
on the next publish. A request survives that because it carries the
generation it was drawn from and is resolved once, immediately. The
Inspector's subject cannot: it is a LEVEL, read every frame, for as long as
somebody leaves the panel open.

So the publisher owes it a correction. Every publish, resolve the id the
panel is holding against the table it came from, find that same thing in
the table being sent, and say so here. The subject then follows the OBJECT
while the numbering moves under it, which is the same guarantee
`set_expanded` asks for and gets for expandable rows.

A publisher whose ids are already stable never has to call this.

It does not scroll and does not open a panel — the only thing it changes is
what the Inspector is about. `set_reveal` is the one that moves a list.

items.name: take_inspect_reveal
items.doc:
Host: a click asked for the Inspector. Consumed, so the pane opens once.

A one-shot for `take_reveal`'s reason and one more: the host answers it by
splitting the layout, and a flag that stayed set would re-split every frame.

items.name: WANT_GRACE
items.doc:
How many publishes a single assertion of interest survives.

Three, not one: the panel and the publisher run on the same thread but in
an order neither controls, so a claim made after this frame's publish must
still be alive at the next one.

items.name: want_census
items.doc:
Panel: I am drawing this. Call it on every frame the panel draws.

`false` gives up immediately, for a host that knows the panel has gone.
Not calling it at all gives up within `WANT_GRACE` publishes, which is the
path that actually carries the weight — see the static above.

A panel torn off into another window still writes this: the census is
process memory, so the panel works anywhere in this process.

items.name: census_wanted
items.doc:
Publisher: is it worth building a census at all.

One relaxed load per frame when the answer is no, which is the common case
and the one that had to be free.

items.name: set_expanded
items.sig: pub fn set_expanded(ids: impl IntoIterator<Item = EntityId>)
items.doc:
Panel: replace the open set.

THE PUBLISHER'S SIDE OF THIS IS A CONTRACT, and it is easy to break by
accident. The ids of EXPANDABLE rows must be stable from publish to
publish, or the set the panel hands back names different rows every time
and the tree opens and shuts on its own.

It is easy to break because the obvious implementation — mint an id per row
as the rows are built — makes a heading's id depend on how many rows came
before it, and therefore on which OTHER headings are open. Opening Planets
then renumbers Stations, and Stations collapses.

A publisher that reserves a fixed slot per heading, filled whether or not
that heading appears, has no such coupling. Rows that are not expandable
may be numbered however is convenient — a click carries its generation, so
those only have to be stable within one publish.

What arrives is the EFFECTIVE open set and not the clicked one. The panel's
tree is open until a person shuts it, so almost every id in here got there
without a click; a publisher told only about the clicks would send no
children for the whole of a tree the panel is drawing wide open.

items.name: is_expanded
items.doc:
Publisher: should this node's children and values be sent.

THE INSPECTED ROW IS ALWAYS OPEN, whatever the tree says. Its values are
the whole content of a panel that can be the only one on screen — the tree
may be behind another tab, in another window, or shut — and a publisher
that filled params for the tree's open set alone would leave that panel
permanently empty for the case it exists to serve.

One extra relaxed load per call, against a lock this already takes.

items.name: expanded
items.doc:
Publisher: the whole open set, for a builder that would otherwise take the
lock once per candidate node.

Carries the inspected row for the reason `is_expanded` does, so the two
cannot disagree — a publisher that switched from one to the other would
otherwise silently stop filling the panel.

items.doc: One thing the panel wants done, and the census it was asked from.

items.name: REQUEST_LIMIT
items.doc:
How many requests the queue holds before it drops the oldest.

A publisher that stops draining — a paused transport, a game mid-load —
must not let a person's clicking grow a Vec without limit. Dropping the
oldest keeps the most recent intent, which is the one they meant.

items.name: drain_requests

the same thing the list is emphasising.

items.name: set_reveal
items.doc:
Publisher: point the panel at a row. Selection made in the viewport.

It aims the Inspector too, and does NOT raise it. Those are deliberately
different: a person who clicked a planet in the game window wants the panel
they already have to be about that planet, and does not want a pane
appearing over what they are looking at. Only a click in the tree opens one.

items.name: take_reveal
items.doc:
Panel: a row to scroll to, consumed. See the banner for why it is a
one-shot: the panel owns its scroll once it has honoured this.

items.name: Census
items.doc: One snapshot of what exists.

items.name: publish
items.sig: pub fn publish(mut c: Census) -> u64
items.doc:
Publisher: install a new snapshot.

The generation field of `c` is overwritten with the next value, so a
publisher does not track it. The value it gets is returned, because the
publisher's key table has to be filed under exactly that number.

items.name: generation
items.doc: The generation of the snapshot now installed, without taking the lock.

items.name: install
items.doc:
Forwarder: install a snapshot that was published somewhere ELSE, keeping
the generation the publisher minted.

The difference from `publish` is the whole reason this exists. `publish`
overwrites the generation because the publisher and the reader share this
counter — one process, one sequence. When the publisher is a game in
another process, they do NOT: the game's key table is filed under the
game's number, and a request the panel draws from this snapshot has to name
that number for the game to resolve it. Renumbering on arrival would send
back a generation the publisher has never issued, and every click would be
refused as aged out.

So the wire is the authority and this end follows it. `GENERATION` is set
rather than incremented, which is also what keeps `census_wanted` working
on this side: the panel's claim expires against a counter that only moves
when a census actually arrives, so a game that stops publishing lets the
interest go stale exactly as a local publisher would.

Going BACKWARDS is refused. Sockets deliver in order, but a transport that
restarts gives the next game a generation of one while the panel is holding
rows from the last one's thousandth, and installing that would make every
id in flight resolve against a table from a world that is gone. A caller
that means "new world" calls `clear` first, which resets nothing here —
see the note there — so the guard is on the number and not on the caller.

Returns whether the snapshot was taken.

items.name: reset_generation
items.doc:
Forwarder: forget the generation, for a world that has ended.

`clear` empties the snapshot but deliberately leaves the counter where it
is, because a local publisher's next `publish` must not reissue a number a
request in flight was drawn from. A forwarder has the opposite problem: the
next world is a different process that starts its own sequence at one, and
`install` refuses anything below what the last one reached.

Separate from `clear` so the ordinary path cannot reach it by accident.
Calling this while a local publisher is running would let it mint a
generation twice.

items.name: with_census
items.sig: pub fn with_census<R>(f: impl FnOnce(&Census) -> R) -> Option<R>
items.doc:
Panel: read the snapshot.

A closure rather than a clone, because the panel reads it once per frame
and cloning forty thousand Strings to draw forty of them is the cost this
whole file is arranged to avoid.

items.name: clear
items.doc:
Drop the snapshot and reset the ask.

For a transport that goes back to Stopped: the world is gone, and a panel
still listing its planets would be reporting a world that no longer exists.

items.name: Value
items.doc:
One editable value, and the only vocabulary the panel knows how to draw.

Deliberately short. Every variant here has ONE obvious control — a
checkbox, a drag field, a swatch — and a type with no obvious control
would have to be drawn as something, which means guessing. A publisher
with a value that does not fit sends it as `Text` and owns the parse, or
splits it into values that do.

items.name: type_name
items.doc:
The name of the variant, for a readout that has to say what a value is
without showing it.

items.name: same_type
items.doc:
Whether two values could be the same parameter.

An edit that arrives as a different type than the row holds is a
publisher and panel that disagree about what a parameter is, and
applying it would write a float into a count. The publisher checks
this before it writes.

Serialisable because the publisher is now usually in another process and

items.name: publish
items.sig: pub fn publish(rev: u64, lines: Vec<Line>)
items.doc:
Publisher: install a snapshot, and say which revision of yours it is.

`rev` is the publisher's own counter and is never interpreted here. It is
compared for equality and nothing else, so any value that changes on every
mutation will do.

items.name: published_revision
items.doc:
The revision of the snapshot now installed, without taking the lock.

A publisher republishes when this differs from the revision it holds.

items.name: with_console
items.sig: pub fn with_console<R>(f: impl FnOnce(&[Line]) -> R) -> Option<R>
items.doc:
Panel: read the scrollback.

A closure rather than a clone, because the panel reads it once per frame
and copying the whole buffer to paint the thirty rows that fit is the cost
the revision protocol exists to avoid.

items.name: MAX_PENDING
items.doc:
How many unrun commands are kept.

Bounded because the far side may not be draining: a stopped application
runs no frames, and a person can keep pressing Return at a panel that looks
alive. The oldest goes, which matches what a queue of intentions should do
when it overflows — the newest command is the one still wanted.

items.name: submit
items.doc:
Panel: run this on the application's next frame.

Blank lines are dropped here rather than at the far end, so a publisher
does not have to guard against a Return pressed at an empty prompt.

items.name: take_submissions
items.doc:
Publisher: everything typed since the last call, oldest first.

Drains, so a command runs once. Order is kept because console commands are
not commutative — `cd learn` then `ls` is not `ls` then `cd learn`.

items.name: has_submissions
items.doc: Whether anything is waiting, without draining it.

items.name: publish_words
items.doc:
Publisher: these are the words worth completing.

Sent whole and replaced whole. A command table is fixed at build time in
most applications, so this is normally called once and never again — but
replacing rather than appending means a publisher whose vocabulary DOES
change has nothing extra to do.

items.name: words_published
items.doc: Publisher: have I sent one already.

items.name: with_words
items.sig: pub fn with_words<R>(f: impl FnOnce(&[String]) -> R) -> Option<R>
items.doc: Panel: borrow the vocabulary to complete against.

items.name: completions
items.doc:
The words that extend `prefix`, in the order the publisher gave them.

Case-sensitive, because a console's commands are. An empty prefix completes
to nothing rather than everything: Tab at an empty prompt should do nothing
visible, not paste the entire command table into the line.

items.name: common_prefix
items.doc:
The longest prefix every candidate shares.

What Tab actually inserts when several words match. Completing to the first
candidate instead would pick one of several equally good answers and be
wrong most of the time; completing to the shared stem is never wrong, and
it is what leaves the caret where a second Tab is useful.

Returns the number of elements written.
Write data to the buffer, growing with power-of-two sizing if needed.

On regrow, the old buffer is deferred-dropped (kept alive for
DEFERRED_DROP_FRAMES so the GPU finishes reading it). This
prevents DX12 heap-free stalls on in-flight command lists.

items.doc: Get a buffer slice for binding to render passes.

items.name: buffer
items.doc: Get the underlying buffer reference.

items.name: capacity
items.doc: Current capacity in elements.

items.name: fit_centered
items.doc:
The largest rect of `aspect`, centred inside `panel`.

`panel` and the result are `[x, y, w, h]`. A non-positive panel returns a
zero-size rect at the panel origin, because a caller that draws it shows
nothing rather than an inverted rect.

Rounded to whole pixels so the image lands on a pixel grid. Without it a
half-pixel origin makes the linear filter blur a still image.

items.name: GameView
new
items.sig: pub fn new( device: &wgpu::Device, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32, generation: u64, ) -> Self
items.doc:
Create the target. Registers with nobody: see `register_in`.

`format` must be the surface format, because the CRT pipeline is built
for that format and this texture replaces the surface as its target.

items.name: ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure( device: &wgpu::Device, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32, )
items.doc:
Create the game view once. Later calls with the same size do nothing,
so this is safe to call every frame.

A size change rebuilds the texture and bumps the generation, which
invalidates every window's registration. A window resize changes the
render size, so the rebuild path runs whenever the user drags a window
edge.

The old `TextureId`s are NOT freed here, and cannot be: an id belongs
to the renderer that issued it, and this call has no window in its
hand. Each window frees its own in `register_in`, which is also what
guarantees nothing samples a stale one — every window re-registers at
the top of its own frame, before it draws.
A FOREIGN image is kept whatever the size, and that case is the reason
this function has an early return that is not about cost. An adopted
surface is the panel's size and this is called with the window's, so
the size test never matches and every frame would have rebuilt over the
game — the editor throwing away the link one frame after making it, and
then showing its own empty scene in the panel as though no game had
launched at all.

items.name: texture
items.doc:
The texture itself, for the one caller that reads it back.

Held private otherwise: everything that DRAWS the game image goes
through `view` or through a registered `TextureId`, and a second way
to reach the texture is a second way to rebuild or write over one that
belongs to another process.

items.name: format
items.doc:
What the pixels in it are, which the readback needs to know whether to
swap the red and blue channels.

items.name: generation
items.doc:
Which build of the texture this is, for a reader that must notice a
rebuild.

A window registers against it; the streaming readback stamps it on
every frame it serves. A region of pixels only means something together
with the build it was cut from — a resize or an adoption replaces the
picture, so the same rectangle is then a different part of a different
image.

items.name: is_foreign
items.doc:
Whether the game image is another process's surface.

Read once per frame by the viewport, which owns the two writes that
must not happen while it is true.

items.name: release_foreign
items.doc:
Give the slot back after a launched game is gone.

Empties it rather than rebuilding, because this has no device in its
hand and `ensure` runs at the top of the next frame anyway. One frame
of "No game image" in the panel is the correct report of the state
between a game ending and the editor's own view existing again.

A no-op when the image is this process's own — Stop pressed on a
linked build must not throw away a texture the frame loop is using.

items.name: owned_elsewhere
items.doc:
Whether the Game panel belongs to another process — picture included,
and from the launch rather than from the first frame that arrives.

`is_foreign` answers "is another process's surface in the slot", which
is a strictly later question: nothing is in the slot until the game has
rendered once, and a game does that after its assets are up. The seven
seconds in between are the ones a person spends looking at a black
panel, and they are exactly the seconds `is_foreign` calls this
process's own.

The launch is read off the INPUT TAP, which is armed in `launch_project`
and disarmed by both `stop_project` and the reaper that notices a game
exited on its own. That is not a borrowed flag standing in for a fact it
does not hold: the tap says the pointer and the keyboard over this panel
belong to another process, and a panel whose input belongs elsewhere
cannot have its picture drawn here. One owner answers both or a click
lands somewhere the pixels are not.

items.name: release_local
items.doc:
Give the slot back when a launch has taken the panel away from this
process, but the game has not published anything to put in it.

The mirror of `release_foreign`, and needed for the same reason in the
other direction. The Game panel is embedded while it is merely VISIBLE,
so `ensure` has already built this process's own view during the whole
time the transport was Stopped and the boot terminal was up. Left in
the slot across a launch, that texture is what the panel goes on
sampling — no longer refreshed, because the blit is gated off, so the
panel would hold the editor's last frame frozen instead of going dark.
A stale picture is worse than no picture: it reads as a game that has
hung rather than one that has not started.

items.name: adopt
items.sig: pub fn adopt(tex: wgpu::Texture, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32)
items.doc:
Take a texture somebody else owns as the game image.

The texture is a GAME'S, imported from the IOSurface it renders into
in another process. Everything downstream of here — `register_in`, the
panel's fit, the published rect, the pointer routing — cannot tell the
difference and must not be able to, which is the whole reason this is
a `GameView` and not a second path beside one.

WHY IT IS NOT `ensure`
----------------------
`ensure` CREATES, and its no-op case is "same size, same format". Both
are wrong here. The texture arrives made, so there is nothing to
create; and a new surface at the SAME size is still a different
texture, so a size comparison would keep the old one and leave the
panel sampling a surface the game has stopped drawing into.

So the caller decides when this runs — on a `Surface` message and at
no other time — and every call rebuilds and bumps the generation,
which re-registers the id in every window on its own next frame.

items.name: register_in
items.sig: pub fn register_in( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, vp: crate::types::ViewportId, )
items.doc:
Give one window's egui a name for the game image.

THIS is what makes the Game panel a panel like any other. A
`TextureId` is an index into the renderer that issued it, so the one
id the primary window held was the reason the panel could not be drawn
anywhere else. The texture itself was never the obstacle: every window
in this process shares one `wgpu::Device`, so the same `TextureView`
registers in as many renderers as ask for it.

Call it once per window per frame, before that window's GUI closure.
It returns immediately after the first, and the ordering is what keeps
a rebuild safe: by the time a window draws, it has re-registered.

Registering is a bind group, not a copy — so the cost of a second
window showing the game is a bind group, once.

items.name: register_nearest_in
items.sig: pub fn register_nearest_in( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, vp: crate::types::ViewportId, )
items.doc:
The SAME texture, named again with a NEAREST filter.

The linear id above is right for the Game panel and wrong for a
MAGNIFIED draw. The CRT pass writes discrete phosphor cells into this
texture, and a linear sampler averages neighbouring cells the moment a
draw asks for less than one texel per output pixel — which is what a
preview box magnifying a patch of the screen does. The cells arrive as
a grey wash, and the person tuning them sees nothing to tune.

Two ids over one `TextureView` cost one bind group. Nothing is copied
and no pass is added: the picture in the box is the finished frame the
window is already showing.

EVERY GUARD HERE IS LOAD-BEARING
--------------------------------
`register_native_texture` MINTS an id and inserts it. It never replaces
one, and the renderer frees nothing it was not asked to — so calling
this per frame without the generation test orphans a bind group per
frame, each one holding the whole render target alive.

Call it once per window per frame, beside `register_in` and before that
window's GUI closure. The order is what lets the panel find its own id:
this marks the window, and the panel reads the mark.

items.name: forget_window
items.doc:
Forget a window that is closing, so its slot does not hold an id into a
renderer that no longer exists.

The ids themselves die with the renderer, so nothing is freed here.

BOTH names of the texture are forgotten. A window holds one id per
filter mode, and a slot left behind is a stale index into a renderer
that is gone — which the next window to take that `ViewportId` would
then free out of its own map.

items.name: GameViewAspect
items.doc: The shape the game is asked to render at, inside its panel.

items.name: label
items.doc: Label for a menu. Ratios read as a ratio, not as two numbers.

items.name: resolve_fixed_source
items.sig: pub fn resolve_fixed_source(self, tex_w: f32, tex_h: f32) -> GameViewAspect
items.doc:
Turn Native into the image's own aspect, for an image whose size THIS
process decides and the panel cannot ask to change.

Only the in-process path calls this. The editor's scene renders at the
editor window's size, so a Native panel of another shape has exactly
two options — letterbox the render aspect, or stretch — and this picks
the first. A hosted game must NOT be resolved this way: its size is a
message away, and resolving would pin it to the shape it already had
and make the resize path a no-op that looks like it works.

A zero-sized image has no aspect to fit, so Native passes through and
fills — which shows the placeholder whole.

items.name: choices
items.doc: The choices a menu offers. Ordered widest last, as Unity orders them.

items.name: GAME_VIEW
items.doc: The primary viewport's single game view (see module header).

items.name: barrel
items.sig: pub fn barrel(p: [f32; 2], curve_x: f32, curve_y: f32) -> [f32; 2]
items.doc:
The image warp: where on the flat framebuffer a screen point reads from.

Two axes, because a Trinitron is a cylinder. `curve_y = 0` leaves the
vertical alone while the horizontal still bows with distance from centre
on both axes, which is the shape of a cylindrical faceplate. Equal
curvatures reproduce the single-scalar barrel this replaced.

`p` is centred, in [-1, 1].

items.name: tube_parallax
items.doc:
How far the mask slides against the phosphors at this point on the tube.

The two planes are at fixed depths behind the glass, so this is closed
form: refract the eye ray at the faceplate, march it to the mask plane and
to the phosphor plane, and return the difference of the two hits. No scene
depth is involved and none could be — the depths are constants of the tube,
not of the picture.

The difference is what is returned, and that is the whole reason this is
usable as a post-process. Each absolute hit carries a magnification from
looking through thick glass, which does not vanish at zero curvature; the
magnification is common to both and cancels here.

items.name: CrtParams
items.doc:
Uniform parameters for the CRT shader.

Field ORDER is load-bearing twice over: `resolution` heads the block and
`time` follows it, because `update_time` writes byte eight directly, and
every member is `f32` after the leading `vec2<f32>` so the struct needs no
interior padding and the Shader Lab can reflect one slider per knob.

items.name: density_scale
items.sig: pub fn density_scale(output_h: u32, ref_h: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
What to multiply a COUNT by, so it means a pitch in pixels.

`scanline_count`, `phosphor_triads_x` and `phosphor_rows` say how many
of a thing fit across the whole picture. That is the question a person
asks, and it is the wrong thing to send to a surface whose size nobody
promised: a panel half the height of a window draws the same count at
half the size, so the same project looks twice as dense in the editor
as it does in the game, and a maximised window on a 4K screen looks
half as dense as either.

`mask_triad_px` never had the problem, because it is already a pitch
in destination pixels. This is what lets the other three keep step
with it.

A reference of zero means the project said nothing, and nothing is
what happens: the counts go to the GPU as written and every existing
project keeps the tube it had.

items.name: passthrough
items.sig: pub fn passthrough(width: u32, height: u32) -> Self
items.doc:
The neutral block: every effect off, so the shader is a straight blit.

It is spelled as a mutation of `Default` and not as a literal on
purpose. A literal would have to name all forty-six fields, and the
next person to add one would get a compile error whose obvious fix is
to write `0.0` — which is right for an intensity and wrong for `mask_boost`,
`glass_ior` and `eye_dist`, where zero is a divide or a black screen.
Starting from the defaults and clearing what must be cleared makes the
safe outcome the automatic one.

items.name: undistort_point
items.sig: pub fn undistort_point(&self, px: f32, py: f32) -> (f32, f32)
items.doc:
Apply the image warp to screen-pixel coordinates.

The shader's `barrel` maps *screen position → source position*, meaning
a pixel at screen position P shows content from `barrel(P)` in the
pre-distortion framebuffer. Mouse events arrive in screen space, so we
apply the same forward warp to find which flat-space content the user
actually clicked on.

The name says undistort and the body distorts. That is not a slip: the
question being answered is "what is under the cursor", and the answer
runs the same direction the shader does.

Only the image warp is applied. The parallax offset moves the MASK
against the picture and not the picture, so it cannot move what a click
lands on.

items.name: scene_texture
items.doc:
The scene target, for the one caller that reads it back.

This texture holds the post-processed scene without the GUI: the chrome
draws into the GUI layer and the two composite later. A save thumbnail
reads the scene here, so the menu the player saved from is never in it.

items.name: scene_size
items.doc: The scene target size in pixels, which the readback needs for the copy.

items.name: scene_format
items.doc:
The scene target format, which tells the readback whether to swap the
red and blue channels.

items.name: PARAMS_SIZE
items.doc:
The size the WGSL `CrtParams` struct must also have.

naga rounds a uniform struct's span up to its own alignment, which is eight
here — the `vec2<f32>` at the head is the widest member. 304 is a multiple
of eight and of sixteen, so the block stays legal even if a later edit
introduces a `vec4`. Seventy four `f32` follow the leading `vec2`.

items.name: TIME_OFFSET
items.doc:
Byte offset of `time` inside `CrtParams`.

`update_time` writes four bytes here every frame rather than the whole
block. The constant exists so the offset is named in one place and asserted
in another, because a reorder that moved `time` would otherwise silently
start writing the clock into whatever field landed at byte eight.

items.name: choose_present_mode
items.doc:
Choose the best present mode for the current surface.

Prefers Mailbox (triple-buffered, non-blocking) which eliminates
vsync stall cascading on DX12. Falls back to AutoVsync (Fifo on
most Windows drivers) if Mailbox is unsupported.

IMMEDIATE, AND WHY IT COMES FIRST WHEN IT COMES AT ALL
-----------------------------------------------------
Metal advertises `[Fifo, Immediate]` and never `Mailbox`, so on macOS
this function could only ever reach `Fifo` — a hard vsync lock, whatever
the frame cap said. `Immediate` was present on the surface the whole time
and unreachable. It is tested first, and only for an application that
declared an above-60 cap, because a game that wants 240 frames wants the
present call not to block and has accepted the tearing that buys.

items.name: apply_display
items.doc:
Copy the `pp_*` fields of the display settings into the params, with
the two switches applied.

The frame and the Android host both call this, so the two cannot
disagree about what a switch does.

`pp_bloom_enabled` false sends an intensity of exactly zero. The
composite then adds `bloom * 0`, so the bloom mips (not written this
frame, and stale) give nothing to the picture, and `bloom_pass_count`
is zero. An intensity below `BLOOM_MIN_INTENSITY` is sent as zero for
the same reason, because those passes are skipped too.

`pp_grade_enabled` false sends the identity grade. The tonemap shader
has no grade flag: at saturation 1, contrast 1, temperature 0 and
brightness 0 each grade line returns its input.

items.name: drain_load_events
items.doc:
Drain all pending events. Call once per frame during Loading phase.
Returns owned Vec; caller processes in order.

No caller in warp_core. The host application is the consumer, through the
re-export in lib.rs, so this is live code with its call site in another
crate. Do not reap it as dead.

items.name: push_load_event
items.doc:
Push one event onto the global load-event queue (loader thread → host).

A full queue drops the oldest progress event. When the queue holds nothing
but state-machine events, a progress event is refused instead, and a
state-machine event still goes on. Both losses are counted.

Progress events emitted by the background asset loader thread.
The host application drains them each frame, and warp_core does not.

items.sig: pub static LOAD_EVENTS: Lazy<Mutex<Vec<LoadEvent>>> = Lazy::new(|| Mutex::new(Vec::with_capacity(64)))

Global bounded queue of load events, oldest first.
Push from the asset loader thread; the host drains it each frame.

Not a ring buffer, whatever this comment said before. A ring drops the
