items.name: try_build
items.sig: pub fn try_build<T>(device: &wgpu::Device, label: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> Option<T>
items.doc:
Run `f` inside a Validation error scope on `device`.

Returns `Some(value)` when the scope is empty. Returns `None` when wgpu
recorded a validation error. In that case the value is dropped, and one
line goes to stderr and to the boot log.

items.name: try_build
items.sig: pub fn try_build<T>(_device: &wgpu::Device, _label: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> Option<T>
items.doc: The web build has no synchronous scope pop. Run `f` with no scope.

items.name: describe
items.doc:
The error text for a log line. For a validation error, wgpu 0.16 puts the
full chain in the Display text: "Validation Error", then "Caused by:" and
one indented line for each cause, which holds the DXC or FXC message. The
source chain repeats those causes, so this function does not walk it.

items.name: MSAA_SAMPLES
items.doc:
How many samples every scene pipeline is built for.

One. It was four, and FXAA replaced it after tonemapping. The name is kept
because eight pipeline definitions read it and "one sample" is what a
multisample state has to be told.

It no longer sizes any texture. Two multisample render targets were built
and resized from it and were bound by nothing — see the removal note in the
commit that deleted them.

items.name: Z_FORMAT
items.doc:
Render target format for HDR scene rendering. All scene pipelines
must target this format instead of the surface sRGB format.

items.name: BLOOM_MIP_COUNT
items.doc: Number of bloom blur levels. 5 gives a wide, soft bloom.

items.body:

pub bloom_intensity: f32,

items.name: BLOOM_MIN_INTENSITY
items.doc: Below this bloom intensity the bloom passes are not run.

items.name: apply_display
items.doc:
Copy the `pp_*` fields of the display settings into the params, with
the two switches applied.

The frame and the Android host both call this, so the two cannot
disagree about what a switch does.

`pp_bloom_enabled` false sends an intensity of exactly zero. The
composite then adds `bloom * 0`, so the bloom mips (not written this
frame, and stale) give nothing to the picture, and `bloom_pass_count`
is zero. An intensity below `BLOOM_MIN_INTENSITY` is sent as zero for
the same reason, because those passes are skipped too.

`pp_grade_enabled` false sends the identity grade. The tonemap shader
has no grade flag: at saturation 1, contrast 1, temperature 0 and
brightness 0 each grade line returns its input.

items.name: bloom_pass_count
items.sig: pub fn bloom_pass_count(enabled: bool, params: &PostProcessParams) -> usize
items.doc:
How many bloom render passes `execute` records: the extract, the
downsample chain and the upsample chain, or zero.

`execute` branches on this, so a test can read the pass plan with no GPU.

Assumes the HDR scene has already been rendered to `self.hdr_view`.
Writes the final LDR result to `output_view`.

When `bloom_pass_count` is zero (bloom switched off, or intensity
near zero), skips all 9 bloom passes
and runs tonemap directly. On DX12, each skipped render pass
saves ~0.3ms of resource barrier overhead.

items.name: create_coverage_bind_group_layout

The coverage sampling layout: one texture, one sampler.

The composite pipeline reads it as group 1, so `Pipelines::new` needs it at
pipeline creation. It is a free function, and not a method, because the
pipeline set is built before any viewport owns a coverage texture.

items.name: LoadEvent
items.doc:
Progress events emitted by the background asset loader thread.
The host application drains them each frame, and warp_core does not.

items.name: LOAD_EVENTS
items.sig: pub static LOAD_EVENTS: Lazy<Mutex<Vec<LoadEvent>>> = Lazy::new(|| Mutex::new(Vec::with_capacity(64)))
items.doc:
Global bounded queue of load events, oldest first.
Push from the asset loader thread; the host drains it each frame.

Not a ring buffer, whatever this comment said before. A ring drops the
oldest entry whatever it is, and two of these events must survive.

items.name: LOAD_EVENT_LIMIT
items.doc:
How many events the queue holds.

One mega-atlas pushes one `MegaAtlasProgress` per texture layer, so a host
that never drains would otherwise grow this queue for the whole boot.

items.name: push_load_event
items.doc:
Push one event onto the global load-event queue (loader thread → host).

A full queue drops the oldest progress event. When the queue holds nothing
but state-machine events, a progress event is refused instead, and a
state-machine event still goes on. Both losses are counted.

items.name: drain_load_events
items.doc:
Drain all pending events. Call once per frame during Loading phase.
Returns owned Vec; caller processes in order.

No caller in warp_core. The host application is the consumer, through the
re-export in lib.rs, so this is live code with its call site in another
crate. Do not reap it as dead.

items.name: load_events_dropped
items.doc: How many events the bound has cost, over the life of the process.

items.name: PREVIEW_SIZE
items.doc:
Side length (px) of the offscreen square. The panel hero is up to 380
logical px, which is 760 device px on a 2x display, so 768 keeps the hero
at one texel per device pixel. Well under the 2048 WebGL2
`max_texture_dimension_2d` floor.

items.doc:
Create the offscreen targets + a private view uniform and register the
colour view with egui. Call once, guarded by the PLANET_PREVIEW global.

The circle pipeline writes two MRT targets (HDR colour + Z), so the pass
must bind both — hence a throwaway `Z_FORMAT` scratch alongside the
sampled `HDR_FORMAT` colour.

items.name: render
items.sig: pub fn render( &mut self, queue: &wgpu::Queue, shared: &SharedGpu, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, base_view: &View, req: &PlanetPreviewRequest, )
items.doc:
Encode one offscreen pass drawing the requested planet + atmosphere.

lighting_wrap, time); framing is overridden to centre and fill the

items.name: GAME_VIEW
items.doc: The primary viewport's single game view (see module header).

items.name: GameView
new
items.sig: pub fn new( device: &wgpu::Device, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32, generation: u64, ) -> Self
items.doc:
Create the target. Registers with nobody: see `register_in`.

`format` must be the surface format, because the CRT pipeline is built
for that format and this texture replaces the surface as its target.

items.name: ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure( device: &wgpu::Device, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32, )
items.doc:
Create the game view once. Later calls with the same size do nothing,
so this is safe to call every frame.

A size change rebuilds the texture and bumps the generation, which
invalidates every window's registration. A window resize changes the
render size, so the rebuild path runs whenever the user drags a window
edge.

The old `TextureId`s are NOT freed here, and cannot be: an id belongs
to the renderer that issued it, and this call has no window in its
hand. Each window frees its own in `register_in`, which is also what
guarantees nothing samples a stale one — every window re-registers at
the top of its own frame, before it draws.
A FOREIGN image is kept whatever the size, and that case is the reason
this function has an early return that is not about cost. An adopted
surface is the panel's size and this is called with the window's, so
the size test never matches and every frame would have rebuilt over the
game — the editor throwing away the link one frame after making it, and
then showing its own empty scene in the panel as though no game had
launched at all.

items.name: texture
items.doc:
The texture itself, for the one caller that reads it back.

Held private otherwise: everything that DRAWS the game image goes
through `view` or through a registered `TextureId`, and a second way
to reach the texture is a second way to rebuild or write over one that
belongs to another process.

items.name: format
items.doc:
What the pixels in it are, which the readback needs to know whether to
swap the red and blue channels.

items.name: generation
items.doc:
Which build of the texture this is, for a reader that must notice a
rebuild.

A window registers against it; the streaming readback stamps it on
every frame it serves. A region of pixels only means something together
with the build it was cut from — a resize or an adoption replaces the
picture, so the same rectangle is then a different part of a different
image.

items.name: is_foreign
items.doc:
Whether the game image is another process's surface.

Read once per frame by the viewport, which owns the two writes that
must not happen while it is true.

items.name: release_foreign
items.doc:
Give the slot back after a launched game is gone.

Empties it rather than rebuilding, because this has no device in its
hand and `ensure` runs at the top of the next frame anyway. One frame
of "No game image" in the panel is the correct report of the state
between a game ending and the editor's own view existing again.

A no-op when the image is this process's own — Stop pressed on a
linked build must not throw away a texture the frame loop is using.

items.name: owned_elsewhere
items.doc:
Whether the Game panel belongs to another process — picture included,
and from the launch rather than from the first frame that arrives.

`is_foreign` answers "is another process's surface in the slot", which
is a strictly later question: nothing is in the slot until the game has
rendered once, and a game does that after its assets are up. The seven
seconds in between are the ones a person spends looking at a black
panel, and they are exactly the seconds `is_foreign` calls this
process's own.

The launch is read off the INPUT TAP, which is armed in `launch_project`
and disarmed by both `stop_project` and the reaper that notices a game
exited on its own. That is not a borrowed flag standing in for a fact it
does not hold: the tap says the pointer and the keyboard over this panel
belong to another process, and a panel whose input belongs elsewhere
cannot have its picture drawn here. One owner answers both or a click
lands somewhere the pixels are not.

items.name: release_local
items.doc:
Give the slot back when a launch has taken the panel away from this
process, but the game has not published anything to put in it.

The mirror of `release_foreign`, and needed for the same reason in the
other direction. The Game panel is embedded while it is merely VISIBLE,
so `ensure` has already built this process's own view during the whole
time the transport was Stopped and the boot terminal was up. Left in
the slot across a launch, that texture is what the panel goes on
sampling — no longer refreshed, because the blit is gated off, so the
panel would hold the editor's last frame frozen instead of going dark.
A stale picture is worse than no picture: it reads as a game that has
hung rather than one that has not started.

items.name: adopt
items.sig: pub fn adopt(tex: wgpu::Texture, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, width: u32, height: u32)
items.doc:
Take a texture somebody else owns as the game image.

The texture is a GAME'S, imported from the IOSurface it renders into
in another process. Everything downstream of here — `register_in`, the
panel's fit, the published rect, the pointer routing — cannot tell the
difference and must not be able to, which is the whole reason this is
a `GameView` and not a second path beside one.

WHY IT IS NOT `ensure`
----------------------
`ensure` CREATES, and its no-op case is "same size, same format". Both
are wrong here. The texture arrives made, so there is nothing to
create; and a new surface at the SAME size is still a different
texture, so a size comparison would keep the old one and leave the
panel sampling a surface the game has stopped drawing into.

So the caller decides when this runs — on a `Surface` message and at
no other time — and every call rebuilds and bumps the generation,
which re-registers the id in every window on its own next frame.

items.name: register_in
items.sig: pub fn register_in( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, vp: crate::types::ViewportId, )
items.doc:
Give one window's egui a name for the game image.

THIS is what makes the Game panel a panel like any other. A
`TextureId` is an index into the renderer that issued it, so the one
id the primary window held was the reason the panel could not be drawn
anywhere else. The texture itself was never the obstacle: every window
in this process shares one `wgpu::Device`, so the same `TextureView`
registers in as many renderers as ask for it.

Call it once per window per frame, before that window's GUI closure.
It returns immediately after the first, and the ordering is what keeps
a rebuild safe: by the time a window draws, it has re-registered.

Registering is a bind group, not a copy — so the cost of a second
window showing the game is a bind group, once.

items.name: register_nearest_in
items.sig: pub fn register_nearest_in( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, vp: crate::types::ViewportId, )
items.doc:
The SAME texture, named again with a NEAREST filter.

The linear id above is right for the Game panel and wrong for a
MAGNIFIED draw. The CRT pass writes discrete phosphor cells into this
texture, and a linear sampler averages neighbouring cells the moment a
draw asks for less than one texel per output pixel — which is what a
preview box magnifying a patch of the screen does. The cells arrive as
a grey wash, and the person tuning them sees nothing to tune.

Two ids over one `TextureView` cost one bind group. Nothing is copied
and no pass is added: the picture in the box is the finished frame the
window is already showing.

EVERY GUARD HERE IS LOAD-BEARING
--------------------------------
`register_native_texture` MINTS an id and inserts it. It never replaces
one, and the renderer frees nothing it was not asked to — so calling
this per frame without the generation test orphans a bind group per
frame, each one holding the whole render target alive.

Call it once per window per frame, beside `register_in` and before that
window's GUI closure. The order is what lets the panel find its own id:
this marks the window, and the panel reads the mark.

items.name: forget_window
items.doc:
Forget a window that is closing, so its slot does not hold an id into a
renderer that no longer exists.

The ids themselves die with the renderer, so nothing is freed here.

BOTH names of the texture are forgotten. A window holds one id per
filter mode, and a slot left behind is a stale index into a renderer
that is gone — which the next window to take that `ViewportId` would
then free out of its own map.

items.name: GameViewAspect
items.doc: The shape the game is asked to render at, inside its panel.

items.name: label
items.doc: Label for a menu. Ratios read as a ratio, not as two numbers.

items.name: resolve_fixed_source
items.sig: pub fn resolve_fixed_source(self, tex_w: f32, tex_h: f32) -> GameViewAspect
items.doc:
Turn Native into the image's own aspect, for an image whose size THIS
process decides and the panel cannot ask to change.

Only the in-process path calls this. The editor's scene renders at the
editor window's size, so a Native panel of another shape has exactly
two options — letterbox the render aspect, or stretch — and this picks
the first. A hosted game must NOT be resolved this way: its size is a
message away, and resolving would pin it to the shape it already had
and make the resize path a no-op that looks like it works.

A zero-sized image has no aspect to fit, so Native passes through and
fills — which shows the placeholder whole.

items.name: choices
items.doc: The choices a menu offers. Ordered widest last, as Unity orders them.

items.name: fit_centered
items.doc:
The largest rect of `aspect`, centred inside `panel`.

`panel` and the result are `[x, y, w, h]`. A non-positive panel returns a
zero-size rect at the panel origin, because a caller that draws it shows
nothing rather than an inverted rect.

Rounded to whole pixels so the image lands on a pixel grid. Without it a
half-pixel origin makes the linear filter blur a still image.

items.name: IDLE
items.doc: Nobody has asked. Not a valid tag.

items.name: MANUAL
items.doc: A person pressed Capture on a card.

items.name: AUTO
items.doc: The game changed screen and the editor is photographing it unasked.

items.name: GAME
items.doc:
The shipped game wrote a save and wants a picture of the scene.

A distinct tag, because the source is distinct. The editor tags read the
GAME_VIEW texture through `serve`; this tag reads the scene target through
`serve_source`. One tag per source keeps a frame with its asker, so a save
thumbnail and a storyboard card cannot collect each other's picture.

items.name: request
items.doc:
Ask the render loop for a frame, as `who`.

Asking twice before a frame is served asks for one picture. A second
asker while one is outstanding is REFUSED rather than queued — the answer
would be the same frame either way, and the one thing that must not happen
is two screens filing one picture between them.

items.name: pending
items.doc: Who has a request outstanding, or `IDLE`.

items.name: abandon
items.doc:
Give up an outstanding request, for an asker that has waited long enough.

Only clears a request that is still this asker's, so a caller timing out
cannot cancel a request somebody else made in the meantime. A frame
already served to this asker is dropped as well, by the same tag rule.

IT MUST DROP THE FRAME TOO. `abandon` used to clear `WANT` alone. A panel
that shut, or an asker that timed out one frame after the loop served it,
left a full picture in `READY` that only `take` on the same tag could
remove — and that caller was gone. The image stayed resident until some
later capture overwrote it: 8.3 MB at 1080p, 14.7 MB at 1440p.

items.name: take
items.doc: The frame, if the one waiting is this asker's. Leaves the slot empty.

items.name: serve
items.doc:
Serve a pending request. Once a frame, from the render loop.

Does nothing at all when nobody asked, which is almost every frame — the
cost of calling this unconditionally is one relaxed atomic load.

items.name: serve_source
items.sig: pub fn serve_source( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, texture: &wgpu::Texture, size: (u32, u32), format: wgpu::TextureFormat, )
items.doc:
Serve a pending `GAME` request against a texture the caller names.

The shipped game has no GAME_VIEW, so `serve` above finds nothing. This
serves the same handshake from a source the caller holds — the scene target
— and it acts ONLY on the `GAME` tag. An editor tag outstanding is left for
`serve`, so a build that runs both loops does not let one steal the other's
frame.

Call it once a frame from the render loop, after the source texture holds
this frame. The compare-exchange is one atomic when nobody asked, which is
almost every frame.

items.name: MAX_EDGE
items.doc: Longest edge of a region this will serve.

items.name: Region
items.doc: A rectangle of the game texture, in texture pixels.

items.name: Peeked
items.doc:
A served region: the pixels, where they came from, and which build of the
texture they came from.

items.name: request
items.sig: pub fn request(key: u64, region: Region)
items.doc:
Ask for `region`, as `key`. Call every frame while a panel wants a stream.
The last asker before `serve` runs is the one served.

A request is TAKEN by `serve` and not kept. A panel that stops calling
this stops the copies with it, so a panel that closes without calling
`abandon` still costs nothing after its last frame.

One short mutex hold, and no GPU work on this thread.

items.name: abandon
items.doc:
Stop asking, as `key`. Drops a ready frame that is this key's.

Both halves are needed. Clearing the request alone leaves the last served
frame in `READY` with nobody to `take` it, and only a `take` on the same
key can remove it. A region is at most 256 KiB, so the leak is smaller than
the one `capture::abandon` fixes, but it is the same leak.

items.name: take
items.doc:
Take the latest served frame, if it is `key`'s. Leaves the slot empty.

DESTRUCTIVE, deliberately. A non-destructive read gives the panel no way to
tell a fresh frame from the previous one it already printed, and holds the
pixels alive after the panel has finished with them.

items.name: serve
items.doc:
Run the readback stream. Once a frame, from the render loop.

Three acts, in this order: poll for finished maps, drain what finished, and
submit the next copy. The order matters — draining before polling would
always be one `serve` behind, and submitting before draining would find no
free slot on the frame a slot became free.

Costs two uncontended mutex locks and a non-blocking poll when nobody asked.

items.name: SHADER_LAB
items.doc: The primary viewport's single shader lab (see module header).

items.name: SHADER_LAB_REQUEST
items.doc: What the panel wants drawn, written once a frame it is visible.

items.name: SHADER_LAB_TEXTURE
items.doc:
What each of the lab's render targets is called in the primary viewport's
egui. One id per colour attachment, in attachment order.

items.name: SHADER_LAB_STATUS
items.doc: What the last build did, for the panel's status line.

items.name: LabSize
items.doc: The preview size, in pixels, and how many colour attachments it needs.

items.name: SHADER_LAB_WANT
items.doc:
The size the panel wants its targets allocated at.

Written every frame the panel draws a canvas and NEVER taken — see the
module header. A panel that stops drawing leaves its last size here, which
`ensure` answers in a comparison and nothing else.

items.name: want
items.doc:
What the panel last asked to have allocated, if it has ever asked.

The frame loop's one read. A `None` means no Shader panel has drawn a
runnable file yet, and nothing is allocated for one that has not.

items.name: disable
items.doc:
Release the lab and stop the frame loop from rebuilding it.

Dropping `SHADER_LAB` frees warp's wgpu handles. It does not free egui's
bind groups over the target views, so this drains `SHADER_LAB_TEXTURE` and
frees each id through the renderer. Clearing `SHADER_LAB_WANT` is what keeps
the lab gone, because the frame loop calls `ensure` on every frame that
`want()` returns `Some`.

No production caller invokes this yet. A panel-close hook must call it, and
the panel contract has no such hook today.

items.name: LabImage
items.doc:
An image the panel wants put into one of the lab's input channels.

RGBA8, tightly packed, `width * height * 4` bytes.
items.body:
pub channel: usize,
pub width: u32,
pub height: u32,
pub rgba: Vec<u8>,

items.name: SHADER_LAB_IMAGES
items.doc:
Images waiting to go to the GPU.

A QUEUE and not a slot, and drained only once a lab exists to put them in.
The panel publishes the first one on the frame it first draws, which is a
frame BEFORE `ensure` has built anything — a slot read on that frame would
take the image and drop it, and the channel would stay the empty texture it
was created as until somebody picked a file by hand.

items.name: MAX_EDGE
items.doc:
Largest preview edge, in pixels.

A shader lab is a place people write per-pixel code, and per-pixel code
gets slower with every pixel. 1024 is generous for a panel — a preview
larger than that is being scaled down by egui to fit the rect anyway on
every layout anybody actually uses — and it bounds the worst case a heavy
raymarcher can inflict on the editor's frame rate.

items.name: MAX_TARGETS
items.doc:
Most colour attachments the lab will allocate.

Two covers every shader in this repository: the scene shaders write HDR
and Z. Four is headroom that costs nothing until a shader asks for it.

items.name: LabBinding
items.doc: One resource the shader declares, and what the lab should put in it.

items.name: LabRequest
items.doc: One frame's worth of instruction from the panel.

items.name: LabStatus
items.doc: What happened on the last build.

items.name: ShaderLab
ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, width: u32, height: u32, targets: usize, )
items.doc:
Build or rebuild the targets, and register every one with egui.

Called from the primary viewport before the GUI closure runs, so the
panel has ids to draw with on the first frame it is opened.

A size or target-count change FREES THE OLD IDS FIRST. This paragraph
used to say the opposite — that egui's ids are freed by the renderer
that issued them and that re-registering replaces them — and neither
half was true. `register_native_texture` mints a NEW id and inserts it;
it never replaces, and the renderer frees nothing it was not asked to.

What the old wording cost: the orphaned bind group holds the texture
view, so wgpu keeps the whole render target alive after this struct's
handle to it drops. The panel publishes its size in raw pixels every
frame with no quantisation, so a divider dragged across it rebuilt once
per distinct width — up to four Rgba16Float targets at a 1024 clamp,
tens of megabytes a step, none of it reachable again.

The game view has always done this correctly and is the pattern copied
here.

The generation moves so the panel knows the picture it is holding is of
the previous size.

items.name: drain_images
items.sig: pub fn drain_images(&mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue)
items.doc:
Take every queued image and put it in its channel.

Called from the frame loop with the lab already locked. Nothing is
drained while there is no lab, so an image published before the first
`ensure` waits rather than being lost.

items.name: size
items.doc: The preview size the lab is currently at.

items.name: set_channel
items.sig: pub fn set_channel( &mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, channel: usize, width: u32, height: u32, rgba: &[u8], )
items.doc:
Fill one input channel with an RGBA8 image.

Recreates the texture when the dimensions change rather than growing
one, because a channel changes at most when somebody picks a different
source image — a per-gesture cost, not a per-frame one.

items.name: render
items.sig: pub fn render( &mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, req: &LabRequest, ) -> Option<LabStatus>
items.doc:
Compile if the request names a pipeline we do not have, then draw.

Returns the status of a BUILD, and `None` when nothing was rebuilt —
so the panel's status line does not flicker between "compiled" and
something else on every frame a slider is dragged.

items.name: OFFICE
items.doc: The primary viewport's single office renderer.

items.name: OfficeFrame
items.doc:
The panel's per-frame draw request: the camera+lighting uniform and the
whole scene geometry, rebuilt each frame. Simple and correct first; a
static/dynamic split is a later optimisation.

items.name: OfficeUniform
items.doc: The camera + lighting uniform, laid out for WGSL (see `office.wgsl`).

items.name: request
items.sig: pub fn request(size: (u32, u32), frame: OfficeFrame)
items.doc:
Panel side: ask for a frame. Writes one inbox entry with the wanted size and
the frame.

items.name: want
items.doc:
The size the panel last asked for, for the viewport's `ensure`. Peeks the
inbox; the size stays after the frame is taken, so `ensure` sizes the target
from it on the next frame.

items.name: set_footprint
items.doc:
Set the building footprint rectangle, as `(fx0, fx1, fz0, fz1)` in world
space. The scene builder calls this on each rebuild from `building.bounds()`.
The fragment shader reads it to gate the sun on a position test, so the call
site is the scene builder and not this renderer.

items.name: set_occupancy
items.sig: pub fn set_occupancy(w: u32, h: u32, cells: Vec<u8>)
items.doc:
Set the building occupancy mask for the next rebuild, as `(w, h, cells)` with
one byte per cell (255 = roofed, 0 = open) in row-major order from the
footprint origin `(fx0, fz0)`. The scene builder calls this beside
`set_footprint`, so the shader's interior test matches the CPU `outdoor_at`.

items.name: texture
items.doc:
The egui texture for a window, or `None` before it has registered. The
texture map lives on the instance, so this locks `OFFICE`. Do not call it
while already holding that lock: `register_in` reads `o.textures` directly.

items.name: degraded
items.doc:
Whether the last render skipped its draw because the scene geometry did not
fit the max buffer size. The panel reads it to name the failed render state
over the stale frame, instead of freezing the last picture with no reason.
See `log_oversized_office`, which sets it, and `MAX_BUFFER_SIZE`.

items.name: forget_window
items.doc:
Drop a closing window's texture slot, so a reused viewport id does not free
an id that belonged to a renderer that is gone.

items.name: take_request
items.doc:
Take this frame's frame, for the viewport's render step. Takes only the
frame; the inbox entry and its size stay, so the next `ensure` still sizes
the target.

items.name: DecalVertex
items.doc:
One decal vertex: a world position, an atlas uv, and the room light reaching
this point. `light` is the wall's baked shade (sun tint plus interior lamp
fill), the stand-in for the per-vertex `shade_frame` colour an opaque wall
carries; the decal shader then runs the same GPU shading stage the opaque
pass runs over `texel * light`, so a decal sits in identical light to a wall
of that colour. `normal` is the wall's inward face normal, which the GPU
shading needs for the hemisphere fill and the sun term. The placement code
(`office/decal.rs`) fills `light` from `scene::wall_light` and `normal` from
the wall face. Must match `office_decal.wgsl` VsIn.
items.body:
pub pos: [f32; 3],
pub uv: [f32; 2],
pub light: [f32; 3],
pub normal: [f32; 3],

items.name: InstanceRaw
items.doc:
One placement of a kit: a world translate, a yaw, a uniform scale, an outdoor
flag, and the interior-fill colour sampled at the anchor. Must match `InstIn`
locations 3-5 in office.wgsl.

items.name: InstDraw
items.doc:
One indexed instanced draw: a run of one kit's indices, its base vertex in
the shared kit vertex buffer, and the run of instances that draw it.
items.body:
pub index_start: u32,
pub index_count: u32,
pub base_vertex: i32,
pub inst_start: u32,
pub inst_count: u32,

items.name: InstancedGeom
items.doc:
The whole instanced-furniture payload for one frame: every kit's vertices and
indices concatenated into one buffer each, every instance concatenated into
one buffer, and a draw range per kit into those buffers. Empty by default, so
a frame that supplies no instances draws none and the path is a no-op.

items.name: ATLAS_DIM
items.doc:
The square side of the decal atlas, in texels. The tiles no longer sit on a
fixed grid; each names its own rect in `DecalTile::spec`, so a wide landscape
and a tall portrait can share one sheet at their own aspect ratios. The top
512 texels hold the hand-packed procedural tiles; the band below `GAL_TOP`
holds the data-driven `GALLERY` of real public-domain paintings, shelf-packed
by `gallery_rects`. 2048 keeps the row pitch (2048*4) a multiple of 256, so
the texture upload needs no per-row padding. The band grew from 1024 to 2048
to hang the portrait collection; the procedural tiles keep their texel rects.

items.name: DecalSpec
items.doc:
One tile's placement facts: its rect in the atlas (texels, `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`),
the art's aspect (width / height), and the height in world units a piece of
this kind wants on a wall. The placement code sizes the quad from `aspect` so
the art is never stretched, and from `world_h` so a clock reads small and a
mirror reads tall.
items.body:
pub px: [u32; 4],
pub aspect: f32,
pub world_h: f32,

items.name: DecalTile
items.doc: One mark in the decal atlas. `spec` returns its rect and size facts.

items.name: WALL_ART
items.sig: pub const WALL_ART: [DecalTile; 16] = [ DecalTile::Whiteboard, DecalTile::Corkboard, DecalTile::Calendar, DecalTile::Schedule, DecalTile::WhiteboardKanban, DecalTile::CorkboardDense, DecalTile::Calendar, DecalTile::Schedule, DecalTile::Whiteboard, DecalTile::Corkboard, DecalTile::Chart,
items.doc:
The office boards the walls hang, weighted toward the working surfaces a
workplace shows most: cork boards, whiteboards, calendars, and schedules. A
chart, a line chart, a poster, an event poster, a screen, and a certificate
fill the rest. `Sticky` and `Clock` are not here: a sticky note belongs on a
desk, and a clock hangs as a small companion beside a board. The arty tiles
(Art, Mountains, Portrait, Photo, Mirror, Spine, Logo) left the set, so the
room reads as a workplace and not a gallery; the gallery is a rare accent the
placement picks on its own.

items.name: spec
items.doc:
The tile's atlas rect and size facts. The rects are packed by hand into
the 2048-texel sheet `decal_atlas` paints.

items.name: uv
items.doc:
The tile's `[u0, v0, u1, v1]` in the atlas, inset half a texel so a
neighbour tile does not bleed in under linear filtering.

items.name: aspect
items.doc: The art's aspect (width / height), so the quad is not stretched.

items.name: world_h
items.doc: The height in world units a piece of this kind wants on a wall.

items.name: variant_count
items.doc:
How many content variants this board draws. A varying board (calendar,
schedule, kanban, line chart) draws `BOARD_VARIANTS` variants so two of
one kind on two walls do not read the same; every other tile draws one.

items.name: variant_rect
items.doc:
The atlas rect of variant `v` of this tile. Variant 0 keeps the tile's
hand-packed `spec` rect. A varying board's later variants shelf-pack into
the free atlas region right of the hand-packed tiles and above the gallery
band. A non-varying tile ignores `v`. The placement calls this per hung
board each frame, so the walk allocates nothing.

items.name: VARYING_BOARDS
items.sig: pub const VARYING_BOARDS: [DecalTile; 4] = [ DecalTile::Calendar, DecalTile::Schedule, DecalTile::WhiteboardKanban, DecalTile::LineChart, ]
items.doc:
The office boards whose drawn content the walls vary. Each draws in
`BOARD_VARIANTS` variants, so a wall of calendars shows different marked
days and a wall of schedules shows different meeting blocks. Every other
tile draws once and ignores the variant index.

items.name: BOARD_VARIANTS
items.doc:
How many content variants a varying board draws. Variant 0 keeps the tile's
hand-packed `spec` rect; variants 1.. shelf-pack into the free atlas region.
Four reads as varied without a large atlas cost.

items.name: variant_uv
items.sig: pub fn variant_uv(tile: DecalTile, v: u32) -> [f32; 4]
items.doc:
The `[u0,v0,u1,v1]` of variant `v` of `tile`, inset half a texel so a
neighbour does not bleed in under linear filtering. The placement code reads
this to hang a chosen variant, the way `DecalTile::uv` hangs variant 0.

items.name: GalleryArt
items.doc:
One framed painting the walls can hang, held as data, not as an enum variant.
`bytes` is a whole image file embedded at build time (the vendored CC0 works
under assets/art/gallery); `aspect` is width / height, so the piece is never
stretched; `world_h` is the height in world units a hung piece of this shape
wants. Adding a painting is one entry here plus a file, not a new tile rect.
items.body:
pub bytes: &'static [u8],
pub aspect: f32,
pub world_h: f32,

items.name: GALLERY
items.sig: pub const GALLERY: &[GalleryArt] = &[ GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g00.jpg"), aspect: 1.3333, world_h: 0.50 }, // William Keith — Landscape Painting GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g01.jpg"), aspect: 1.0601, world_h: 0.58 }, // Paul Gauguin — Two Figures GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g02.jpg"), aspect: 0.7653, world_h: 0.66 }, // Walter Shirlaw — Self-Portrait GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g03.jpg"), aspect: 0.7937, world_h: 0.66 }, // John Philip Simpson — The Captive Slave GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g04.jpg"), aspect: 0.5639, world_h: 0.66 }, // William Michael Harnett — For Sunday's Dinner GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g05.jpg"), aspect: 0.8230, world_h: 0.58 }, // De Scott Evans — The Irish Question GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g06.jpg"), aspect: 1.1928, world_h: 0.58 }, // William Michael Harnett — Just Dessert GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g07.jpg"), aspect: 1.2739, world_h: 0.50 }, // John Singer Sargent — Thistles GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g08.jpg"), aspect: 1.2097, world_h: 0.50 }, // John F. Francis — Wine, Cheese, and Fruit GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g09.jpg"), aspect: 1.2526, world_h: 0.50 }, // Claude Monet — Apples and Grapes GalleryArt { bytes: include_bytes!("../panels/sauron/office/assets/art/gallery/g10.jpg"), aspect: 1.2685, world_h: 0.50 }, // Pierre-Auguste Renoir — Seascape
items.doc:
The gallery of real public-domain paintings the walls draw from. Every work is
from the Art Institute of Chicago Open Access collection under CC0; source,
title, and artist per file are in assets/art/gallery/ATTRIBUTION.md. The
placement in `office/decal.rs` picks from this list by hash, so a wall reads
as hung with varied art. To add more, drop a file and add a row.

items.name: GAL_TOP
items.doc:
The gallery band's top edge in the atlas, in texels. The procedural tiles keep
the region above it; the paintings pack the region below.

items.name: gallery_rects
items.doc:
Shelf-pack the gallery into the atlas band below `GAL_TOP`, left to right and
wrapping to a new shelf when a piece would overrun the right margin. Returns
one `[x0,y0,x1,y1]` per `GALLERY` entry, index-aligned, so the atlas blit and
`gallery_uv` agree on where each work sits. A piece that would fall past the
band bottom gets a zero rect; the count and band are sized so none do, and a
test guards it.

items.name: gallery_len
items.doc: The number of gallery paintings the walls can hang.

items.name: gallery_uv
items.doc:
The `[u0,v0,u1,v1]` of gallery painting `i`, inset half a texel so a neighbour
does not bleed in under linear filtering. The uv spans the whole packed rect,
frame included, so the hung quad carries the frame the same way a `DecalTile`
picture does.

items.name: gallery_aspect
items.doc:
Gallery painting `i`'s aspect (width / height of the framed piece), so the
hung quad is not stretched.

items.name: gallery_world_h
items.doc: Gallery painting `i`'s wanted height on a wall, in world units.

items.name: decal_atlas
items.doc:
Build the decal atlas: a 2048x2048 `Rgba8Unorm` (linear) sheet. The top 512
texels hold the hand-packed procedural tiles; the band below `GAL_TOP` holds
the shelf-packed `GALLERY` of real paintings. Returns `(width, height,
pixels)`, four bytes per texel. The field is transparent; each tile paints its
own art in linear rgb, so a decal sits in the same light as the flat-shaded
room. Slogans and mug text arrive later via the epaint atlas.

items.name: atlas_ready
items.sig: pub fn atlas_ready() -> Option<(u32, u32, std::sync::Arc<Vec<u8>>)>
items.doc:
The atlas for the live render, when it has landed. Starts the job on first
call; `None` means the decal pass draws nothing this frame and tries again
on the next.

items.name: atlas_blocking
items.doc:
Block until the atlas lands. The headless shot and the verification test
render one frame to a file and read it back, so they need the decals in the
pixels; the live renderer never calls this.

items.name: ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure(device: &wgpu::Device, w: u32, h: u32)
items.doc:
Create or resize the office targets. Registration is a separate act
(`register_in`), one per window, because a `TextureId` belongs to the
renderer that issued it. Called by the primary viewport from `want()`.

items.name: register_in
items.sig: pub fn register_in(device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, vp: ViewportId)
items.doc:
Give one window's egui a name for the office texture. Call once per
window per frame, before that window's GUI closure. Returns at once
after the first, until a resize bumps the generation.

items.name: render
items.sig: pub fn render( &mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, req: &OfficeFrame, )
items.doc: Encode one office pass into the frame encoder.

items.name: shot
items.sig: pub fn shot(path: &str, w: u32, h: u32) -> Result<(), String>
items.doc:
Render one stand-in office frame to a PNG at `path`. Returns an error string
on a machine with no usable GPU adapter, which is not a failure of the code.

items.name: shot_zoom
items.sig: pub fn shot_zoom(path: &str, w: u32, h: u32, zoom: Option<f32>) -> Result<(), String>
items.doc:
As `shot`, but `zoom` (a world-space half-extent) frames a sub-region around
the scene centre instead of the whole scene. A small `zoom` is how the shadow
map's texel density is checked at a zoom the live camera reaches — the fit
follows the visible region, so the shadows must stay crisp when zoomed in.

items.name: MAX_EDGE
items.doc:
The largest target edge this will allocate. A panel dragged to fill a 6K
display would otherwise ask for a pair of 32-bit float buffers the size of
the screen and a path tracer that runs at one frame every few seconds.

items.name: fit
items.sig: pub fn fit(width: u32, height: u32) -> (u32, u32)
items.doc:
The biggest target of the SAME SHAPE that fits inside `MAX_EDGE`.

The ceiling has to be applied to both axes together. Clamping them
separately keeps the size legal and silently changes the aspect, and the
panel then stretches that texture over a rect of the original shape: at a
UI scale of 2 a 722 by 515 point viewport asks for 1440 by 1024, gets 1280
by 1024 — near enough square — and draws it 12 percent too wide. The whole
picture is distorted and nothing anywhere reports an error.

It scales rather than crops because the shader is handed `w / h` as its
aspect and fills whatever it is given; a cropped target would be the right
shape and the wrong field of view.

items.name: MAX_SAMPLES
items.doc:
Stop accumulating here. Past this the image has not changed in a way anyone
can see, and the frame is better spent on the rest of the editor.

items.name: SLOTS
items.doc:
How many panes may have a GPU picture at once.

ONE TARGET BECAME FOUR BECAUSE THREE MODES NOW NEED ONE
------------------------------------------------------
This was a single global holding one target for one camera, and the panel's
rule that only one pane may be Rendered came straight out of it. That rule
was two rules glued together: ACCUMULATION is genuinely single — one
converged average belongs to one camera, and two panes averaging different
views would each throw away the other's samples every frame — but TARGETS
are not.

Solid and Shaded moved onto this pipeline and neither accumulates, so a
quad layout can legitimately want four pictures at once. One slot per pane.

The accumulating rule survives unchanged and is still enforced in the
panel: at most one pane may be in `Mode::Trace`.

items.name: CORNELL
items.sig: pub static CORNELL: Mutex<[Option<Cornell>; SLOTS]> = Mutex::new([None, None, None, None])
items.doc: One tracer per pane slot.

items.name: CORNELL_WANT
items.sig: pub static CORNELL_WANT: Mutex<[Option<(u32, u32)>; SLOTS]> = Mutex::new([None; SLOTS])
items.doc:
The size each pane wants. Read, never taken — the viewport sizes the target
from LAST frame's value, which is the only one that exists at that point in
the frame. Taking it would empty the mailbox and no target would be built.

items.name: CORNELL_REQUEST
items.sig: pub static CORNELL_REQUEST: Mutex<[Option<Request>; SLOTS]> = Mutex::new([None, None, None, None])
items.doc: What to draw, per slot. Taken once per frame.

items.name: CORNELL_TEXTURE
items.sig: pub static CORNELL_TEXTURE: Mutex<[Option<egui::TextureId>; SLOTS]> = Mutex::new([None; SLOTS])
items.doc: The id each pane samples. `None` until that slot's first `ensure`.

items.name: CORNELL_SAMPLES
items.sig: pub static CORNELL_SAMPLES: Mutex<[u32; SLOTS]> = Mutex::new([0; SLOTS])
items.doc: How many samples are in each slot's average, for the panel's status line.

items.name: want
items.sig: pub fn want(slot: usize) -> Option<(u32, u32)>
items.doc: The size a slot asked for last frame.

items.name: texture
items.doc: The id a slot draws with, if there is one yet.

items.name: samples
items.doc: How many samples a slot's image is the average of.

items.name: request
items.sig: pub fn request(slot: usize, size: (u32, u32), req: Request)
items.doc: Ask a slot for a picture. A slot past the end is ignored rather than fatal.

items.name: disable
items.sig: pub fn disable(gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, slot: usize)
items.doc:
Release a slot's target and stop the frame loop from rebuilding it.

Dropping the slot's `Cornell` frees warp's wgpu handles. It does not free
egui's bind group over the display view, so this takes the renderer and
calls `free_texture`. Clearing `CORNELL_WANT` is what keeps the slot gone,
because the primary viewport calls `ensure` for every slot whose `want()`
is `Some`. A slot past the end is ignored rather than fatal.

No production caller invokes this yet. A preset that hides a pane must call
it, and the panel does not today.

items.name: mark_hidden
items.doc:
Mark a slot for release, because a preset stopped showing it.

The panel calls this; the primary viewport drains it and calls `disable`. A
slot already marked is dropped, so a slot marked on every frame until the
drain runs enqueues once. A slot past the end is ignored.

items.name: drain_hidden
items.doc: Take the slots marked for release since the last drain.

items.name: Mode
items.doc:
What the panel asks to be drawn.

Semantic rather than packed: the panel sends the scene as the tracer's own
types and this module does the vec4 packing. The alternative — the panel
building the uniform bytes — would put the shader's memory layout in the
UI, where a field reordered in the WGSL becomes a silent misread.
What a pane is asking the GPU to draw.

SOLID AND SHADED RUN ON THE TRACER'S PIPELINE AND ARE NOT TRACES
---------------------------------------------------------------
They go through the same shader, the same uniform block and the same pass
as `Trace`, and they take one ray with no bounces and no lighting. What
that buys is that the geometry — the march, the fields, the transforms — is
written once and cannot come to disagree between a preview and a render.

They were on the CPU until now, one ray per pixel in bands across several
frames, which is a raytracer without a GPU and is why they crawled. On the
pipeline that already renders this scene they are one fullscreen pass.

items.name: accumulates
items.doc:
Whether this mode averages frames together. Only one does, and it is
the only one whose picture is thrown away when the scene changes.

items.name: Request
ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure( device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, slot: usize, width: u32, height: u32, )
items.doc:
Build or rebuild the targets, and register the display view with egui.

Called from the primary viewport before the GUI closure runs, so the
panel has an id to draw with on the first frame it is opened. A size
change rebuilds and RESTARTS the average, because the samples already
taken were of a different set of pixels.

items.name: headless
items.sig: pub fn headless(device: &wgpu::Device, w: u32, h: u32) -> Cornell
items.doc:
The same tracer, with no egui renderer and no global slot.

`ensure` needs a `egui_wgpu::Renderer` because it registers the display
view as a texture id, and it parks the result in a process-wide array.
A test wants neither: it wants one tracer it owns, that it can render
into and read back. Everything below `ensure` already worked that way,
so this is the private constructor and no second code path.

items.name: readback_bytes
items.doc:
How many bytes `encode_accum_readback` writes.

Sixteen per texel, because the accumulator is `Rgba32Float`. A copy to
a buffer must have a row pitch that is a multiple of 256, so a width
that is not a multiple of 16 would need per-row padding. The caller is
told to pick a good width instead, because the only caller is a test
and a test can pick its own size.

items.name: encode_accum_readback
items.sig: pub fn encode_accum_readback(&self, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, dst: &wgpu::Buffer)
items.doc:
Copy the half of the average that is CURRENT into `dst`.

Linear radiance, before the display pass tonemaps it. That is the side
of the tonemap a comparison wants: `aces` is a lossy curve and two
images that differ by a little in the dark end can agree exactly after
it.

Panics on a width that is not a multiple of 16 — see `readback_bytes`.

items.name: render
items.sig: pub fn render( &mut self, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, slot: usize, req: &Request, )
items.doc:
Add this frame's samples to the average, then tonemap it.

Encoded into the frame's command encoder after the egui mesh is built
and before the GUI pass samples the display texture, so the picture is
this frame's and not last frame's.

items.name: SPLAT
items.doc: The one renderer. Built by `ensure` in the primary viewport.

items.name: SPLAT_WANT
items.sig: pub static SPLAT_WANT: Mutex<Option<(u32, u32)>> = Mutex::new(None)
items.doc:
The size the panel wants. Read, never taken — the viewport sizes the target
from LAST frame's value, which is the only one that exists at that point in
the frame. Taking it would empty the mailbox and no target would be built.

items.name: SPLAT_REQUEST
items.doc:
What to draw this frame. Taken once per frame, so a frame on which the
panel is closed draws nothing and costs nothing.

items.name: SPLAT_TEXTURE
items.doc: The id the panel samples. `None` until the first `ensure`.

items.name: SPLAT_STATUS
items.sig: pub static SPLAT_STATUS: Mutex<Status> = Mutex::new(Status { count: 0, asked: 0, degree: 0, asked_degree: 0, bytes: 0, })
items.doc: What is on the GPU now.

items.name: want
items.doc: The size the panel asked for last frame.

items.name: texture
items.doc: The id the panel draws with, if there is one yet.

items.name: status
items.doc: What reached the GPU.

items.name: request
items.sig: pub fn request(size: (u32, u32), req: Request)
items.doc: Ask for a picture at this size.

items.name: upload
items.doc:
Queue a cloud's static half for upload.

The packing runs HERE, on the calling thread, and not in `render`. A six
million splat cloud is about 400 MB to pack, and doing it inside the frame
would stop the editor for the length of it. The loader thread calls this;
the next frame writes the result into buffers.

items.name: unload
items.doc: Drop the static half. The next frame draws an empty target.

items.name: disable
items.doc:
Release the splat target and stop the frame loop from rebuilding it.

Dropping `SPLAT` frees warp's wgpu handles. It does not free egui's bind
group over the target, so this takes the renderer and calls `free_texture`.
Clearing `SPLAT_WANT` is what keeps the target gone, because the primary
viewport calls `ensure` on every frame that `want()` returns `Some`.

No production caller invokes this yet. A panel-close hook must call it, and
the panel contract has no such hook today.

items.name: view_from_basis
items.sig: pub fn view_from_basis( eye: [f32; 3], right: [f32; 3], up: [f32; 3], forward: [f32; 3], ) -> [[f32; 4]; 4]
items.doc:
The view matrix the shader expects, column-major.

Camera space is x RIGHT, y UP and z FORWARD, so a splat in front of the eye
has a positive z. The EWA Jacobian divides by that z twice and the quad is
placed from the same value, so a convention with z pointing backwards puts
every splat on the wrong side of the screen while the ellipses stay the
right shape — a picture that looks plausible and is mirrored.

The three axes must be orthonormal. This builds the inverse of a rigid
transform by transposing the rotation, which is only the inverse when they
are.

items.name: focal
items.sig: pub fn focal(height: u32, fov_y: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
The focal length in pixels for a vertical field of view.

Pixels are square, so the horizontal focal length is the same number and
the aspect enters only through the width of the target.

items.name: MAX_BINDING
items.doc:
The largest one storage binding may be, in bytes.

`wgpu::Limits::default()` sets `max_storage_buffer_binding_size` to this,
and `gpu/device.rs` never asks for less (fn raised_limits). The split uses
this floor, so it holds on every device. It is the single number the buffer
split below answers to.

items.name: MAX_SPLATS
items.doc:
How many splats the geometry buffers can hold.

Position, scale, rotation and colour are 16 bytes each, so each of the four
reaches the binding cap at the same count. A cloud above this is clamped by
`upload` and the loss is reported in `Status`.

items.name: band_floats
items.sig: pub const fn band_floats(band: u8) -> usize
items.doc:
How many floats of harmonic one band costs per splat.

Band `b` has `2b + 1` coefficients and each carries three channels. Band 0
is not here: it is one coefficient per splat and lives in the `dc` buffer.

items.name: oct_encode
items.doc:
A unit vector as two numbers in -1..1, octahedrally.

The sphere is projected onto an octahedron, which is unfolded into a
square. It is a well behaved mapping — no pole, and an error under a
thousandth of a degree at this precision — and the reason it is used here
is that it FITS: the scale and colour buffers each carry a padding float
that vec4 alignment demands and nothing reads.

A normal buffer of its own would be a ninth binding against a limit of
eight, and another sixteen bytes a splat against a cap this layout is
already shaped around. Two floats that were being written as zero anyway
cost nothing at all.

items.name: oct_decode
items.doc: The inverse, for the tests. The shader has its own copy.

items.name: sh_degree_fit
items.doc:
The highest harmonic degree a cloud of `count` splats can carry.

Each band is its own binding, so the test is on the LARGEST band and not on
their sum. Band 3 is 84 bytes per splat, band 2 is 60 and band 1 is 36, so
a degree that fits implies every lower one fits.

The answer is the memory lever the panel reports. A cloud whose band 3 does
not fit renders at degree 2 with no error anywhere, and a person comparing
it against another viewer needs to be told which one they are looking at.

items.name: MAX_EDGE
items.doc:
The largest target edge this will allocate.

A panel dragged across a 6K display would otherwise ask for a target that
costs more to rasterize than the sort costs to compute, and the splat draw
is fill bound: every splat covers many pixels and every pixel is blended.

items.name: MAX_QUAD_PIXELS
items.doc:
The largest quad half axis, in pixels.

A splat close to the eye projects to an ellipse larger than the screen, and
a handful of them make the whole frame one blend chain. The cap trades the
exactness of a very near splat for a frame that finishes.

items.name: OVERDRAW_STEP
items.doc:
What one splat adds to a pixel in `Mode::Overdraw`.

Fifty splats saturate the channel, which is the density at which a cloud
starts to cost real time.

items.name: fit
items.sig: pub fn fit(width: u32, height: u32) -> (u32, u32)
items.doc:
The biggest target of the SAME SHAPE that fits inside `MAX_EDGE`.

Both axes are clamped together. Clamping them apart keeps the size legal
and silently changes the aspect, and the panel then stretches that texture
over a rect of the original shape.

items.name: Light
items.doc:
A single directional light, and what it does to the cloud.

WHY A CLOUD IS NOT LIT BY DEFAULT

A captured splat already carries the light that fell on it when the
photographs were taken. Lighting it again puts a second light on a surface
that has one baked in, which is not what the capture looked like and is
not physically anything.

It earns its place as an INSPECTION tool. A scan's colour is often flat
and evenly exposed, and shape that the eye cannot find in it appears at
once under a raking light. So this is off unless somebody turns it on, and
the panel says what it is for.

items.name: direction
items.doc:
The unit vector pointing TOWARD the light, in world space.

Built in a frame whose vertical is `up`, so the angles mean the same
thing whichever axis the capture calls up.

items.name: light_terms
items.doc:
The two uniform vectors a light resolves to.

A free function and not a step of `uniforms_for`, because that one is a
method on a `Splat`, a `Splat` needs a device, and the test harness has no
device. The arithmetic that decides whether a cloud is lit at all should
not be the part that cannot be checked.

items.name: Upload
items.doc:
A cloud in the exact shape the storage buffers take.

Built on the loader thread and handed across. Each field is one binding, so
`render` writes it with no further work.

items.name: of
items.doc:
Pack a cloud.

The scale and the opacity are copied as they stand. `splat/mod.rs`
applied the exponential and the sigmoid once at load, and applying
either again here would shrink every splat.

items.name: ensure
items.sig: pub fn ensure(device: &wgpu::Device, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer, width: u32, height: u32)
items.doc:
Build or rebuild the target, and register it with egui.

Called from the primary viewport before the GUI closure runs, so the
panel has an id to draw with on the first frame it is opened. The
static buffers survive a resize: they are not a function of the target.

items.name: loaded
items.doc: How many splats and which degree are on the GPU.

items.name: render
items.sig: pub fn render( &mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, req: &Request, )
items.doc:
Draw one frame into the target.

Encoded into the frame's command encoder after the egui mesh is built
and before the GUI pass samples the target, so the picture is this
frame's and not last frame's.

items.name: Mode
items.doc:
Which picture to draw.

The numbers are the ones `shaders/splat.wgsl` branches on. A test below
reads that file and asserts they agree, because a mismatch is silent: the
panel says one mode and the shader draws another.

items.name: Request
items.doc:
One frame's description.

Semantic rather than packed. The panel sends a camera and an order, and
this module does the uniform packing — the alternative puts the shader's
memory layout in the UI, where a field reordered in the WGSL becomes a
silent misread.

items.name: Status
items.doc:
What actually reached the GPU.

The panel reports this rather than what the cloud holds, because the two
differ exactly when a person needs to be told: a cloud too large for a
binding loses a harmonic band and looks slightly flat.

items.name: Mode
items.doc:
One debug channel.

`id` is the value written into `View::debug_mode` and matched by the
`DBG_*` constants in view.wgsl. The position in `MODES` is also the file
index a dump writes, so the two must stay in step — `modes_are_in_order`
asserts it.

items.name: MODES
items.sig: pub const MODES: [Mode; 19] = [ Mode { id: 0, label: "OFF", name: "Shaded", accent: [0.85, 0.85, 0.88], tip: "The shipped frame. Bloom, tonemap, DoF, FXAA and CRT all run; every other channel skips them." }, Mode { id: 1, label: "KIND", name: "Primitive kind", accent: [0.95, 0.95, 0.98], tip: "What each fragment IS: rect, triangle, circle, planet, star, atmosphere, glow, corona, sprite, dust, explosion, wormhole. The legend every other channel is read against." }, Mode { id: 14, label: "TEX", name: "Texture layer", accent: [0.75, 0.85, 0.95], tip: "Array layer this fragment sampled, hashed to a stable color. Two objects that should share an atlas page and do not show as two colors." }, Mode { id: 18, label: "WIRE", name: "Primitive border", accent: [0.30, 0.95, 1.00], tip: "The edge of each primitive in its own local space, over a dark fill. The only channel that keeps the sprite quad the alpha test throws away — so it shows the geometry a sprite actually costs." }, Mode { id: 2, label: "ALB", name: "Albedo", accent: [0.85, 0.72, 0.30], tip: "Base color before tint and before light. A sprite that looks wrong here has a texture problem, not a lighting one." }, Mode { id: 3, label: "TINT", name: "Instance tint", accent: [0.90, 0.60, 0.35],

items.name: SECTIONS
items.doc:
The chips grouped into columns, the way the game panel draws them. Values
index `MODES`, not `Mode::id` — the two differ because the grid is ordered
for reading and the ids are ordered for the shader's switch.

items.name: KINDS
items.doc:
The KIND legend, in the order `dbg_kind_color` switches on. Kept beside the
table it explains rather than in the UI module, because the colors are the
shader's and a copy in egui would drift from them.

items.name: index_of
items.doc: Index into `MODES` for a `Mode::id`, or 0.

items.name: DumpReport
items.doc: What one completed dump produced.
items.body:
pub dir: PathBuf,
/// The one image that is worth sending someone.
pub sheet: PathBuf,
pub buffers: usize,
pub size: (u32, u32),

items.name: active
items.doc:
True when a channel other than the shipped frame is selected, which is the
condition the whole post chain is skipped under.

items.name: request_dump
items.doc:
Ask the next rendered frame to write the full set. Ignored while the game
is not being drawn, because there would be no scene to re-shade.

items.name: set_dump_root
items.doc:
Point dumps at a project. Called with the project's directory; the buffers
land in `debug_buffers/` under it, next to the thing they are about.

items.name: dump_dir
items.doc:
The directory one dump writes, wiped and recreated per dump so exactly one
set ever lives there and two dumps are never mixed.

items.name: DebugBlit
items.doc:
Copies one texture to another with no grading.

One pipeline, because the two things it writes — the LDR image the game
view samples, and the readback texture a dump copies from — are both
created at the surface format. Keeping the dump at the surface format is
also what lets OFF go through the real tonemap pipeline, which is built for
that format and no other.
items.body: pub pipeline: wgpu::RenderPipeline,

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(device: &wgpu::Device, ldr_format: wgpu::TextureFormat) -> Self

items.name: bind
items.sig: pub fn bind(&self, device: &wgpu::Device, src: &wgpu::TextureView) -> wgpu::BindGroup
items.doc:
A bind group over one source view. Cheap enough to build per pass; the
alternative is caching against a TextureView with no identity to key on.

items.name: Frame
items.doc: One rendered channel, already de-padded to tight RGBA8 rows.
items.body:
pub label: &'static str,
pub name: &'static str,
pub pixels: Vec<u8>,

items.name: write_dump
items.sig: pub fn write_dump( dir: &std::path::Path, w: u32, h: u32, frames: &[Frame], ) -> Result<DumpReport, String>
items.doc:
Write every frame as its own PNG, plus one contact sheet.

The sheet is the deliverable. Twenty separate files are what you open when
you already know which channel you want; one labelled grid is what you send
to somebody who does not, and it is the only form in which "the star's
emission is fine but its alpha is not" is a single glance.

The directory is wiped first, so two dumps never interleave and a channel
that failed to render this time cannot leave last time's picture behind
pretending to be current.

items.name: reveal
items.doc:
Reveal a dumped file in the platform's file manager, so "share this" is one
click and not a path to retype. A no-op where there is nothing to ask.

items.name: accumulates
items.doc:
Whether this mode averages frames together. Only one does, and it is
the only one whose picture is thrown away when the scene changes.

items.name: SURFACE
items.doc: The window surface, under the scale blit.

items.name: LDR
items.doc: The LDR image the post chain writes and the blit samples.

items.name: HDR
items.doc: The HDR scene, before the post chain.

items.name: on
items.doc: Whether the probe colours replace the black clears.

items.name: clear
items.doc: `probe` while the probe is on, and black at every other time.

items.name: CAPTURE_FORMAT
items.doc:
The offscreen capture format. `Rgba8Unorm` reads back without a channel
swap on every backend, so the same scene gives the same bytes everywhere.

items.name: headless
items.doc:
A device and queue with no surface, or None where no adapter answers.

The visual tests run on developer machines and on headless CI. A machine
with no GPU still runs the rest of the suite, so the caller skips rather
than fails when this returns None. A software adapter is asked for second,
because headless CI on Windows (WARP) and Linux (llvmpipe) can still serve
one when the hardware path is empty.

items.name: offscreen
items.sig: pub fn offscreen( device: &wgpu::Device, width: u32, height: u32, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, ) -> wgpu::Texture
items.doc:
A colour target the CPU can read back.

The target carries `COPY_SRC` so a later copy to a buffer is legal, and
`RENDER_ATTACHMENT` so a pass can draw into it.

items.name: read_rgba
items.sig: pub fn read_rgba( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, texture: &wgpu::Texture, width: u32, height: u32, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, ) -> Option<Vec<u8>>
items.doc:
Copy a target back to the CPU as tight RGBA bytes, or None on a zero extent.

THE ROW PADDING IS NOT OPTIONAL. `copy_texture_to_buffer` aligns each
destination row to 256 bytes, so the read skips the tail of every row.
Reading the block flat is the bug that shears the picture a few pixels per
row. The channel order is normalised to RGBA here, so a BGRA target and an
RGBA target of one image return the same bytes.

items.name: hash_rgba
items.doc:
Reduce RGBA bytes to one stable number. The hasher is the standard library's
default, which `image/cache.rs` already relies on for a fixed-key,
run-stable digest.

items.name: hash_texture
items.sig: pub fn hash_texture( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, texture: &wgpu::Texture, width: u32, height: u32, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, ) -> Option<u64>
items.doc: Read a target back and reduce it to one number in one call.

items.name: SOCKET_FLAG
items.doc:
The argv flag the editor passes the game so it knows to attach.

Named here rather than in either binary, because the writer and the reader
of a command line that do not share a constant drift apart in exactly one
direction: silently, into a game that launches standalone and looks fine.

items.name: crash_file_path
items.doc:
Where a game writes its crash report and the editor reads it.

Named by pid, so the editor — which spawned the child and holds its pid —
finds exactly the report it is looking for and not a sibling game's. It
shares `link_dir` with the sockets, which is already the directory both
processes agree on.

items.name: read_crash_report
items.doc:
Read the crash report a game wrote for `pid`, if it wrote one.

Here rather than in the editor because the parse is serde, and serde_json is
a warp_core dependency the editor does not name. The editor reads the report
through this so it needs no crate for one call.

items.name: Guest
items.doc: The game's side of the link.

items.name: connect
items.doc:
Attach to an editor. None when there is no editor to attach to, which
is the shipped game launched by hand and is not an error.

items.name: editor_alive
items.doc:
False once the editor's socket has closed. A hosted game exits when its
host does; nothing else would ever close its window.

items.name: socket_from_args
items.doc:
Read the socket address off a command line, if this process was
launched by an editor. The game calls this instead of parsing argv
itself.

It reads text and does not touch the filesystem, which is what lets one
function serve a unix path and a windows `host:port/token` alike.

items.name: apply_transport
items.doc:
Write a received transport message into the engine's own statics.

This is the whole of what replaces the shared address space. In-process
the editor wrote `EDITOR_PLAY_STATE` and the game's sim loop read it;
out of process the editor sends and THIS writes the same static, in the
game's own copy of the engine. Every reader downstream is unchanged,
which is why the sim loop and the render loop did not have to learn
that they are now in a different process.

items.name: Host
items.doc:
One game, one socket.

Unlike `handoff::Server` this accepts a SINGLE connection and drops the
listener afterwards. A second connection on a game socket is not a second
game — it is something that should not have found the path, and accepting
it would give it the transport.

items.name: start
items.doc:
Start listening. None when no socket can be made, which leaves the
editor working with no game rather than failing to open.

items.name: socket
items.doc:
Where the game should connect. Goes on its command line after
`SOCKET_FLAG`.

items.name: is_connected
items.doc:
Whether a game has attached. False both before the first connection and
after the process goes away, which are the same thing to every caller.

items.name: drain
items.doc:
Everything that arrived since the last call.

Draining is also what releases a reader thread that is waiting for
room, so the editor must keep calling this once a frame even on the
frames it ignores the result.

items.name: queued
items.doc:
Messages the game has sent that no frame has taken yet.

A number sitting at `INBOX_QUEUE` is a queue nobody is draining,
which is the shape the leak had before the bound went in.

items.name: send
items.doc:
Tell the game something. A game that has gone is not an error: Stop
races the process exiting, and both orders are normal.

items.name: Browse
items.doc:
A move through a page's own history, as a toolbar button means it.

Its own enum rather than three arms on `ToGame`, because the three are one
control group in every browser chrome ever drawn and a caller that had to
remember which of three arms to send would eventually send the wrong one.
items.body:
Back,
Forward,
Reload,

items.name: MemoryPressureLevel
items.doc:
How close the machine is to running out of memory, as the editor sees it.

A GAME MAY USE ALL THE MEMORY THERE IS. THIS IS NOT A QUOTA.
The editor is the parent, so it is the one process placed to watch the whole
machine rather than its own heap alone. It does not budget the game a
number. It watches how much memory the MACHINE has left and sends this only
when the reserve the editor and the OS need is at risk. So these levels are
a courtesy, not a limit: the guarantee that a game cannot take the editor
down rests on the editor being able to stop it, not on the game obeying.

items.name: CrashKind
items.doc:
Why a game process ended, when it ended badly.

Four kinds from three producers. `Panic` and `Signal` are the game's own,
carried by `ToEditor::Crash`. `OutOfMemory` is the editor's, set when the
editor is the one doing the killing. `Exit` is the editor's fallback for a
non-zero status that arrived with no report to explain it.

items.name: CrashReport
items.doc:
What a game says on its way out, or what the editor reconstructs when the
game could not say anything.

ONE TYPE, TWO PRODUCERS, so the crash surface has one renderer and not two
that drift. The game's panic hook fills a rich one — message, location, a
backtrace. The editor fills a coarse one from an exit status when no report
arrived. A panel that had a private path for each would draw the common case
and be wrong on the rare one, which is the case that matters most.

items.name: ToGame
items.doc: Editor to game.

items.name: ToEditor
items.doc: Game to editor.

items.name: reap
items.doc:
End a launched game: the process, the shell that started it, and whatever
that shell left running.

THE GROUP AND NOT THE PROCESS, and that is the whole reason this exists.
A manifest target with a `command` key runs a SHELL, and the shell runs the
game — `./run.sh` builds and then launches, and one of its modes pipes the
game into `tee` instead of `exec`ing it. `Child::kill` signals one pid, so
Stop killed the script and left the game rendering into a surface nobody
read and printing its frame loop into the editor's terminal. The terminal
panel learned this first and states it in the same words.

The caller sends `Shutdown` before this. The first loop is the chance that
message asks for, and it is the only place a game with unsaved state gets
one; a game that ignores it costs the Stop frame `GRACE_TRIES` steps and no
more. Then the group is asked, then the group is told.

`launch_project` puts the child in a group of its OWN. Without that step
every signal here would name the editor's group and the editor would be in
it, so this function would stop warp.

items.name: contain
items.doc:
Put a child the editor has just started in a job object, so `reap` can end
the whole tree it grows.

WHY THE SPAWN SITE MUST CALL THIS AND `reap` CANNOT DO IT ALONE
--------------------------------------------------------------
A process joins a job and every process it starts AFTERWARDS joins with it.
Processes it started BEFORE do not. So a job made at Stop time holds the
handle and nothing else, and a `command` target — a shell that launched the
game and waits on it — loses exactly the grandchild the unix `killpg` was
written to reach. Call this on the frame the child is spawned.

It still races the child's own first spawn, and std offers no way to close
that: `CREATE_SUSPENDED` needs the thread handle back from `CreateProcess`,
which `std::process::Child` does not give out. The race is microseconds
against a shell that has not been loaded yet, so in practice the job is set
before the shell runs a line.

False means no job was made. The caller carries on: `reap` then falls back
to the handle alone, which is what `Child::kill` always did.

items.name: Shared
items.doc:
A frame buffer both processes hold.

Not Clone. Two owners would mean two `CFRelease` calls for one retain,
and the second is a use-after-free of a buffer the other process is
still rendering into.

items.name: create
items.sig: pub fn create(width: u32, height: u32) -> Option<Self>
items.doc: Allocate. The guest process calls this, because the guest renders.

items.name: adopt
items.doc:
Take ownership of a share in a surface somebody else allocated.

For a producer that hands out an `IOSurfaceRef` of its own — an
off-screen browser's paint callback, a capture session, anything
that renders where warp does not. The caller keeps its reference;
this takes one of its own.

None when the surface is null, has no extent, or is not BGRA. The
format check is the load-bearing one — see the module header for
what a silent mismatch costs.

items.name: lookup
items.doc: Attach to a surface another process made and published.

items.name: publish
items.doc:
Make this surface reachable, and return the name to send over the
JSON channel. None when the namespace refused the registration, in
which case the host simply never gets a picture — it does not fail.

items.name: stride
items.doc:
Bytes per row. Deliberately exposed rather than computed from the
width: the OS pads rows for alignment, so `width * 4` is wrong for
most widths and the error is a sheared image.

items.name: as_raw
items.doc:
For the texture import, which lives next to the device it imports
into rather than here.

items.name: create
items.sig: pub fn create(_width: u32, _height: u32) -> Option<Self>

items.name: SharedRings
items.doc:
A block of scope rings both processes have mapped.

Not Clone: the mapping is unmapped on drop, and a second owner would
unmap a region the audio callback in the other process is still
writing into.

items.name: create
items.doc:
Allocate a segment, stamp it as a block, and keep it mapped.

The game calls this, because the game is where the audio callback
runs. An editor that allocated would be publishing rings before
knowing whether a process exists to fill them.

items.name: attach
items.doc:
Map a segment another process created and published.

A miss is reported and dropped rather than retried. The name comes
off the channel and is valid for the life of the game that sent it,
so a failure here is a real one — a build mismatch or a game that
died between sending and this call — and retrying a dead name is a
spin, not a recovery.

items.name: name
items.doc: The name to send over the JSON channel.

items.name: as_ptr
items.doc: For `scope::adopt`, which is the only thing that should hold it.

items.name: poll
items.doc: Drain the channel and act on it. Once a frame.

items.name: memory_pressure
items.doc:
The memory-pressure level the editor last sent, or None when it has sent
none. Read by `memcap` once a frame.

None both in a game with no editor and in a hosted game the editor has not
warned — the same answer, because both are "nobody is asking for memory
back", which is the case where a game keeps everything it has.

items.name: attach
items.doc:
Connect, if this process was launched by an editor.

Returns whether it did. Call once, before any window or GPU work, so the
first frame already knows what it is rendering into.

items.name: hosted
items.doc: Whether this process has an editor. False is the shipped game.

items.name: report_crash
items.doc:
Send a crash report to the editor, if one is attached and reachable.

`try_lock`, NOT `lock`. This is called from the panic hook, which may be
running on the very thread that holds the session lock — a game that
panicked inside a pump, say. A blocking lock there would replace a legible
crash with a deadlock, so a contended session simply falls back to the
crash file the hook also writes.

items.name: detach
items.doc:
Drop the connection and every surface with it. For tests, and for a clean
exit path that wants the socket closed before the window goes.

items.name: report_screen
items.doc:
Say which screen the game is on, in the game's own words.

Called from the game's frame loop with whatever it calls the phase it is
in — `title_screen`, `briefing`, `playing`. Cheap enough to call every
frame: a game with no editor returns on the first line, and one with an
editor compares two strings.

The name is the game's to choose and the storyboard's to match. A card
whose `state_id` is this string is the card that gets the picture, and a
name nothing on the board claims simply files a PNG nobody draws — which
is the correct outcome for a screen the storyboard has not been told
about yet.

items.name: pump_screen
items.doc:
Send the screen if it moved. Once a frame, beside the other pumps.

Split from `report_screen` so the game can report from wherever the phase
is decided — which is not necessarily a place holding a socket — and the
send still happens once, on the frame loop's own terms.

items.name: pump_census
items.doc:
Forward the census the world just published, when it published one. Once a
frame, after the application has rendered.

AFTER, because the publisher builds its rows from a cache that is rebuilt
during the frame, and a pump that ran first would forward last frame's
world — every position one frame stale, which on a moving body is a row
that never quite matches the picture beside it.

WHAT ARMS THE PUBLISHER IS THE FIRST LINE, NOT THE LAST
-------------------------------------------------------
`census_wanted` is the publisher's own brake and it is checked before a
single row is built. In one process the panel set it directly. Here the
panel's ask arrives as a message, is parked in `CENSUS_WANT`, and is
