re-asserted from this function on every frame — which is what makes the
claim expire the way the channel says it does. Applying it once on receipt
would leave a game publishing forever for an editor that had closed the
panel, or died with it open.

THE GATE IS THE PUBLISHER'S GENERATION, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS NOT PER-FRAME
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
The header next door refuses per-frame messages, and a census is the
largest thing on this channel — so it is sent when the publisher says
there is a new one and not when a frame ends. Stella Nova publishes one
frame in six; forwarding on every frame would encode identical rows five
times out of six to redraw a panel that cannot tell the difference.

The two ids ride with the rows because they NAME rows in them. `inspecting`
is the publisher's correction for its own renumbering — ids are indices
into a table it rebuilds, so the subject moves under the Inspector on every
publish — and sending it separately would let it arrive against a census it
does not describe.

items.name: pump_profile
items.doc:
Carry the frame just closed into the profile window, and send a Report when
one is ready. Once a frame, after `profile::frame()`.

Cheap in the shipped game and cheap in a hosted one nobody is profiling:
both leave on the first line, and the second costs one relaxed load.

WHY THE GAME REDUCES AND THE EDITOR DOES NOT
--------------------------------------------
The obvious build ships every frame's spans across and windows them on the
editor's side, where the panel already windows its own. It is wrong on the
only axis this channel cares about: that is sixty JSON encodes a second of
a payload that grows with how well the game is instrumented, to produce a
picture that is redrawn four times a second. Reducing at the source sends
the same reading in one message.

The Report is the same type the editor builds for its own frames, so the
two sources reach the panel identically and neither has a private path.

items.name: pump_perf
items.doc:
Take this frame's cost and send a quarter second of them at a time. Once a
frame, after the render loop has stored its three spans.

WHY THE PANEL COULD NOT JUST READ THE ATOMICS
---------------------------------------------
It did, and that was the bug. `RENDER_DRAW_US` and the two beside it are
process globals filled by whichever render loop is running, so a
Performance panel in the editor was reading the EDITOR'S frames — and
reporting them under a status line that said the game was running. The
panel was not empty and did not error; it drew a healthy sixty at two
milliseconds while the game next door did whatever it was doing.

This is the same static, read where it is written. The interval is measured
here too rather than sent as a fourth span, because the gap between two
calls of this function IS the game's frame period — the same argument the
panel makes for timing its own `poll`, one process over.

AFTER THE FRAME, AND AFTER `pump_profile`
------------------------------------------
`RENDER_GPU_US` is stored when the submission returns, which is the last
thing the frame arm does before these pumps run. A sample taken any earlier
carries the previous frame's GPU span beside this frame's draw — three
numbers from two frames, summed into one column.

items.name: pump_console
items.doc:
Keep the console publisher armed, and send the scrollback when it moved.
Once a frame, AFTER the game has published — which is after its own frame,
because the publisher is part of the game's gui and not of the engine.

THE ARM MUST HAPPEN EVEN THOUGH IT IS A FRAME LATE
--------------------------------------------------
`devconsole::want_console` is what the game's publisher checks first, and
nothing in this process was ever going to set it: the panel that used to
set it is now in the editor, writing the editor's copy of the static. So a
game with a Debug Console open on it did not build a snapshot to send. It
built nothing at all, which is why the panel's failure looked like an empty
console rather than a stale one.

Arming here rather than in `poll` costs one frame at the moment a panel is
opened and buys the property that the whole console bridge is one function.
A frame is nothing against a person reaching for a panel; the want then
stays armed for as long as the editor keeps saying so.

WHY THE REVISION IS READ AND NOT THE BUFFER
-------------------------------------------
Most frames print nothing, and on those this is two relaxed loads and a
comparison. The buffer is only cloned on the frames the game's own
publisher decided something changed, which is what keeps a channel that
carries a whole scrollback off the per-frame list this protocol refuses.

items.name: pump_controls
items.doc:
Forward the binding table when it has moved. Once a frame.

NO WANT, UNLIKE EVERY PUMP ABOVE IT
-----------------------------------
The census, the profiler and the console are all gated on somebody
looking, because each of them costs the game real work to BUILD — rows off
a forty-thousand-entry cache, a span tree, a scrollback clone. A binding
table costs a revision load on the frames nothing changed, and on the
frames something did it is a hundred short strings. There is nothing here
to brake.

Ungated also means the panel is populated the moment it is opened, with no
round trip. A want would put an empty Control Map on screen for the frame
after a person clicked the tab — which is exactly the state this whole
message exists to stop showing.

WHY THE GAME'S REVISION AND NOT THE EDITOR'S ASK
-----------------------------------------------
The rebinds arriving on `ToGame::Rebind` move this counter themselves, so
one comparison covers both directions: an edit made in the panel comes back
as the table the game actually has, and a rebind the GAME made — its own
settings screen, a default that moved in a new build — reaches the panel by
the same path with nothing extra to arrange.

items.name: pump_mem
items.doc:
Give memory back if the editor asked, and report the footprint. Once a
frame, beside the other pumps.

TWO JOBS, BOTH CHEAP WHEN NOTHING IS HAPPENING
----------------------------------------------
The shed runs first and does nothing unless the editor has raised pressure
and raised it further than last time — see `memcap::shed_if`. The report is
throttled to a second a sample, because the editor measures this process
from outside as well: this figure is the game-attributed meter, not the
governor's input, so it does not need frame-rate freshness.

items.name: requested_size
items.doc:
What the editor last asked the game image to be. None before it has asked,
which is every frame before the panel has a rect.

items.name: take_resize
items.doc:
The requested size, once, on the frame it changes — for the caller that
owns the WINDOW.

WHY THE WINDOW AND NOT JUST THE SURFACE
---------------------------------------
`requested_size` above is enough to allocate an IOSurface of the panel's
shape, and for a long time that was the whole of the resize path. It is not
enough to DRAW at the panel's shape. A hosted game renders at its own
window's size — the manifest size, set once at launch and never touched —
and `present::publish_frame` filled the panel-shaped surface with a
fullscreen triangle over that image. The sampler stretched it. A panel of
any other aspect than the launch window's got a non-uniformly scaled
picture, and nothing in the chain said so.

It also meant the game's own layout never learned the panel existed. Its
window stayed at the launch size, so every reflow, every anchored HUD
element and every `available_rect` inside the game was computed against a
shape the person looking at it could not see.

So the size goes to the window. Everything downstream — the surface config,
the render dimensions, the post chain, the game's egui screen rect — is
already wired to a window resize and follows for free, and the publish blit
becomes 1:1 because the two sizes are finally the same number.

Returns None when nothing changed, so the frame loop pays one atomic load
on the overwhelming majority of frames. Marks the size applied on the way
out: a caller that drops the value still will not be handed it again, which
is correct, because the next real change supersedes it anyway.

items.name: focused
items.doc:
Whether keys are aimed at the Game panel. Always false with no editor,
because then nothing else is competing for them.

items.name: visible
items.doc:
Whether anybody is looking at the game image.

True with no editor, because then the window is the picture and the person
looking at it is the only opinion there is. The `hosted` test is first so
a shipped game answers on one relaxed atomic load and never reads the flag
an editor would have written.

WHAT A FALSE ANSWER IS ALLOWED TO STOP
-------------------------------------
The publish blit, and the RATE of the frame loop. Not the loop itself: it
still drains the channel, still takes a resize, still answers `Shutdown`,
and still renders — a hidden panel raised again must show a picture of the
world as it is now, and a loop that had stopped would show the frame it
stopped on until it caught up.

It is therefore a throttle and not a switch, and the consequence is worth
stating where somebody will find it: a game that runs its world inside its
own render call runs that world at the idle rate while its panel is hidden.
Warp cannot fix that from here, because `render` is the one call where the
application walks its own world and the engine has no way to separate the
two halves of it.

items.name: should_exit
items.doc: The editor went away, or asked for a clean exit.

items.name: ensure_surface
items.sig: pub fn ensure_surface(width: u32, height: u32) -> bool
items.doc:
Allocate and publish a surface, when the size has changed.

Idempotent at a given size, so a caller can put it in the frame loop and
pay a comparison for every frame that did not resize.

Returns whether a surface is available at the requested size afterwards.

items.name: surface_generation
items.doc:
Which allocation the current surface is. See `SURFACE_GEN`.

Starts at 0 and is bumped before the first surface exists, so a cache that
initialises to 0 is stale on the first frame rather than accidentally
current — the value is only ever compared, never counted from.

items.name: with_surface
items.sig: pub fn with_surface<R>(f: impl FnOnce(&Shared) -> R) -> Option<R>
items.doc:
Borrow the surface being rendered into, if there is one.

A closure rather than a returned reference, because the surface lives
behind the session mutex and handing out a borrow of it would either leak
the guard or need a lifetime nobody at the call site can satisfy.

items.name: IMPORT_FORMAT
items.doc:
What an imported texture always is.

sRGB, and the SRGB IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART. An IOSurface's pixel format
is a byte layout — 'BGRA' — and carries no colour space, so this is a free
choice about how the bytes are read. It has to match the pipeline that
writes them, and that pipeline is the CRT blit, which is built for the
window surface format. On macOS that is `Bgra8UnormSrgb`.

It was `Bgra8Unorm` and the mismatch was not a wrong colour. wgpu refuses
a render pass whose attachment format differs from the pipeline's, so the
game panicked inside the publish blit — the surface handshake completed,
the editor imported a texture, and the process died on the first frame it
tried to draw. `a_launched_process_attaches_and_publishes_a_surface` now
outlives the publish for exactly this reason.
On Windows the free choice is already made: a D3D12 resource carries a
typed format, and `surface.rs` creates it as `B8G8R8A8_UNORM_SRGB`, which
is what wgpu-hal maps this constant to. The two must agree there as well,
and there the disagreement is caught — a view in a format the resource
cannot be cast to is refused by the runtime.

items.name: texture_from_shared
items.doc:
See `surface.rs`'s stub note: a host that cannot import shows the boot
terminal, which is what it shows before the first frame anyway.

items.name: adopt_device
items.doc:
Tell `surface.rs` which GPU device to allocate shared surfaces on.

Windows only in effect, and a no-op everywhere else, so the GPU init calls
it unconditionally and carries no `cfg` of its own. Call it once, right
after the device is made and before any surface is created: every
`Shared::create` and `Shared::lookup` on Windows fails until it has run.

It lives here and not in `surface.rs` because it needs `as_hal`, and this
file is the one place in warp that touches wgpu-hal.

items.name: adopt_device
items.doc: The no-op half. macOS allocates an IOSurface with no device at all.

items.name: InputEvent
items.doc:
One input event, in the picture's own coordinates.

The winit types are carried as themselves rather than as numbers of our
own, which is what winit's `serde` feature is for. A key code re-encoded as
a u32 here would be a second table to keep in step with winit's, and the
failure of such a table is a keyboard where most keys work.

items.name: accept
items.doc:
Queue events for the next `replay`. From `child::poll`, and from a game
that makes its own events. A gamepad cursor is the second case: the game
turns the pad into these events, so that egui and the input helper read
the pad as a pointer.

items.name: forget
items.doc:
Drop anything queued. On detach, so a game that loses its editor does not
replay a click from it afterwards.

items.name: pending
items.doc:
True when `accept` queued events that no `replay` took yet. The event loop
replays when this is true, so a game with no editor reaches `replay` too.

items.name: replay
items.sig: pub fn replay(window_px: (u32, u32), surface_px: (u32, u32)) -> Vec<WindowEvent<'static>>
items.doc:
Take the queue as events the child's own window could have produced, and
mirror every key press onto the focus-immune raw ring on the way past.

Empty when nothing arrived, which is most frames — a person is not moving
the mouse on most of them.

THE RING IS WRITTEN HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE IN THIS PROCESS
--------------------------------------------------------
The engine writes the ring from the primary window's `WindowEvent` arm. A
hosted game's window is hidden and produces no window events, so nothing
wrote the ring in a launched game at all. Every action that reads the ring
AND the input helper lived on its helper half and hid that; an action that
reads the ring alone answered nothing. The game's debug console is
single-path on the ring on purpose — the two paths double-fired one press
against each other — so its key opened nothing under the editor and opened
the console in the same game started from a shell.

`push_raw_key` and not `push_raw_key_from`: this process has no panels,
`game_view_embedded` is false in it, and `capture` already applied
`game_keys_from` before the key crossed the socket. A second gate here would
be answered by the wrong window.

KEY ROUTING, THE SAME THREE ARMS A REAL EVENT GETS
-------------------------------------------------
The window arm in `lib.rs` decides which of three places a key lands in:
a pointer-release key drops the pointer grab, a key under keyboard capture
goes to the capture queue, and everything else mirrors onto the raw ring.
A hosted game reaches no window arm, so this function is where a hosted
game answers the same three questions.

Keyboard capture was the arm that was missing. `INPUT_CAPTURED` was set by
the app, nothing ever wrote `CAPTURED_KEYS`, and the subsystem holding the
keyboard — the game's DOOM framebuffer — drained an empty queue for every
key. The same game answered the keyboard when it was started from a shell.

Every key still reaches `out`, capture or not. That is what the window arm
does: it feeds egui before it routes, and capture diverts the RING, not the
window's own egui half.

items.name: capture
items.sig: pub fn capture( vp: crate::types::ViewportId, event: &WindowEvent, window_px: (u32, u32), render_px: (u32, u32), )
items.doc:
Tap one window event on its way to the editor's own game hooks.

`vp` is the window the event came from, which is not always the primary
one — the Game panel can be torn off, and then that window's pointer is
the game's.

items.name: drain
items.doc: Take what has been tapped since the last call. Once a frame, by the editor.

items.name: set_forwarding
items.doc:
Arm or disarm the tap.

Off by default and off in every shipped game, so `capture` costs one
relaxed load on a path that runs for every window event in the editor.

items.name: publish_frame
items.sig: pub fn publish_frame( device: &wgpu::Device, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, pipeline: &wgpu::RenderPipeline, bind_group: &wgpu::BindGroup, gui_pipeline: &wgpu::RenderPipeline, gui_bind_group: &wgpu::BindGroup, )
items.doc:
Draw the composed frame into the editor's surface.

`pipeline` and `bind_group` are the ones the window blit uses, and must
stay that way: the pipeline is built for the surface format, the imported
texture is `Bgra8Unorm`, and on macOS those are the same format. Handing a
pipeline built for anything else is a wgpu validation failure at encode.

`gui_pipeline` and `gui_bind_group` are the chrome composite, and they are
the SECOND HALF of the same frame rather than an extra. The game's own GUI
stopped being inside the image `bind_group` reads the day it got its own
target; without this draw a hosted game publishes a picture with no menu on
it, and the editor panel shows a game nobody can drive.

items.name: forget
items.doc:
Release the imported texture.

Called on detach, so a process that loses its editor is not holding a
GPU texture over an IOSurface nobody will read again.

items.name: Shared
items.doc:
A frame buffer both processes hold.

Not Clone. Two owners would mean two `CFRelease` calls for one retain,
and the second is a use-after-free of a buffer the other process is
still rendering into.

items.name: create
items.sig: pub fn create(width: u32, height: u32) -> Option<Self>
items.doc: Allocate. The guest process calls this, because the guest renders.

items.name: adopt
items.doc:
Take ownership of a share in a surface somebody else allocated.

For a producer that hands out an `IOSurfaceRef` of its own — an
off-screen browser's paint callback, a capture session, anything
that renders where warp does not. The caller keeps its reference;
this takes one of its own.

None when the surface is null, has no extent, or is not BGRA. The
format check is the load-bearing one — see the module header for
what a silent mismatch costs.

items.name: lookup
items.doc: Attach to a surface another process made and published.

items.name: publish
items.doc:
Make this surface reachable, and return the name to send over the
JSON channel. None when the namespace refused the registration, in
which case the host simply never gets a picture — it does not fail.

items.name: stride
items.doc:
Bytes per row. Deliberately exposed rather than computed from the
width: the OS pads rows for alignment, so `width * 4` is wrong for
most widths and the error is a sheared image.

items.name: as_raw
items.doc:
For the texture import, which lives next to the device it imports
into rather than here.

items.name: create
items.sig: pub fn create(_width: u32, _height: u32) -> Option<Self>

items.name: register_device
items.doc:
Name the device to allocate on. `import.rs` calls this, because
`import.rs` owns the one `as_hal` call in warp.

Takes ONE reference and never gives it back. The device outlives every
surface made on it, and a release here is a use-after-free inside
whichever driver thread reads it next.

items.name: MAX_MEGA_ATLAS_LAYERS
items.doc: Maximum textures per mega-atlas (wgpu limit is typically 2048).

items.name: atlas_set
items.doc:
The registered atlas set, or an empty one.

The reference is `'static`, so callers can hold `&'static str` borrows of
atlas ids for the process lifetime. The load event channel needs that.

items.name: register_atlas_set
items.sig: pub fn register_atlas_set(mut set: AtlasSetDescriptor) -> Result<(), Vec<String>>
items.doc:
Validate a descriptor and store it. The first call wins.

Returns every problem found, so a wrong descriptor needs one run to fix
rather than one run per mistake.

items.name: AtlasDesc
items.doc: One mega-atlas: a slot in the render path, plus the texture families in it.

items.name: groups
items.sig: pub fn groups(id: &str, index: usize) -> Self
items.doc: An atlas that loads its groups at `resolution` 256.

items.name: placeholder
items.sig: pub fn placeholder(id: &str, index: usize) -> Self
items.doc: An atlas that holds a placeholder layer and no groups.

items.name: with_resolution
items.sig: pub fn with_resolution(mut self, resolution: u32) -> Self

items.name: with_pak_name
items.sig: pub fn with_pak_name(mut self, pak_name: &str) -> Self

items.name: with_dir
items.sig: pub fn with_dir(mut self, dir: &str) -> Self

items.name: with_manifest
items.sig: pub fn with_manifest(mut self, manifest: &str) -> Self

items.name: tiling
items.doc:
Declare that every layer of this atlas tiles.

The Texture Forge writes materials in the group layout this walks, so
an atlas pointed at a directory of them wants this and a sprite atlas
does not.

items.name: edge
items.doc: The edge rule this atlas's texture set is built with.

items.name: with_group
items.sig: pub fn with_group(mut self, group: AtlasGroupDesc) -> Self

items.name: group
items.doc: The group with this name, or None.

items.name: group_base_id
items.doc:
The first `type_id` of the named group. The application reads its own
type-id bases back through this, in place of the constant modules the
engine used to hold.

items.name: entry_count
items.doc: How many `MegaAtlasEntry` values this atlas produces.

items.name: worst_case_layers
items.doc: Texture array layers this atlas can take at its caps.

items.name: entries
items.doc:
The load entries for this atlas, in declaration order, with paths
resolved against the asset root.

Both the runtime loader and the offline packer call this, so the
type-id arithmetic exists once.

items.name: AtlasGroupDesc
items.doc:
One texture family inside an atlas. Each path becomes one
`MegaAtlasEntry`, and the entry at position `i` gets `type_id = base_id + i`.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(name: &str, base_id: u32, max_variants: u32, paths: &[&str]) -> Self
items.doc: A group that loads normals and masks. Use the builders to turn either off.

items.name: with_normals
items.sig: pub fn with_normals(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: with_masks
items.sig: pub fn with_masks(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: type_id_range
items.doc:
First and last `type_id` this group occupies, both inclusive.
An empty group returns `base_id` twice, and validation rejects it.

items.name: worst_case_layers
items.doc: Texture array layers this group can take at its cap.

items.name: AtlasSetDescriptor
items.doc: Every atlas the application declares.

items.name: new
items.doc: An empty set. `const` so the unregistered fallback needs no lock.

items.name: with_atlas
items.sig: pub fn with_atlas(mut self, atlas: AtlasDesc) -> Self

items.name: with_image_atlas
items.sig: pub fn with_image_atlas(mut self, atlas: ImageAtlasDesc) -> Self

items.name: atlases
items.doc: Every atlas, in slot order once the set is registered.

items.name: atlas
items.sig: pub fn atlas(&self, slot: usize) -> Option<&AtlasDesc>
items.doc: The atlas in this slot. A Vec index, not a search.

items.name: slot_of
items.doc:
The slot of the named atlas. Application code that needs a slot
number resolves it once at startup and then addresses by index.

items.name: primary_image_atlas
items.doc:
The first declared image atlas. The engine holds exactly one
`ImageAtlas` slot today, so the first declaration fills it.

items.name: summary
items.doc:
One line per atlas: slot, id, entry count, worst-case layers.
The loader prints it, so a wrong descriptor is visible in the log
before any texture reads.

items.name: AtlasSource
items.doc: Where the layers of an atlas come from.

items.name: ImageAtlasDesc
items.doc: One directory loaded into an `ImageAtlas` rather than a mega-atlas.

items.name: new
items.doc: An atlas that loads normals and masks, and packs at 1024 with 256 layers.

items.name: with_pak_name
items.sig: pub fn with_pak_name(mut self, pak_name: &str) -> Self

items.name: with_normals
items.sig: pub fn with_normals(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: with_masks
items.sig: pub fn with_masks(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: with_pack_size
items.sig: pub fn with_pack_size(mut self, resolution: u32, max_textures: u32) -> Self

items.name: MAX_ATLAS_SLOTS
items.doc:
How many atlas slots the render path can address.

RenderContext, Viewport and RenderResources each hold one entry per slot,
all NUM_MEGA_ATLASES long, so the descriptor cannot declare more atlases
than the render path allocates. Widening the render path is that one
constant.

items.name: create_image_bind_group_layout
items.doc:
Create the standard bind group layout for image rendering.

Layout:
- binding 0: albedo texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)
- binding 1: sampler (filtering)
- binding 2: normal texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)
- binding 3: mask texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)
- binding 4: metallic texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)
- binding 5: roughness texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)
- binding 6: emission texture array (texture_2d_array, float, filterable) (texture_2d_array, float, filterable)

items.name: MegaAtlasEntry
items.doc: Defines a texture source directory for mega-atlas loading.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(path: impl AsRef<Path>, type_id: u32, max_variants: u32) -> Self

items.name: with_normals
items.sig: pub fn with_normals(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: with_masks
items.sig: pub fn with_masks(mut self, load: bool) -> Self

items.name: construct
items.sig: pub fn construct(progress: f32, start_edge: u32) -> u32
items.doc:
The flag bits for a construction draw: the flag, the progress (clamped to
0..=1) and the start edge (0..=3, wrapped).

items.name: construct_of
items.sig: pub fn construct_of(flags: u32) -> Option<(f32, u32)>
items.doc:
The progress and start edge in a flags word, or None when the flag is
clear. The shader reads the same fields with the same arithmetic.

items.name: construct_quiet
items.sig: pub fn construct_quiet(progress: f32, start_edge: u32) -> u32
items.doc:
The flag bits of a quiet construction draw: construct() plus the quiet bit,
so the reveal shows the panels with no weld glow.

items.name: research
items.sig: pub fn research(progress: f32, still: bool) -> u32
items.doc:
The flag bits of a research draw: the construct flag, the progress (clamped
to 0..=1) and the research bit. `still` sets the quiet bit, so the bubbles
do not move.

items.name: research_of
items.doc:
The progress in a research flags word, or None when the word is not a
research draw. The shader reads the same field with the same arithmetic.

items.name: tiles
items.doc:
The flag bits that repeat a texture `count` times over the quad, per axis.

Clamped to what the field holds. Zero and one both mean once, so
`flags | tiles(1)` is `flags`.

items.name: tiles_of
items.doc:
The repeat count in a flags word, never less than one.

The shader reads the same field with the same arithmetic. This is here so
a test can hold the two together.

items.name: IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_EDGE_SHIFT
items.doc:
Where the start edge starts in the flags word. Two bits, in sprite UV:
0 is u = 0, 1 is u = 1, 2 is v = 0, 3 is v = 1.

items.name: IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_MASK
items.doc: How wide the build progress is.

items.name: IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_QUIET
items.sig: pub const IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_QUIET: u32 = 1 << 30;  /// The flag bits for a construction draw: the flag, the progress (clamped to /// 0..=1) and the start edge (0..=3, wrapped). pub fn construct(progress: f32, start_edge: u32) -> u32 { let p = (progress.clamp(0.0, 1.0) * 255.0).round() as u32; IMAGE_FLAG_CONSTRUCT | ((p & IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_MASK) << IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_SHIFT) | ((start_edge & 3) << IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_EDGE_SHIFT) }  /// The flag bits of a quiet construction draw: construct() plus the quiet bit,
items.doc:
Bit 30: the damage draw. The construction reveal shows no weld glow and no
frame band, so a panel is plated or shows the blue survey outline. A
damaged module uses it while nobody repairs it: the lost panels look like
the panels of a module that is not built yet.

items.name: IMAGE_RESEARCH
items.sig: pub const IMAGE_RESEARCH: u32 = 1 << 31;  /// The flag bits of a research draw: the construct flag, the progress (clamped /// to 0..=1) and the research bit. `still` sets the quiet bit, so the bubbles /// do not move. pub fn research(progress: f32, still: bool) -> u32 { let quiet = if still { IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_QUIET } else { 0 }; construct(progress, 0) | IMAGE_RESEARCH | quiet }  /// The progress in a research flags word, or None when the word is not a /// research draw. The shader reads the same field with the same arithmetic.
items.doc:
Bit 31: the research draw. It goes with IMAGE_FLAG_CONSTRUCT and reads the
same progress field (bits 20-27), so it uses the construction path. The
shader then shows a blue liquid fill that moves along the sprite u axis with
the batch progress, with bubbles that rise through it. The start edge
(bits 28-29) has no function in this mode. The quiet bit (30) stops the
bubbles, for the reduce motion setting.

items.name: forge
items.sig: pub fn forge(progress: f32, still: bool) -> u32
items.doc:
The flag bits of a forge draw: a research draw with the forge edge value.
The shader shows a molten orange fill to the batch progress, with embers
that rise from it. `still` stops the embers, for the reduce motion setting.

items.name: forge_of
items.doc:
The progress in a forge flags word, or None when the word is not a forge
draw. A forge word is also a research word, so research_of reads it too.

items.name: IMAGE_FORGE_EDGE
items.doc:
Start-edge value that turns a research draw into a forge draw. The research
mode does not read the start edge (bits 28-29), so the value is free to
select the fill look: 0 is the blue research fill, 1 is the orange forge
fill of a production machine.

items.name: IMAGE_CONSTRUCT_SHIFT
items.doc: Where the build progress starts in the flags word. Eight bits, 0..=255.

items.name: IMAGE_FLAG_CONSTRUCT
items.doc:
Draw the sprite as a module under construction. The fragment shader cuts
the sprite into panels and shows each panel as a survey outline, a cyan
frame, or finished plating, from the build progress in bits 20-27. The
panels go on from the start edge in bits 28-29. Bit 7, the last free bit
below the tile-count field.

Eight //  bits, so 1 to 255 repeats per axis, and a zero there means one — which is //  what every instance written before this held, so nothing moved. // //  IN THE FLAGS WORD, AND NOT A FIELD OF ITS OWN

Eight //  bits, so 1 to 255 repeats per axis, and a zero there means one — which is //  what every instance written before this held, so nothing moved.
items.doc:
UV sub-rect crop, for half-tiles and quarter-tiles. Each flag narrows the
sampled UV range to one half of the texture, so a half-size quad shows the
matching half of the art at 1:1 instead of squashing the whole texture into
it. Combine one X flag with one Y flag for a quarter. Bits 16-19, clear of
the tile-count field (bits 8-15).

items.name: IMAGE_FLAG_ENV_REFLECT
items.doc:
Take the matcap environment reflection. A lit sprite gets the matcap term
only with this bit. The application sets it on station metal (modules,
walls and floor plating), so ships, rocks and props stay clear and show no
reflection. Bit 6, clear of the tile-count field (bits 8-15).

items.name: IMAGE_FLAG_OVERLAY_TINT
items.doc:
Use overlay blend instead of multiply for tint color.
Overlay preserves luminance contrast on greyscale textures.

items.name: IMAGE_FLAG_RECEIVE_SHADOW
items.doc:
Receive the station shadow coverage. A sprite with this bit reads the
coverage buffer at its screen position and darkens by it. The application
sets it on colony interior sprites only, so walls, ships and space objects
keep the bit clear and do not darken. Bit 5, clear of the tile-count field
(bits 8-15) and the sub-rect crop field (bits 16-19).

items.name: IMAGE_FLAG_UV_CROP
items.doc:
Crop UV coordinates inward to remove texture edge padding.
Amount is controlled by UV_CROP_AMOUNT in image_shader.wgsl.

items.name: load_multi
items.sig: pub fn load_multi( device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, layout: &wgpu::BindGroupLayout, entries: &[MegaAtlasEntry], resolution: u32, name: &'static str, pak_name: &str, atlas_id: u8, edge: Edge, ) -> Self
items.doc:
Load multiple texture directories into a single unified atlas.

Integrates disk caching: after directory scanning, a fingerprint is
computed from source file metadata. On cache hit, pre-processed
pixel data is loaded directly. On miss, the full decode→resize
pipeline runs and results are saved for subsequent launches.

`edge` says whether the layers of this atlas are tiles. It reaches the
texture set, which is the only thing that can act on it: the sampler's
address mode and the mip reduction are both its.

`name` is 'static because every MegaAtlasProgress event carries it to
the render thread, which reads it a frame or more later. `atlas_id` is
the atlas slot number, and it tells the boot terminal which atlas the
counter belongs to.

items.name: parse
items.doc:
Parse and validate. The version gate runs before the rules, so a future
format fails with one clear message instead of a list of field errors.

items.name: read_model
items.doc:
The read model of text that parses, whatever rules it breaks.

`parse` is the gate a LOADER wants: a project that breaks a rule must
not start. An EDITOR wants the other thing. It has to draw the fields
of the file somebody is part way through fixing, and the moment it
cannot, the section that holds the mistake disappears and takes the
only control that could correct it.

Duplicate an atlas id, or leave a gap in the slots, and this is the
difference between a red problem line and an editor that says the file
does not parse — about a file that parses.

The version check stays. A manifest of another format is not a model
this code can read at all, so there is nothing to draw from it.

items.name: load
items.doc: Read a manifest from disk, then parse it.

items.name: discover
items.doc:
Find the manifest. WARP_APP_MANIFEST first, then the directory that
holds the executable, then the working directory and its parents.

items.name: resolve
items.doc:
Turn whatever a person named into the manifest path.

A directory becomes the `warp_app.toml` inside it. Anything else — a file,
a path that does not exist, a symlink — comes back untouched.

WHY THIS EXISTS AT ALL. Every way into a project used to demand the file
itself: the command line, the Open dialog, the recent lists, the
satellite's `--project=`. That is the wrong unit to ask for. The name of
the file is a constant, so naming the directory already names the file,
and a directory is what a person has selected in every other tool they
use to open a project. Requiring the extra click added no information.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. It does not walk upward and it does not
look inside subdirectories. A missing manifest stays missing, and the
caller reports that against the directory it was handed. Searching was
removed from the editor's startup on purpose — see `EditorState::discover`
— because a project found by walking is a project nobody chose, and this
function must not smuggle that back in one directory at a time.

It does not check that the result exists either. The caller is about to
open the file and will produce a better message from the failure than a
bool here could.

items.name: platform_invocation
items.sig: pub fn platform_invocation(&self, key: &str, triple: Option<&str>) -> Invocation
items.doc:
The invocation that builds one platform when no target declares it.

WHY THIS EXISTS. `[[build.target]]` is a list a person writes, and the
editor's template writes exactly one entry, `native`. Four platform
tiles then had one target between them: the Build panel compiled that
target whichever tile was pressed, so Windows, Linux and macOS all
packed the same host binary into three folders.

IT IS NOT ALWAYS `cargo build`, and that is the half that makes a
cross build work at all. warp_core pulls rusqlite, ratatui and vte for
every target that is not android or wasm, and rusqlite vendors sqlite
as C. A plain `cargo build --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` on a mac
hands that C to the host `cc`, which stops on

fatal error: 'stdlib.h' file not found

because there is no Windows SDK behind it. `cargo xwin` supplies one.
The same is true of Linux and `cargo zigbuild`, which supplies a libc
and the glibc floor. Both routes are already named in the manifest and
already probed by `ready.rs`; this reads the same two fields.

Release only. A distribution folder is not where a debug build goes,
and the panel that calls this is the distribution panel.

entry to read a profile and a triple from. Both push the triple

items.name: artifact
items.sig: pub fn artifact(&self, target_id: &str, target_dir: &Path) -> Option<PathBuf>
items.doc:
Where cargo puts the binary this target builds.

`<target_dir>/[<triple>/]<profile dir>/<build.bin>`, which is cargo's
layout written down. The one rule that is not the profile name spelled
out is the dev profile, whose directory is `debug`.

It answers for cargo targets only. A `command` target runs a program
the project named and this module knows nothing about what that
program builds or where it puts it.

The caller supplies `target_dir` rather than this deriving it: the
directory belongs to the cargo workspace, not to the manifest, and a
package inside a workspace builds into the WORKSPACE's target — a
distinction this file has no way to see.

think about them in. Sorting by id would put `dist-mac` before `run`.

A command target gives its own program. A cargo target gives "cargo"
and the argv that `cargo_args` builds. So one caller starts either kind
without a branch of its own.

`draw_rect` and every other primitive take `[u8; 4]`; egui takes

one definition rather than two that can disagree.

Serialised as a hex string. `"#1a1a1f"` in a manifest is a value a person
can read and a designer can paste; `[26, 26, 31]` is neither.

items.doc: The same colour at a different opacity, for a wash over the scene.

items.name: from_hex
items.doc:
Read `#rgb`, `#rrggbb` or `#rrggbbaa`. The leading hash is optional.

An unreadable word gives `None` rather than an error. The caller keeps
its default, so one bad key in a manifest costs one role and not the
project.

items.name: Role
items.doc:
What a colour is FOR. The vocabulary is closed; the values are not.

Named for what a game has rather than what a widget has. A tool has rows
and fields; a game has a ground, a surface, ink on it, one colour that
says "this one", and three that say how it went.

items.name: ALL
items.sig: pub const ALL: [Role; 15] = [ Role::Background, Role::Surface, Role::SurfaceRaised, Role::SurfaceSunken, Role::Ink, Role::InkDim, Role::InkStrong, Role::InkInverted, Role::Highlight, Role::Accent, Role::Ok,
items.doc: Every role, in the order the Theme panel lists them.

items.name: key
items.doc:
The key this role has in `[settings.theme]`, and the words a panel
puts beside its swatch. Stable across builds: a rename orphans the
override of everybody who already made one.

items.name: group
items.doc:
The heading a panel files this role under.

Five groups and not fifteen rows, because a person changing "the
background" wants the four grounds together and does not want to read
past the status colours to find them.

items.name: GROUPS
items.doc: Every group, in the order a panel lists them.

items.name: title
items.doc: The words beside the swatch. Title case, and shorter than the key.

items.name: Metric
items.doc:
The shape of a box, in design units.

Design units and not pixels. `ui::theme::px` turns one into a pixel count
at the interface scale in force, so a themed box answers the zoom keys
the way the rest of the interface does.

items.name: ALL
items.sig: pub const ALL: [Metric; 5] = [ Metric::Rounding, Metric::Border, Metric::PadX, Metric::PadY, Metric::Gap, ]

items.name: range
items.doc:
The band a person works in, not what the renderer tolerates.

A rail cut to the largest legal value puts the whole useful range in
its first tenth, and a small change becomes impossible to place.

items.name: Palette
items.doc:
Every role and every metric, as one value.

The serialised view of the live table, and what `[settings.theme]` holds.
Named fields rather than an array, because `project_settings::merge`
writes only the keys that differ from the default — so a project's block
lists the four roles it changed and not all twenty.

items.name: DEFAULT
items.doc:
The look a game has before anybody themes it.

Dark, low chroma, one blue that carries every "this one". It is a
starting point that reads correctly on a projector and in a bright
room, not a house style — the whole point of the table is that a
project moves off it.

items.name: get
items.sig: pub const fn get(&self, role: Role) -> Rgba
items.doc:
One role out of a copy. This is the lookup a draw loop wants: the
copy was one pass over the table, and every `get` after it is a move.

items.name: metric
items.sig: pub const fn metric(&self, m: Metric) -> f32
items.doc: One metric out of a copy, in design units.

items.name: color
set_color
items.sig: pub fn set_color(role: Role, c: Rgba)
items.doc:
Put a colour on a role, for this process.

The Theme panel calls this as a person drags. It does not write the
manifest — `project_settings` does that on save, from `section`.

items.name: metric
items.doc: One metric, in design units. Multiply by `ui::theme::px` for pixels.

items.name: set_metric
items.sig: pub fn set_metric(m: Metric, v: f32)

items.name: palette
items.doc:
The whole table, as one value.

Take this once and name fields on it when a loop reads several roles. The
copy is twenty loads; twenty lookups against the live table would be
twenty each time round.

items.name: set_palette
items.doc: Install a whole table. What `[settings.theme]` does on project open.

items.name: reset
items.doc: Put every role back to the default.

items.name: section
items.doc:
`[settings.theme]`, for `project_settings`.

Registered as a builtin rather than by the application, and that is the
point of the whole module. A game that calls nothing still gets its
project's palette, because the engine loaded it before the first frame.

items.name: frame
frame_of
items.doc:
A themed box filled with any role.

The border is `Line` whatever the fill is, because a border that tracked
the fill would vanish on the one surface that most needs an edge — a
panel laid straight over the scene.

items.name: frame_raised
items.doc: The same, one step up: a button, a header, the card in front of a card.

items.name: frame_sunken
items.doc: The same, one step down: a field, a well, the track of a bar.

items.name: gap
items.doc:
The gap between one box and the next, in pixels at the current scale.

`ui.add_space(palette::gap())` rather than a literal, so the rhythm of a
HUD moves with the theme the same way its colours do.

items.name: MAX_SPANS
items.doc:
Spans one thread will record in one frame before it stops recording.

Four thousand is far past what an instrumented frame loop produces and far
short of what would cost memory worth thinking about. It is here for the
unbounded case — a `scope!` inside a loop over ten thousand entities, or a
worker thread whose buffer nothing drains — where the alternative is a Vec
that grows until the process dies.

items.name: WANT_GRACE
items.doc:
How many frames a reader's interest outlives its last `want(true)`.

The census's constant and the census's reason: a reader that stops asking
gives up within a few frames rather than at once, so interest survives a
frame where the panel did not happen to draw.

items.name: Span
items.doc:
A block of named work, and where it sits in the frame's tree.

`&'static str` and not a String, which is what keeps the recording free of
allocation: the name of an instrumented block is a literal in the source.
A caller with a name it computed has to leak it or pick a literal, and
picking a literal is the right answer — a flame chart with one row per
entity id is not a reading of anything.

items.name: dur_ns
items.doc: What the span cost, in nanoseconds.

items.name: Frame
items.doc: One frame's spans, in pre-order.

items.name: children
items.sig: pub fn children(&self, i: usize) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + '_
items.doc:
The direct children of the span at `i`.

The pre-order walk the header describes: everything after `i` that is
deeper, stopping at the first that is not, and of those only the ones
exactly one level down.

items.name: subtree_end
items.sig: pub fn subtree_end(&self, i: usize) -> usize
items.doc: One past the last span of the subtree rooted at `i`.

items.name: work_ns
items.doc:
The instrumented work of the frame: every top-level span added up.

NOT `total_ns`, and the difference decides which frame a window keeps.
`total_ns` is the PERIOD — the wall clock from one `frame()` to the
next — and the Performance panel next door spends a section header on
why that is a different quantity: submissions are gated at the frame
budget, so the period bottoms out there however cheap the frame was.

Ranking by period therefore picks the frame that WAITED longest, which
is usually the one that did least. Worse, the first frame after
profiling is turned on has a period stretching back to whenever the
loop last called `frame()` and contains no spans at all, so it wins its
window outright and the flame chart is empty with a large number over
it. Work is zero for that frame, which is the right answer.

items.name: self_ns
items.sig: pub fn self_ns(&self, i: usize) -> u32
items.doc:
What the span at `i` cost with its children's time taken out.

The number a profiler is actually read for. Total time on a span near
the root is the frame restated — it is large because everything is
inside it, not because anything in it is slow.

items.name: Scope
items.doc:
Time the block this is dropped at the end of.

Constructed by `scope!`, which is how it should be reached — a guard bound
to a named variable is a guard somebody can accidentally drop early, and a
guard bound to `_` is dropped IMMEDIATELY, which times nothing and is the
classic way to get a flame chart full of zero-width spans.

items.name: want
items.doc:
Say that something is reading. Call it every frame a reader is open.

`false` gives up at once. Not calling it at all gives up within
`WANT_GRACE` frames, which is the path that carries the weight — a panel
that was closed, or an editor that exited, says nothing at all.

items.name: enabled
items.doc: Whether a scope entered right now would record anything.

items.name: generation
items.doc: Frames closed since the process started.

items.name: frame
items.doc:
Close the frame on this thread, publish it, and start the next.

Call once per frame from the loop, whether or not anything is reading. It
is the clock `want` expires against, so a loop that only called it while a
panel was open would leave the gate stuck at whatever it last was.

Spans still open here are closed at this instant and counted. That is a
caller putting `frame()` inside something it also timed, and the choice is
between a well-formed tree with one span longer than it should be and a
tree with a hole in it. The first can be read.

items.name: take_frame
items.doc:
The frame `frame()` last published, taken out of the slot.

None when nothing has been published since the last call, which is the
normal answer for a reader polling faster than the loop runs.

items.name: reset
items.doc:
Drop the recording in progress and anything published. For tests, and for
a reader that wants to be sure the next frame it sees began after a Clear.

items.name: Bar
items.doc: One bar of the flame chart: a span of the worst frame in the window.

items.name: Report
items.doc:
What a quarter second of frames came to.

The unit the panel draws and the unit the socket carries. See the header:
deliberately one type for both.

items.name: fps
items.doc: Frames per second over the window. None before a window has closed.

items.name: children
items.sig: pub fn children(&self, i: usize) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + '_
items.doc:
The direct children of bar `i` of the worst frame.

The same pre-order walk `Frame::children` does, over the wire form.

items.name: subtree_end
items.sig: pub fn subtree_end(&self, i: usize) -> usize

items.name: depth
items.doc: The deepest level the worst frame reached, counting the root as one.

items.name: Row
items.doc: One name, totalled over every frame of the window.

items.name: Window
items.doc: Frames in, a Report every `WINDOW_MS`.

items.name: accept
items.sig: pub fn accept(&mut self, frame: Frame)
items.doc:
Fold one captured frame in, rolling the window if it is time.

Rolling here and not on a timer of its own, because a window that
closed while no frames were arriving would publish an empty Report over
a live one — a game that stalled would look like a game that stopped
doing anything, which is the opposite of the reading.

items.name: latest
items.doc:
The Report from the last window that closed. None until one has.

The same Report for every frame of the window it covers, which is what
a panel wants: the picture holds still to be read.

items.name: take_fresh
items.doc:
The Report from the last window that closed, ONCE.

For a reader that forwards rather than draws. See the `fresh` field:
answering `latest` there would put the same quarter second on the
socket sixty times over.

items.name: clear
items.doc:
Drop everything: the window in progress and the last Report with it.

The Report goes too, because a Clear that left the picture standing has
not cleared the thing the person was looking at.

items.name: ProfilerState
items.doc: The panel's own memory: two sources, and where the pointer is.

items.name: poll
items.doc:
Arm the capture if the panel is being looked at, and take whatever it
published. Once a frame, from the host.

Unlike the Performance panel's `poll` this does NOT run the measurement
while the panel is closed. See the header: instrumentation costs a
timestamp per span per frame and a monitor is not worth that when
nobody has it open.

items.name: wants_profile
items.doc:
Whether the game should be instrumenting itself.

For whoever owns the `hostlink::Host`: this is what goes in
`ToGame::Profile`. It is a want and not a start/stop, so sending it
every frame is correct and cheap.

items.sig: pub fn accept_game(&mut self, report: Report)
items.doc: A Report that arrived from the game.

items.name: game_lost
items.doc:
The game process went away — stopped, or died.

The last Report is KEPT and marked, not dropped. The moment a game
stops is the moment somebody wants to see what it was doing, and a
panel that blanked itself on Stop would take that away exactly then.

items.name: SETTINGS_TABLE
items.doc: The manifest key every section lives under.

items.name: Section
items.doc:
One subsystem's settings block.

Function pointers and not closures, so a `Section` is a plain value that
costs no allocation and can be built in a `const`. Neither pointer takes
the subsystem's state as an argument: a section reads and writes its own
global, because that global is what a frame already reads.

items.name: register
items.doc:
Add a section, replacing any section already registered under its name.

Replacing and not pushing: an application that registers twice — two
windows, a satellite, a test that runs after another test — would otherwise
get two writers of one table, and which of them won would depend on
registration order.

items.name: reset_all
items.doc:
Install every registered section's default.

Closing a project is not the same as opening one with no settings, but the
engine state it should leave behind is identical.

items.name: save_all
items.doc:
Merge every registered section into a document's `[settings]` table.

Creates the table on demand and REMOVES it again when every section came
out empty, so a project that has tuned nothing keeps a manifest with no
`[settings]` in it at all. An empty table left behind would be a diff on
the first save of every project that never touched a slider.

items.name: fingerprint
items.doc:
What `save_all` would write right now, as text.

The editor compares this against the last one it saw to decide whether a
slider has moved. It is deliberately defined AS the save rather than beside
it: a fingerprint computed some other way could say "unchanged" about a
value that a save would write, and the person would lose the edit at the
one moment they were told there was nothing to lose.

Equal strings therefore mean equal files, and the comparison is exact
rather than a hash — there is no collision to reason about, and the string
is a few hundred bytes at most because only non-default keys are in it.

items.name: read
items.sig: pub fn read<T: serde::de::DeserializeOwned + Default>(table: Option<&toml::Value>) -> T
items.doc:
Deserialise one section's table, or its default when there is none.

A table that does not deserialise gives the default too, and says nothing.
The alternative is refusing to open a project over a settings key somebody
hand-edited into a typo, and a look is not worth a project that will not
open. The value is visibly wrong on screen, which is the report.

`T` must treat every missing field as its default — `#[serde(default)]` on
the struct — because the table on disk holds ONLY the keys that differ.

items.name: merge
items.sig: pub fn merge<T: serde::Serialize + PartialEq>(into: &mut toml_edit::Table, value: &T, default: &T)
items.doc:
Write the keys of `value` that differ from `default`, and remove the rest.

One implementation serves every field of every section, which is what the
registry is for: eighty-four display fields need no per-field code, and the
next section needs none either.

The removal half is as load-bearing as the writing half. Without it a
slider dragged away from its default and back would leave the value behind
in the file, and the project would carry a key that says nothing forever.

items.name: compose_frame_graph
items.sig: pub fn compose_frame_graph( base: &[GraphResource], extensions: &[&dyn RenderPassExtension], active_owners: &[&str], ) -> FrameGraph
items.doc:
Build one frame graph from the engine base and the loaded extensions.

The base resources seed the graph. Each extension that is on, and owned by
a loaded product, fills the builder through `declare`. An extension that is
off, or owned by a product that is not loaded, adds nothing. This is how a
stopped game leaves the runtime graph whole.

The caller validates the result. Composition does not validate, so a
caller can compose once and validate once, and read every fault together.

`active_owners` are the products loaded this run. A pass owned by a
product not in the list is rejected, so a stopped game cannot leave a
pass on a live viewport.

items.name: engine_frame_graph
items.doc:
The engine's frame, stated through the graph contract.

`ENGINE_ROWS` is the draw order inside one pass. This is the pass order
around it: clear, scene, overlay, post, gui, present. It is the sequence
`execute_render_pass` walks, written as data a caller can validate now and
drive the frame from later.

Every pass here is the engine's, so the owner is `warp`. A product adds its
own passes through `compose_frame_graph`, which seeds a builder from this
base. The scene pass writes the HDR target that post reads.

The frame path calls this, so an invalid engine declaration stops the
renderer at once, and not only under a test. The graph is the engine's
own, so a fault here is an engine bug, and a panic is the right answer.

Execute the main render pass.

The order lives in `layers`. This walks it and nothing else — a row with a
count of zero binds nothing at all, which is what the thirteen `if count > 0`
blocks before it did and what keeps an empty slot free.

GUI (Layer 13) is rendered separately, after this returns.

Instance counts for all renderable types.

SERIALISED BECAUSE THE POPULATION CROSSES A PROCESS BOUNDARY
------------------------------------------------------------
This is a render-path struct and a wire type, which normally wants two
types and a conversion. It does not get them, for the reason `Display`
gives on the same channel: it is a POD of `u32` that is already cloned out
from under a mutex on every read, and a hand-written wire copy would buy
nothing but a second place for a new layer to be forgotten — in the one
panel whose subject is which layer is large.

Every count, in submission order, paired with the row it belongs to.

Same order as `layers`, and that is the point: a row added to one and
not the other is what this is for. The names are the ones a person
reading the draw code already uses.

A registered row sorts by the position its descriptor gave it. Where
the registry is absent — the editor process reading a count off the
wire — every registered row sorts last and keeps its name.

items.name: total
items.doc:
Everything the CPU pushed this frame, summed across rows.

Instances, not bytes and not vertices: the strides differ per row, so
this is a population and not a size. It answers "how much is there",
which is the question that decides whether retaining any of it is worth
the machinery.

items.name: summary
items.doc:
One line per non-empty row, largest first, for a log or a panel.

Empty rows are dropped rather than printed as zero. A frame draws maybe
six of the sixteen, and ten zeroes above the number somebody is looking
for is how a readout stops being read.

A handle to one object, good for the life of the store that minted it.

Two objects never share one, and a despawned id is never handed out again.
It is a bare `u64` and not an index: nothing here is borrowed by holding
one, and a stale one is a lookup that answers `None` rather than a lookup
that answers the wrong object.

items.name: Transform
items.doc:
Where an object sits, relative to its parent.

A root object's parent is the world, so its transform is already the world
one. Everything else composes up the chain.

items.name: compose
items.doc:
This transform expressed in `parent`'s frame — the child seen from the
world when the parent is where it is.

Order matters and is the usual one: the child's offset is scaled by the
parent, then rotated by the parent, then moved to the parent. Rotating
before scaling would make a rotated parent shear its children, which is
the bug this note exists to prevent someone reintroducing.

picture, and the two would drift.
