Remove an object and everything under it.

Returns what went, parents before children, so a caller can drop the
same ids from a selection or push them onto an undo stack. An id that
is not here returns an empty list rather than panicking: a double
delete is a person pressing the key twice, not a bug to crash on.

items.name: clear
items.doc:
Every object, gone. The id counter does NOT reset: a handle held across
a clear stays stale rather than coming back pointing at something new.

items.name: get
items.sig: pub fn get(&self, id: ObjectId) -> Option<&Object>

items.name: get_mut
items.sig: pub fn get_mut(&mut self, id: ObjectId) -> Option<&mut Object>

items.name: alive
items.sig: pub fn alive(&self, id: ObjectId) -> bool

items.name: iter
items.doc: Every object, in spawn order.

items.name: iter_mut
items.sig: pub fn iter_mut(&mut self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &mut Object>

items.name: roots
items.doc: The roots, in spawn order. Where a hierarchy starts drawing.

items.name: children
items.sig: pub fn children(&self, id: ObjectId) -> Vec<ObjectId>
items.doc: Direct children only, in spawn order.

items.name: set_parent
items.sig: pub fn set_parent( &mut self, child: ObjectId, parent: Option<ObjectId>, ) -> Result<(), ParentError>
items.doc:
Move an object under another, or to the root with `None`.

The object keeps its LOCAL transform, so re-parenting moves it on
screen. That is the honest default for a store whose transform field is
the local one: preserving the world position instead would silently
rewrite a number the person can see in the inspector.

items.name: subtree
items.sig: pub fn subtree(&self, id: ObjectId) -> Vec<ObjectId>
items.doc: An object and everything below it, parents before children.

items.name: world_transform
items.sig: pub fn world_transform(&self, id: ObjectId) -> Option<Transform>
items.doc:
Where an object actually is, with every ancestor applied.

`None` when the id is not here. A broken parent chain — an id whose
parent has gone — resolves against what remains rather than failing,
because a partly-torn-down store still has to draw a frame.

items.name: APP_NAME
items.doc:
Product name of the host application. `run` and `run_web` store it from
`Config` before the window exists, because the GPU failure dialog in
gpu/device.rs must name the product and cannot take a parameter: its
caller chain runs through State, which the engine owns.

items.name: app_name
items.doc: The host application name, or a neutral placeholder before `run` stores one.

items.name: set_app_name
items.doc: Store the host application name. The first call wins.

items.name: INPUT_CAPTURED
items.doc:
True while an app subsystem owns the raw keyboard. The app sets it; the
event loop reads it when it routes each KeyboardInput event.

items.name: CAPTURED_KEYS
items.sig: pub static CAPTURED_KEYS: LazyLock<Mutex<VecDeque<(RawKey, bool)>>> = LazyLock::new(|| Mutex::new(VecDeque::new()))
items.doc:
Key transitions diverted by keyboard capture, oldest first. `true` means
the key went down. Producer: the event loop. Consumer: whatever app code
owns the capture.

items.name: CAPTURED_KEY_LIMIT
items.doc:
How many pending transitions the capture queue holds.

The queue makes room by dropping the oldest press, together with the
release that closes it. A release alone is never dropped, so the count can
go above this limit by the releases of the keys a person holds down. That
overshoot is bounded by the keyboard, and it is the safe direction.

items.name: CAPTURE_PASSTHROUGH_KEYS
items.sig: pub static CAPTURE_PASSTHROUGH_KEYS: LazyLock<Mutex<Vec<RawKey>>> = LazyLock::new(|| Mutex::new(Vec::new()))
items.doc:
Keys that stay global while keyboard capture is active. A console toggle
belongs here: the user must always be able to leave.

items.name: POINTER_RELEASE_KEYS
items.sig: pub static POINTER_RELEASE_KEYS: LazyLock<Mutex<Vec<RawKey>>> = LazyLock::new(|| Mutex::new(Vec::new()))
items.doc:
Keys that drop pointer capture when pressed. Such a press also reaches the
raw ring, so one keystroke can both release the pointer and mean something.

items.name: POINTER_CAPTURED
items.doc: True while the pointer is locked to the window center.

items.name: POINTER_DELTA_X
items.doc: Pointer drift accumulated under capture, as f32 bits.

items.name: POINTER_BUTTONS
items.doc: Mouse buttons held under capture: bit0 left, bit1 right, bit2 middle.

items.name: set_input_capture
items.doc: Grab or release the raw keyboard.

items.name: input_captured
items.doc: True while an app subsystem owns the raw keyboard.

items.name: set_pointer_capture
items.doc: Grab or release the pointer.

items.name: pointer_captured
items.doc: True while the pointer is locked to the window center.

items.name: set_capture_passthrough_keys
items.doc: Name the keys that stay global under keyboard capture.

items.name: is_capture_passthrough
items.doc: True if this key stays global under keyboard capture.

items.name: set_pointer_release_keys
items.doc: Name the keys that release pointer capture.

items.name: is_pointer_release_key
items.doc: True if this key releases pointer capture.

items.name: push_captured_key
items.sig: pub fn push_captured_key(key: RawKey, pressed: bool)
items.doc:
Queue one diverted key transition.

── A RELEASE IS NEVER THE ENTRY THAT GOES ─────────────────────────────
This queue carries TRANSITIONS, not presses. The consumer reads one edge
at a time and holds the key between the two, so the two edges of one key
must live or die together.

The queue used to refuse the new entry when it was full. That is the one
policy this queue cannot have: with the queue full of presses, every later
RELEASE was refused while the presses stayed. The consumer then held keys
that nobody was touching, which is the stuck-key fault the pointer and
keyboard paths in hostlink/input.rs describe.

Plain drop-oldest is not enough either. A consumer that has already taken
a press leaves the matching release at the front, and drop-oldest takes
exactly that entry. So the queue drops the oldest PRESS and the release
that closes it, in one step, and never a release on its own.

A press is refused only when the queue holds no press to evict. Losing a
press loses an action; losing a release locks one on.

items.name: captured_keys_dropped
items.doc:
How many diverted transitions the bound has cost, over the life of the
process.

items.name: pop_captured_key
items.doc: Take the oldest diverted key transition.

items.name: clear_captured_keys
items.doc: Drop every pending diverted transition.

items.name: take_pointer_delta
items.doc: Take the pointer drift accumulated since the last call.

items.name: pointer_buttons
items.doc: Mouse buttons held under pointer capture.

items.name: PENDING_SCROLL
items.doc:
Scroll accumulated across event batches between render frames.
The event loop adds scroll_diff() at each MainEventsCleared.
handle_input() drains this instead of reading scroll_diff() directly,
which would return 0 on frames where the render budget was skipped.

items.name: PENDING_MOUSE_RELEASE_LEFT
items.doc: Mouse release flags accumulated across skipped render frames.

items.name: DISPLAY_SETTINGS_TEST_LOCK
items.doc:
Held by every test that installs a value in `DISPLAY_SETTINGS` and then
reads back something derived from it.

The settings are ONE global for the whole process and cargo runs tests in
parallel, so two such tests interleave: one installs a tube, another resets
the block, and the first reads the reset. The failure surfaces in whichever
test lost the race, which is never the one that needs changing, and it does
not reproduce when that test is run alone.

It lives beside the global rather than in any one test module because the
tests that need it are in three of them, and a second lock would not
exclude the first.

items.name: display_settings
items.doc:
Read a copy of the settings.

Poison is stepped over rather than unwrapped, which is what the rest of the
engine does with its globals. A panic somewhere in a GUI frame must not
turn every later read of the picture's settings into a second panic — the
value behind the lock is a plain struct that no partial write can corrupt.

items.name: set_display_settings
items.doc: Replace them.

items.name: with_display_settings
items.sig: pub fn with_display_settings<R>(f: impl FnOnce(&mut DisplaySettings) -> R) -> R
items.doc:
Borrow them mutably for the length of a call.

The lock is held across `f`, so `f` must not call back into anything that
locks it again. Everything that does — the Display section, the game's
settings window — receives the borrow rather than reaching for the global.

items.name: display_is_borrowed
items.doc:
Whether a frame is holding the display settings right now.

A flag and not `try_lock`: `try_lock` cannot tell "this thread already has
it" from "another thread has it for a moment", and the second is ordinary —
a hosted game applies an editor's push from the socket thread.

items.name: DisplaySettings
items.doc:
Serialisable because the game is a second process now. The Post-processing
section edits the copy in the EDITOR, and the picture is composed by the
child — so the struct has to cross a socket or the panel writes a global
nobody with a framebuffer is reading.

`PartialEq` for the same reason: the editor sends this on the change and
not on the frame, so something has to answer whether it changed.
`serde(default)` is the contract with `project_settings`. The table on disk
holds ONLY the keys that differ from `DEFAULT`, so every absent field must
fall back to it rather than fail the whole block for being incomplete.

items.name: DEFAULT
items.doc:
What a game gets before it asks for anything, as a const so a
`static Mutex` can hold it.

`Default::default()` is not callable in a const initializer, and the
settings are one global now — so the values live here and `Default`
returns this rather than the other way round.

EVERY EFFECT IS OFF, AND THE VALUES BESIDE THE SWITCHES ARE NOT
---------------------------------------------------------------
A new project draws what it drew: the rects and lines its `render`
method submits, at the colours it chose. It used to draw those through
an HDR chain and a barrel-distorted CRT filter, because this const held
the look of one game — so the first picture anybody made in this engine
came out bloomed, saturated and bent, and nothing in the project said
where that came from.

The tuned numbers stay. They are the look those two passes had, and a
game that wants it sets `pp_enabled` and `crt_enabled` and gets it back
whole; a game that wants its own moves the fields beside them. What
changed is which of the two states costs a line of code.

AND THE TUBE GREW THIRTY-ONE MORE FIELDS WITHOUT MOVING THE PICTURE
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The CRT filter gained a phosphor mask, a parallax model, a per-channel
convergence block and a set of visualisation modes. A project that sets
only `crt_enabled = true` today must get exactly the picture it got
before them, so every one of those features is off in this const:
`crt_mask_type` 0, `crt_mask_strength` 0, `crt_parallax_strength` 0,
all six `crt_conv_*` 0, `crt_viz_mode` 0, and `crt_phosphor_on` false.
`crt_curve_aspect` is 1.0, which makes the two-axis barrel equal to the
single scalar it replaced.

The fields those switches multiply keep real values rather than zero —
`crt_mask_triad_px`, `crt_slot_height_px`, `crt_eye_dist`, `crt_glass_ior`
and `crt_mask_boost` are divisors, periods or a gain of one, where zero
is a divide or a black screen and not a no-op.

`crt_phosphor_gui_exempt` defaults to 1.0 and is dormant. The default
is left where it was because the field is only carried, never read;
changing it would rewrite every saved project for no visible effect.

items.name: copy_crt_tuning_from
items.doc:
Copy every `crt_*` field except `crt_enabled` from `src`.

The tube's tuning is sixty-odd fields that a game sets as one block,
so `warp_sdk::post::CrtTuning` carries them in a `DisplaySettings`
and moves them with this. The list is in ONE place: a field added to
the struct and not here is a field the SDK drops, and the test below
fails on it: it changes every `crt_*` key the struct serialises.

items.name: display_section
items.doc:
The viewport's settings block, as the project settings registry wants it.

It lives here and not in `project_settings` because the two pointers reach
the global in this file, and a section that reads its own subsystem's
global from another module is a second place that has to be kept in step
with the accessors.

`load` calls `set_display_settings` and not `with_display_settings`: the
block is installed WHOLE. A merge over the live value would leave the
previous project's tube in every field the new project does not name, and
"absent means default" is the rule the file is written against.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_EMBEDDED
items.doc:
True while the host draws the scene inside an egui panel. False restores
the shipped path exactly: egui on the LDR image, one blit to the surface.

THIS DECIDES WHETHER THE CHROME IS POST-PROCESSED, so it is a declaration a
host makes about itself and not a fact a widget discovers.

It used to be written by `playbar::game_view` as a side effect of that
panel drawing, which made "is the toolbar barrel-distorted" a consequence
of which tab happened to be in front. With a fixed layout the panel drew
every frame and the coupling never showed; with a dock it is one closed tab
away from the entire window going through the CRT shader.

A host that embeds the game now says so once, at startup, through
`set_game_view_embedded`. The panel still publishes its RECT every frame,
because that genuinely is a layout fact and it changes as panels move.

items.name: set_game_view_embedded
items.doc:
Declare whether this host presents the game inside a panel.

Call it once, when the application is built. See the static above for why
this is a host's declaration rather than a widget's side effect.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_FOCUSED
items.doc:
True while the Game panel is the panel this window's keys are aimed at.

The rect above answers where the POINTER is; a key has no position, so it
needs the other question — which panel is being worked in. The two are
separate on purpose: a cursor resting over the toolbar must not deafen the
game to the movement keys, and a click in the code editor must silence its
hotkeys even if the cursor then drifts back over the game.

Without it both egui contexts saw every key press, and one Command-plus
zoomed the editor's panel AND rescaled the game's HUD — two effects from a
keystroke that named one.

A host publishes it each frame, from whatever it already uses to decide
where a shortcut goes; the engine cannot work it out, because a panel is
not a thing the engine has. Never written under a game with no editor, so
it stays at the default and the gate never runs.

items.name: set_game_view_focused
items.doc:
Say whether the Game panel is what a key press means right now.

Once a frame, before the GUI pass. A host that stops calling it leaves the
game deaf, which is the safe direction to fail: keys land in the chrome.

items.name: game_view_focused
items.doc:
Whether a key press belongs to the game this frame. Outside embedded mode
nobody asks: the game is the window, and `gate_keys_to_game_view` returns
before it reads this.

items.name: game_focus_vote
items.sig: pub fn game_focus_vote(vp: ViewportId, holds: Option<ViewportId>) -> bool
items.doc:
Whether window `vp` is the one entitled to answer for the flag above.

── ONE WINDOW GETS A VOTE, AND EVERY WINDOW MUST BE ABLE TO CAST IT ────
The flag is one global and the host calls it once per window per frame, so
the windows that do not hold the panel must say nothing — or the last one
drawn decides whether the game hears anything, and draw order is not a
thing a person controls.

`holds` is the window the Game panel is laid out in, which the dock knows.
`None` is a shut panel, and then the primary window answers: without that
arm the last `true` would stand, and the game would keep swallowing keys
with no panel on screen.

A pure rule rather than a branch inside the host, because the host's own
frame method returns early for every window except the primary one. The
vote lived below that return, so a panel in a tool window was voted on by
nobody and the flag held its tear-off value for the life of the process:
permanently deaf, or permanently deaf to the chrome instead.

items.name: publish_game_focus
items.sig: pub fn publish_game_focus(vp: ViewportId, holds: Option<ViewportId>, has_keys: bool)
items.doc:
Cast this window's vote, and store it when the window is the one entitled.

The pair above, in the order a host wants them. Every window calls it every
frame with its own id.

items.name: game_keys_from
items.doc:
Whether a key event that came from window `vp` belongs to the game.

── THE FLAG ANSWERS FOR A PANEL, AND A PANEL IS IN ONE WINDOW ──────────
`game_view_focused` says the Game panel holds the keyboard. It does not say
WHERE, because it is one process-global with no window on it. A consumer
that reads it alone therefore takes keys from EVERY window at once, and the
window the panel is not in is exactly the window a person types the editor's
own text into.

Both halves together are the rule: the panel holds the keyboard, AND this is
the window it draws in. `game_view_host` is the second half, published by the
panel's own draw and cleared when the panel stops drawing.

True unconditionally outside embedded mode. A shipped game has no panel and
no host to publish one, so the flag stays at its default — and a gate that
read it there would make every shipped game deaf for the life of the process.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_TEXTURE
items.sig: pub static GAME_VIEW_TEXTURE: Mutex<Vec<(ViewportId, egui::TextureId)>> = Mutex::new(Vec::new())
items.doc:
egui texture id of the finished game image, PER WINDOW.

One wgpu texture, registered separately in every window's egui renderer.
A `TextureId` is an index into the renderer that issued it and means
nothing to another one — so a single id was the whole reason the Game
panel could not leave the primary window. The texture itself crosses
freely: every window in this process shares one `wgpu::Device`.

A Vec and not a map: the count is the number of open windows, which is
ones, and `Vec::new` is const so the static needs no lazy init.

Empty until the first frame of embedded mode, and missing an entry for any
window that has not registered yet — so a panel must handle the absence
rather than unwrap.

items.name: game_view_texture
items.doc: What this window's egui calls the game image, if it has registered it.

items.name: set_game_view_texture
items.sig: pub fn set_game_view_texture(vp: ViewportId, tex: Option<egui::TextureId>)
items.doc:
Record what one window's egui calls the game image, or forget it.

`None` is what a window closing says, and what a texture REBUILD says for
every window that has not re-registered yet — a stale id outlives the
texture it named and would sample freed memory.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_TEXTURE_NEAREST
items.sig: pub static GAME_VIEW_TEXTURE_NEAREST: Mutex<Vec<(ViewportId, egui::TextureId)>> = Mutex::new(Vec::new())
items.doc:
The SAME game image, named a second time with a NEAREST sampler.

One texture, two names. `GAME_VIEW_TEXTURE` above is registered with a
linear filter, which is right for the Game panel: that rect almost never
matches the texture size, and a nearest filter would alias the whole
picture while the panel moves.

A MAGNIFIED draw wants the opposite. The CRT pass writes the phosphor cells
into this texture, and a linear sampler blends neighbouring cells into a
grey smear as soon as one output pixel covers less than one texel. So the
preview box in the CRT panel draws through this id instead, and sees the
cells the shader wrote.

items.name: game_view_texture_nearest
items.doc: What this window's egui calls the nearest-sampled game image.

items.name: set_game_view_texture_nearest
items.sig: pub fn set_game_view_texture_nearest(vp: ViewportId, tex: Option<egui::TextureId>)
items.doc:
Record what one window's egui calls the nearest-sampled game image, or
forget it. The mirror of `set_game_view_texture`, and `None` means the same
two things: a window closing, and a texture rebuild that no window has
re-registered against yet.

items.name: note_game_view_nearest_window
items.doc: Say which window is about to draw. Called by `register_nearest_in`.

items.name: take_game_view_texture_nearest
items.doc:
The nearest-sampled id THIS window may draw, once.

It CLEARS the marker, and that is the safety property rather than a
micro-optimisation. A window that never calls `register_nearest_in` leaves
the marker pointing at some earlier window, and an id from another
renderer is either absent there — egui-wgpu skips the mesh — or is a
different texture entirely, which draws the wrong picture with nothing
reporting it. Consuming the marker turns that case into no picture, which
the caller already draws a placeholder for.

items.name: GameViewRect
items.doc:
Where the host drew the game image last frame, and how large that image
is.

Every field is in the RENDER space OF `viewport`, not window space. egui
lays out at that window's `render_size`, and the engine already scales
pointer events from window pixels into that space before anything here
runs. So a panel rect read from egui and a remapped pointer are the same
space, and this type never needs the window size.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_RECT
items.doc:
The rect published by the host during the GUI closure. The pointer remap
reads it. None while the game fills the window.

ONE rect, for however many windows there are, and that is not an
approximation: the dock guarantees a `PanelId` names one leaf across every
window, so there is one Game panel and it publishes from one window. The
`viewport` field says which. Were two panels able to exist, both would
write here every frame and the last one drawn would own the pointer.

items.name: game_view_host
items.doc:
Which window the Game panel drew in last frame, if it drew.

The engine's answer to "where is the game", for the input path: the window
whose pointer and keys the game is entitled to. None while the panel is
closed, while the transport is Stopped, and on the first frame of embedded
mode before anything has been published.

items.name: game_view_embedded
items.doc: True while the game runs inside a panel and the rect is known.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_TICK
items.doc:
RENDERED FRAMES since start, bumped by the host inside its frame gate.

Frames and not event-loop turns, and the difference is the whole value of
the counter. Under `ControlFlow::Poll` the loop turns about 110,000 times a
second and renders 60 — count turns and the "one tick of grace" below spans
a sixty-thousandth of the gap it was written to span.

items.name: GAME_VIEW_SEEN
items.doc: The tick the panel last published a rect on.

items.name: tick_game_view
items.doc:
Open a frame. Called once per event-loop turn by the host that owns the
window, which is the only place that knows where a frame begins.

In `run` only. A satellite is another process with its own copy of these
statics and no Game panel to publish into them.

items.name: mark_game_view_drawn
items.doc: Stamp the rect as drawn on this tick. Called by the panel as it publishes.

items.name: game_view_rect
items.doc:
The published rect, copied out — if the panel still draws it. The lock is
released before the caller sees the value, so a caller can lock something
else without a deadlock.

── A RECT IS ONLY TRUE WHILE THE PANEL IS DRAWING IT ───────────────────
The rect is published as a side effect of `playbar::game_view`, so it is
written only on frames the panel actually draws. Under a fixed layout that
was every frame and the static could be read at face value. Under a dock
it is not: Code, Strudel and Sauron are tabs of the Game panel's own leaf,
so selecting one leaves the panel undrawn — and the last rect standing,
naming the very screen area that tab now covers.

What that cost was the POINTER. `game_view_contains_in` answered true for
a point over the Code panel, `gui`'s cursor arbiter read that as "the game
owns this pointer" and let the game's `CursorIcon::None` through, and
egui-winit's per-State icon cache meant the chrome never asked for the
cursor back. Hovering the Code panel made the mouse vanish.

So a rect expires. One tick of grace, because events for frame N+1 are
read BEFORE that frame redraws and republishes: expiring at zero would
blank the rect for every event between two frames, which is where the
clicks are. Two ticks without a draw is a panel that has stopped.

Clearing at the top of each frame instead would be simpler and wrong: with
the panel torn off into its own window, each window walks its own dock, so
whichever walked second would wipe a rect the first had just published.
A stamp does not care what order the windows draw in.

items.name: game_view_remap
items.sig: pub fn game_view_remap(px: f32, py: f32) -> (f32, f32)
items.doc:
Panel-rect pixels to game-image pixels, both in render space. Outside
embedded mode, and before the host publishes a rect, this is the identity
— so every call site is safe to convert unconditionally.

The game keeps believing the screen is the image it renders, which is what
Unity does: in play mode `Screen.width` reports the Game view, not the
monitor. That already holds here, because the game is told the screen is
`render_size` and the game view texture is `render_size`. Only the pointer
moves, so no picking or camera path changes.

For the GAME's own mouse code, which has a pointer and no notion of a
window. It does not need one: the pointer it is handed comes from whatever
window is showing the Game panel, because that is the only window whose
events reach the game at all. So this resolves the host itself.

items.name: game_view_contains
items.sig: pub fn game_view_contains(px: f32, py: f32) -> bool
items.doc:
True when the game's pointer lies inside the published rect. Outside
embedded mode every point is inside, because the game fills the window.

items.name: game_view_remap_in
items.sig: pub fn game_view_remap_in(vp: ViewportId, px: f32, py: f32) -> (f32, f32)
items.doc:
The same remap, for a caller that knows which window its point came from.

A point from any window OTHER than the one the panel drew in passes through
unchanged, because there is no rect for it to be inside: the panel is not
there. Answering anyway is the failure this argument exists to prevent —
the maths is affine and returns a plausible coordinate for a click three
windows away, with nothing to report.

warp_core's own input path uses this and never the pair above: a
`GuiHandler` always knows whose events it is reading, and a handler that
guessed would be the bug this exists to make unrepresentable.

items.name: game_view_contains_in
items.sig: pub fn game_view_contains_in(vp: ViewportId, px: f32, py: f32) -> bool
items.doc:
True when a point from window `vp` lies inside the published rect.

False for every point of a window the panel is not in — see the remap
above for why that is a test and not an oversight.

False as well while a Peek panel is placing its scope. A click that places
a scope must not also reach the game, or arming the tool fires whatever the
game does on click. This is the one function that decides whether a point
belongs to the game, so the one condition here covers every pointer path.

The keyboard already had a gate of the same shape: `publish_game_focus`
stops the chrome and the game both taking one key. The pointer had no
equivalent until the placement gesture needed one.

items.name: View
width
items.doc:
The render width in pixels: the low 16 bits of `xy`.

```ignore
let w = view.width();
```

items.name: height
items.doc:
The render height in pixels: the high 16 bits of `xy`.

```ignore
let h = view.height();
```

items.name: pack_xy
items.sig: pub fn pack_xy(width: u32, height: u32) -> u32
items.doc:
Pack a render size into the `xy` word. Each value keeps its low 16 bits.

```ignore
view.xy = View::pack_xy(1280, 720);
```

items.name: RECT_FLAG_RECEIVE_SHADOW
items.doc:
Receive the station shadow coverage. A rect with this bit reads the coverage
buffer at its screen position and darkens by it. The rect shader binds the
coverage buffer at group 1, and the flag gates the read, so a rect without
the bit reads nothing and does not darken. It is the rect analogue of
`IMAGE_FLAG_RECEIVE_SHADOW`, in the rect flags word rather than the image
one. The application sets it on procedural furniture that stands on a floor,
like the planter box, and leaves it clear on floors and world-space marks.

items.name: PlayState
items.doc: What the transport says the simulation should be doing.

items.name: EDITOR_PLAY_STATE
items.sig: pub static EDITOR_PLAY_STATE: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU8 = std::sync::atomic::AtomicU8::new(PlayState::Stopped as u8)
items.doc: The transport state. Stopped until a play bar, or the host, sets it.

items.name: EDITOR_STEP_ONCE
items.doc:
Set by Step. The sim loop runs exactly one pass while paused, then clears
it, which is what `EditorApplication.Step()` does.

items.name: EDITOR_TRANSPORT_ACTIVE
items.doc:
True once the host has handed the transport to a play bar. While false the
sim loop ignores every field above, so a game with no editor shell runs the
shipped path untouched.

items.name: EDITOR_PLAY_DEBUG
items.doc:
Which configuration the next boot uses. Set by the debug-play button,
cleared by Stop and by a plain Play.

WHY THE ENGINE HOLDS A FLAG IT CANNOT ACT ON
--------------------------------------------
warp_core has no idea what a debug configuration IS for any given game.
For this one it is a hardware tier, a seed, a fixed dt, a skipped tutorial
and eight console commands — none of which are engine concepts, and all of
which the launch script has been passing as argv to a fresh process.

The hosted game has no argv. It is compiled into the editor, so
`std::env::args()` there belongs to the editor and the game's own flag
parsing never sees a `--debug`. That is the whole reason this is a global
rather than a parameter: it is the seam the argv used to come through.

So the bar writes it and the game reads it at the moment it builds a
world — the same contract as the three fields above, which the bar writes
and the sim loop reads. The engine stays ignorant of what it means.

WHAT IT CANNOT REACH
--------------------
`./run.sh --debug` also adds `--features sauron_panel` to the build. That
is a compile-time feature of the binary the editor is ITSELF part of, so
no runtime flag can turn it on. The hosted debug boot gets the scenario
and the dev flags; it does not get the sauron pane. The launch button in
its own window is still the one that does.

items.name: play_debug
items.doc:
True when the world the transport is asking for is the debug one.

Read this where the game builds a world, not once at startup. The answer
changes between a Stop and the next Play, which is the point: a person
switches configuration by pressing a different button, not by relaunching.

items.name: set_play_debug
items.doc:
Choose the configuration the next boot uses.

The play bar calls this before it sets Playing, and clears it on Stop.

items.name: transport_active
items.doc: True while a play bar owns the transport.

items.name: set_transport_active
items.doc: Hand the transport to a play bar, or give it back to the game.

items.name: request_step
items.doc: Ask for one step. Ignored unless the transport is Paused.

items.name: take_step_request
items.doc: Consume a pending step request. True means run one pass now.

items.name: step_pending
items.doc:
Is a step waiting to be run? Does NOT consume it.

`take_step_request` is owned by the sim loop and there can only be one
consumer: two swaps against one flag means whichever thread wins runs the
pass and the other silently loses the request. So a second reader gets a
peek instead.

It exists for a thread that has a stake in a step it does not own. The sim
loop owns the consuming `take_step_request`; two swaps against one flag
would mean a step one reader saw was a step the sim never ran, so any other
reader gets this peek instead.

NO CALLER TODAY, and the reason is worth recording. The render thread used
to read it: an editor pause parked a viewport selection, and the thing that
let a parked one land was time moving. Selection is no longer gated on the
transport, so nothing asks. The peek is kept because the shape of the
problem has not gone away — a step is invisible in `play_state`, which
reports Paused throughout one.

items.name: take_play_state_change
items.doc:
Report the transport state once per change, and nothing in between.

A host that maps the transport onto its own state — a render phase, a
camera, a scene — must write that state only when the transport moves.
Writing it every frame overwrites whatever the application did in the
meantime, and the application then cannot leave the state the host keeps
re-asserting.

The first call returns None and records the current state, so a host that
starts up does not disturb an application still working through its own
boot sequence.

items.name: post_store_get
items.doc:
A copy of the newest post fields. Callable from any thread, and from inside
`Renderer::gui`.

items.name: post_store_update
items.sig: pub fn post_store_update(f: impl FnOnce(&mut DisplaySettings)) -> u64
items.doc:
Change the post fields, and return the new revision. The frame applies the
change to the global at its next `sync_post_store`.

The store is locked while `f` runs. `f` must not call `post_store_get` or
`post_store_update`, or the thread hangs.

items.name: post_store_revision
items.doc:
How many `post_store_update` calls the process has made. A change in this
number tells a reader that the post fields changed.

items.name: sync_post_store
items.doc:
Step 2 of the frame order in the module header. Returns true when it wrote
the store into `display`.

items.name: DisplayWindow
items.doc: How the primary window covers the screen.

items.name: DisplayMode
items.doc:
The display state a game asks for. All fields apply together, at the
next frame.

items.name: DEFAULT
items.doc:
The state of a window that `run` opened with no change: windowed, no
vsync (the engine picks Mailbox), the manifest frame cap.

items.name: MonitorInfo
items.doc: One monitor, as winit reports it.

items.name: display_store_get
items.doc:
A copy of the newest display mode. Callable from any thread, and from
inside `Renderer::gui`.

items.name: display_store_update
items.sig: pub fn display_store_update(f: impl FnOnce(&mut DisplayMode)) -> u64
items.doc:
Change the display mode, and return the new revision. The primary
viewport applies it at its next frame.

The store is locked while `f` runs. `f` must not call another
`display_store_*` function, or the thread hangs.

items.name: display_store_revision
items.doc: How many `display_store_update` calls the process has made.

items.name: sync_display_store
items.doc:
Step 2 of the frame order. Gives the display mode once for each new
revision. With no new revision, copies `fullscreen` (the real window
state) into the window field and gives `None`.

`fullscreen` is `None` while a window mode request waits in
`WINDOW_MODE_REQUESTED`. The event loop has not applied it, so
`FULLSCREEN_STATE` is old, and the window field stays as the game set it.

items.name: take_display_vsync_pending
items.doc: The vsync value that the next frame must apply to the surface, once.

items.name: display_store_exclusive_size
items.doc:
The exclusive video mode size the game asked for, when the window field
is `ExclusiveFullscreen`. The event loop tries it before the desktop size.

items.name: display_store_set_present_modes
items.doc:
Record the present modes of the primary surface. The viewport build
calls it with the surface capabilities.

items.name: display_store_present_modes
items.doc: The present modes of the primary surface. Empty before the first build.

items.name: pick_present_mode
items.sig: pub fn pick_present_mode(vsync: bool, supported: &[wgpu::PresentMode]) -> wgpu::PresentMode
items.doc:
Pick a present mode from `supported`.

Vsync on: Fifo. Vsync off: Mailbox (no tear, no wait), else Immediate
(tears), else Fifo. A list with none of the three gives its first entry.
An empty list gives Fifo, which wgpu makes all surfaces support.

items.name: frame_cap_budget_us
items.doc:
The frame budget in microseconds for a cap in hertz. `None` for no cap
(`None` or `Some(0)`).

items.name: display_store_note_manifest_cap
items.doc:
The budget to put back when the game sets `frame_cap` to `None`.
`current_us` is the engine budget now. The first call keeps it.

items.name: display_store_set_monitors
items.doc: Replace the monitor list. The frame calls it on the main thread.

items.name: display_store_monitors_stale
items.doc:
True when the frame must read the monitors again: at start, and after
each applied display mode.

items.name: display_store_mark_monitors_stale
items.doc: Mark the monitor list old, so the next frame reads it again.

items.name: display_store_monitors
items.doc: A copy of the monitor list. Empty before the first frame.

items.name: unique_resolutions
items.sig: pub fn unique_resolutions(mut sizes: Vec<[u32; 2]>) -> Vec<[u32; 2]>
items.doc:
Sort and remove the duplicates of a list of video mode sizes, largest
area first.

items.name: GUI_ATLAS_TEXTURES
items.sig: pub static GUI_ATLAS_TEXTURES: std::sync::Mutex<Vec<(String, egui::TextureId)>> = std::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new())
items.doc:
Atlas texture IDs registered with egui for glossary sprite rendering.
Populated by Viewport::register_atlas_textures_for_gui after asset load.
Vec of (key, TextureId) pairs. Keys: "res:{resource_kind}", "str:{type_index}".

items.name: PlanetPreviewRequest
items.doc:
One frame's request to render a live planet preview into the offscreen
PlanetPreview texture. Written by the planet selection panel every frame it
is shown (during the GUI closure, viewport.rs ~line 359), and consumed by
the primary viewport the SAME frame, before the GUI is drawn — so the
preview shows the currently-selected planet with no latency.

items.name: PLANET_PREVIEW_TEXTURE
items.doc:
egui texture id of the offscreen planet preview, published once the primary
viewport has created + registered it. The panel reads this to draw the live
square; None until the first primary-viewport frame.

items.name: RawKey
items.doc: A physical key, as winit reports it.

items.name: RAW_KEY_WATCH
items.sig: pub static RAW_KEY_WATCH: LazyLock<Mutex<Vec<(&'static str, Vec<RawKey>)>>> = LazyLock::new(|| Mutex::new(Vec::new()))
items.doc:
The keys the app wants on the focus-immune path, one slot per subsystem
that asked. Empty by default, so an app that installs no list gets no ring
entries at all.

egui consumes a key event whenever any TextEdit holds keyboard focus, and
WinitInputHelper then never sees that key. A console whose own text field
has focus therefore goes deaf to the key that closes it. The event loop
mirrors every watched press into RAW_KEY_PRESSES from the raw WindowEvent
arm, before egui gets the event, so one path always survives focus.

The watch list exists to bound the ring. Mirroring every press would let
held movement keys and OS key repeat evict a real press within seconds.

ONE LIST, SEVERAL OWNERS
------------------------
This was a single Vec that every caller replaced wholesale, and a process
with two subsystems on the ring silently lost one of them. The editor
hosting the game is exactly that process: the game registers its bound keys
before the window opens, and the code panel then registered its three
punctuation keys from `Renderer::new` — which ran later and cleared the
game's. The backtick was no longer mirrored, so the debug console, whose
toggle reads only this ring, could not be opened at all.

The rule the old shape needed — "a host that needs its own keys registers
them together with the others" — cannot be honoured across a crate
boundary, because neither crate can name the other's keys. So the list is
keyed by owner and the effective watch is the union: a subsystem replaces
only its own slot, and no registration can delete somebody else's key.

items.name: RAW_WATCH_APP
items.doc: The slot `set_raw_key_watch` writes: the application's own keys.

items.name: RAW_KEY_PRESSES
items.sig: pub static RAW_KEY_PRESSES: LazyLock<Mutex<VecDeque<RawKey>>> = LazyLock::new(|| Mutex::new(VecDeque::new()))
items.doc:
Pending watched presses, oldest first. A full ring drops its oldest entry,
so the newest press always lands. std Mutex on purpose — warp_core has no
parking_lot dependency.

items.name: RAW_KEY_RING_LIMIT
items.doc: How many pending presses the ring holds.

items.name: watch_raw_keys
items.doc:
Declare which keys one subsystem needs on the focus-immune path.

Replaces that owner's earlier list and touches nobody else's, so this is
also how a subsystem follows a rebind: call it again with the new keys.
`owner` is a stable name for the caller, never shown to a person.

items.name: set_raw_key_watch
items.doc:
Declare the application's own keys. The `RAW_WATCH_APP` slot of
`watch_raw_keys`, kept because it is what every host already calls.

items.name: raw_key_watched
items.doc: True if any subsystem watches this key.

items.name: push_raw_key
items.doc:
Record a press. Ignores keys outside the watch list.

The ungated form, for a host with no panels: a shipped game, and the wasm
event loop. An editor hosting a game calls `push_raw_key_from` instead.

items.name: push_raw_key_from
items.sig: pub fn push_raw_key_from(vp: ViewportId, key: RawKey)
items.doc:
Record a press that came from window `vp`, if that window may make it.

── THE RING IS FOCUS-IMMUNE, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS PANEL-IMMUNE ─────
The ring exists to survive EGUI focus: egui swallows a key whenever any
TextEdit holds it, so a console whose own field has focus could not be
closed. That is a fact about one widget and the ring is right to ignore it.

It is not a licence to ignore which PANEL is being worked in. The app slot
is not the two keys the ring was built for — `refresh_raw_watch` in the game
registers every key its whole action catalog is bound to, and re-registers
them after a rebind. So a ring written from every key press meant that
typing into Sauron, the terminal or the code editor fired game actions, on a
path none of the other three gates could see.

The app slot alone is gated, and the union rule is what makes that possible:
the code panel's own three punctuation keys live in a different slot and are
unaffected, so this cannot make the editor's own keys depend on where the
game is. A key both slots want is admitted for the code panel's sake, which
is the safe direction — the editor's key is the one a person is looking at.

items.name: take_raw_key
items.doc:
Remove every pending press of one key, and report whether the ring held
one. This is the drain for a single meaning, such as pause or a console
toggle. Repeated presses of the same key inside one frame collapse to a
single true, which is what the atomic flags this replaced also did.

items.name: drain_raw_keys
items.doc: Take every pending press, oldest first.

items.name: clear_raw_keys
items.doc: Drop every pending press. A screen that must swallow keys calls this.

items.name: RENDER_DRAW_US
items.doc: CPU draw time (renderer.render call), microseconds.

items.name: RENDER_UPLOAD_US
items.doc: GPU buffer upload time (state.set_* calls), microseconds.

items.name: RENDER_GPU_US
items.doc: GPU render + postprocess + egui + present time, microseconds.

items.name: RENDER_FRAME_US
items.doc: Total render frame time (draw + upload + GPU), microseconds.

items.name: GPU_DESCRIPTION
items.doc:
The adapter and the primary surface configuration, as `key value` lines.
Written once by `create_device_and_surface`. Empty until the device exists.

items.name: WINDOW_PHYS_W
items.doc: The primary window in physical pixels, written by each primary frame.

items.name: WINDOW_PHYS_H
items.doc: See `WINDOW_PHYS_W`.

items.name: WINDOW_SCALE_BITS
items.doc: The primary window's OS scale factor, as `f32::to_bits`.

items.name: SURFACE_W
items.doc: The primary surface configuration size in pixels.

items.name: SURFACE_H
items.doc: See `SURFACE_W`.

items.name: ViewportId
items.doc:
Unique identifier for a render viewport.

Each viewport corresponds to one OS window with its own wgpu surface,
postprocess chain, egui context, and camera state. The simulation
thread is shared — all viewports read the same frame's entity data.

items.name: PRIMARY_VIEWPORT
items.doc: The main game window. Always exists. Created first during startup.

items.name: SECONDARY_VIEWPORT_REQUESTED
items.doc:
Flag for secondary viewport lifecycle.

Set to `true` by game GUI to request opening a secondary window.
Set to `false` to request closing it. The event loop in lib.rs
polls this each frame during MainEventsCleared.

items.name: alloc_viewport_id
items.doc:
Name a window that does not exist yet.

The application allocates the id, then asks the engine to open a window
carrying it. The alternative — the engine allocating on creation and the
application learning the id a frame later — cannot work for tear-off: the
dock has to put the panel into its new window on the frame the drop
happens, and a window it cannot name yet is a window it cannot fill.

Ids are never reused. A closed window's id stays spent, so a stale one
names nothing rather than naming somebody else's window.

items.name: WindowRequest
items.doc:
One thing the application wants the event loop to do to a window.

A queue rather than a flag, because tear-off can produce two of these in
one frame — a window opens as another empties and closes — and a flag can
only carry the last one.

items.name: WINDOW_REQUESTS
items.doc: Requests waiting for the event loop. Drained once per frame.

items.name: request_window
items.doc: Ask the event loop for something. Applied at the next MainEventsCleared.

items.name: drain_window_requests
items.doc: Take everything queued. Called by the event loop and by nothing else.

items.name: WindowGeometry
items.doc:
Where one window is on the desktop, in physical pixels.

TWO SPACES, AND THE FACTOR BETWEEN THEM
---------------------------------------
`origin` and `size` are desktop pixels. A window's own egui counts in
POINTS, and for one window kind those are not the same length: a Viewport
lays the chrome out at a fixed internal resolution and blits up to the
window, so one of its points is `pixels_per_point` desktop pixels. A
ToolWindow lays out at its own surface size, where the factor is one.

The dock aims across windows in desktop pixels, so every conversion goes
through `to_desktop` and `to_local` here. They used to be a bare add and
subtract of `origin`, which is correct only while the factor is one. On a
primary window smaller than its render floor the factor is about 0.75, and
every drop target, tear-off position and follower chip landed up to a third
of the window away from the pointer. The error changed with the window's
size, so it changed when the window moved to another monitor.

items.name: rect
items.doc: The window's client area as a screen-space rect.

items.name: to_desktop
items.sig: pub fn to_desktop(&self, p: egui::Pos2) -> egui::Pos2
items.doc: A position this window's egui painted at, on the desktop.

items.name: to_local
items.sig: pub fn to_local(&self, p: egui::Pos2) -> egui::Pos2
items.doc: A desktop position, in the coordinates this window paints in.

items.name: to_desktop_size
items.sig: pub fn to_desktop_size(&self, v: egui::Vec2) -> egui::Vec2
items.doc: A length this window's egui measured, as a desktop length.

items.name: to_desktop_rect
items.sig: pub fn to_desktop_rect(&self, r: egui::Rect) -> egui::Rect
items.doc: A rect this window's egui painted, on the desktop.

items.name: to_local_rect
items.sig: pub fn to_local_rect(&self, r: egui::Rect) -> egui::Rect
items.doc: A desktop rect, in the coordinates this window paints in.

items.name: WINDOW_GEOMETRY
items.sig: pub static WINDOW_GEOMETRY: Mutex<Vec<(ViewportId, WindowGeometry)>> = Mutex::new(Vec::new())
items.doc:
Every live window's position and size, republished each frame.

This is what makes a drag between windows possible. The pointer belongs to
whichever window the OS is routing motion to, and every OTHER window has to
decide whether that pointer is over one of its panels — which needs its own
position on the desktop, not just inside its own client area. egui knows
nothing about where its window sits, so the engine publishes it.

Keyed by ViewportId. The primary window is in here too.

items.name: set_window_geometry
items.doc: Replace the published geometry. Called by the event loop each frame.

items.name: window_geometry
items.doc: Where one window is, if it is open.

items.name: all_window_geometry
items.doc: Every live window's geometry.

items.name: to_desktop
items.sig: pub fn to_desktop(vp: ViewportId, p: egui::Pos2) -> egui::Pos2
items.doc:
A position `vp`'s egui painted at, on the desktop.

The identity for a window the engine has not published yet, which is the
one frame between asking for a window and having it. Cross-window aim is
wrong for that frame and nothing else is.

items.name: to_local
items.sig: pub fn to_local(vp: ViewportId, p: egui::Pos2) -> egui::Pos2
items.doc: A desktop position, in the coordinates `vp` paints in.

items.name: to_desktop_size
items.sig: pub fn to_desktop_size(vp: ViewportId, v: egui::Vec2) -> egui::Vec2
items.doc: A length `vp`'s egui measured, as a desktop length.

items.name: WINDOW_CLOSED
items.doc:
Windows the OS closed, waiting for the application to notice.

A tool window can go away without the application asking: someone presses
the red button. The dock still holds that window's tree, so it has to hear
about it or the panels inside stay "open" with nowhere to be drawn.

items.name: push_window_closed
items.doc: Record that a window went away. Called by the event loop.

items.name: drain_window_closed
items.doc: Take the list of windows that closed since the last call.

items.name: PANEL_CLOSED
items.doc:
Panel kinds the user closed, waiting for the frame loop to release them.

The dock knows which panel a person closed, but holds no renderer. A tool's
egui `TextureId` lives in a renderer the frame loop owns. This is the bridge:
the dock records the closed kind here, and the primary frame drains it and
calls `window::disable`, the same shape as `WINDOW_CLOSED` above.

items.name: push_panel_closed
items.doc: Record that a panel kind was closed. Called by the dock's close path.

items.name: drain_panel_closed
items.doc: Take the panel kinds closed since the last call.

items.name: NewWindowPreview
items.doc: The window a drop would create, if it happened where the pointer is.

items.name: DragProxyState
items.doc: What the follower window should say, and where it should be.

items.name: DRAG_PROXY
items.doc: The follower window's wanted state, or None while nothing is in flight.

items.name: set_drag_proxy
items.doc:
Ask for the follower, or dismiss it. Called every frame by whatever owns
the drag; the event loop reads it and does not clear it.

items.name: drag_proxy
items.doc: What the follower should be showing right now.

items.name: FULLSCREEN_TOGGLE_REQUESTED
items.doc:
One-shot signal: Display tab sets true, event loop swaps to false and
toggles window.set_fullscreen(). Same pattern as SECONDARY_VIEWPORT_REQUESTED.

items.name: FULLSCREEN_STATE
items.doc:
Tracks current fullscreen state for GUI readback. Seeded from Config at
launch, updated by event loop when toggle completes.

items.name: WINDOW_MODE_REQUESTED
items.doc:
One-shot display-mode request. The event loop reads it, applies the winit
mode, and stores 255 back. This mirrors FULLSCREEN_TOGGLE_REQUESTED, but a
value instead of a toggle carries three modes in one word.
0 = windowed
1 = borderless fullscreen
2 = exclusive fullscreen
255 = no request

items.name: WINDOW_SIZE_REQ_W
items.doc:
One-shot windowed-size request, in physical pixels. Both words nonzero
means a resize is wanted. The event loop applies set_inner_size and stores
0 back. This is standalone only: a hosted window follows its panel, so the
drain skips the request when the process is hosted.

items.name: KIND_PREFIX
items.doc:
What every registered window's id starts with.

The prefix is the whole of the editor's answer to "is this one of mine".
A host tests the prefix and then asks this module, which means the host
holds no list of registered ids and cannot fall out of date with one.

It is not `INSTANCE_SEP`'s separator. The dock cuts an id at ':' to find a
kind, so a registered window's full kind is `window.hello` and never
`window:hello` — the second would make every registered window an instance
of one kind called `window`.

items.name: Group
items.doc:
Where a window asks to be filed in the View menu.

The engine names no menu. These are the coarse kinds an editor can map onto
whatever groups it has, and `Tools` is the answer for a window that does
not care — which is most of them, and is what the editor already does with
a panel no group arm names.

items.name: title
items.doc: The group's name, for a host with no mapping of its own.

items.name: WindowSpec
items.doc:
Everything about a window that is not its body.

One value answers every question the fourteen host sites ask. A field added
here is a question the host can start asking without a new lookup.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(name: &str, title: impl Into<String>) -> Self
items.doc:
A window of this name and title, with every permission at its default.

`name` is bare. The prefix is added here so that no caller writes it,
and so that a caller who writes it anyway does not get it twice.

items.name: group
items.sig: pub fn group(mut self, group: Group) -> Self
items.doc: File it under this group in the View menu.

items.name: pinned
items.doc: Cannot be closed.

items.name: primary_only
items.doc: Cannot leave the primary window.

items.name: standalone
items.doc: Can become its own process.

items.name: undocked
items.doc: Keep it out of a reset layout. It stays reachable from the View menu.

items.name: source
items.sig: pub fn source(mut self, path: impl Into<PathBuf>) -> Self
items.doc: The file that declares this window.

items.name: summary
items.sig: pub fn summary(mut self, text: impl Into<String>) -> Self
items.doc: One line about what it is for.

items.name: name
items.doc: The name without the prefix, for a panel that lists windows by name.

items.name: WarpWindow
items.doc:
One window: what it is, and how it draws.

Two methods, and the first is a constant for almost every implementation.
That is the whole contract — an author who implements this and registers it
has a panel with a tab, a menu row, a place in the layout, and a tear-off
to a real window.

items.name: register
items.sig: pub fn register(window: Box<dyn WarpWindow>) -> Result<(), String>
items.doc:
Add a window. Call before `run`, from the application's `main`.

A second window of a name already registered REPLACES the first and says
so. Two windows of one id would give the dock a panel it could show twice
and close once, and silently keeping the first is the failure that takes
longest to see.

items.name: owns
items.doc:
Is this panel id one of ours?

The prefix and nothing else, so a host can ask before it has a spec and
without holding a list.

items.name: specs
items.doc: Every registered window's facts, in registration order.

items.name: spec_of
items.doc: One window's facts, by kind.

items.name: count
items.doc: How many windows are registered.

items.name: close_all
items.doc:
Tear down every registered window, in registration order.

The host calls this once at shutdown, so a registered tool reaps a port, a
child process, or a target the way the built-in panels do. It generalises
the editor's hand-written stop list: a tool the shell never names still gets
its `on_close`. A poisoned table is skipped, because a panic on the quit
path would strand the very resources this reaps.

items.name: register_disable
items.sig: pub fn register_disable( kind: impl Into<String>, f: impl Fn(&mut egui_wgpu::Renderer) + Send + 'static, ) -> Result<(), String>
items.doc:
Register the closure that releases a panel kind's reopenable resources.

A tool calls this once, before `run`. A second disabler for a kind already
registered REPLACES the first and returns `Err`, the same contract as
`register`, so a double registration is seen and not silent.

items.name: disable
items.sig: pub fn disable(kind: &str, gui: &mut egui_wgpu::Renderer) -> bool
items.doc:
Release a panel kind's reopenable resources. False when no kind matches.

The dock calls this on per-panel close, with the renderer it holds at close
time. A poisoned table is skipped, so a close gesture cannot panic. A
disabler must not call back into this registry, because the table stays
locked for the call, the same rule `close_all` keeps for `on_close`.

items.name: draw
items.sig: pub fn draw(kind: &str, ui: &mut egui::Ui) -> bool
items.doc:
Draw one window's body. False when no window has that kind.

`try_lock` and not `lock`: see the module header. A window that draws
itself from inside itself gets a line of text, not a frozen editor.

items.name: spec
items.doc:
Everything about this window that is not its body. Read every frame,
so a title may carry live state the way the Code panel's does.

items.name: ui
items.doc:
Draw the body. The `Ui` is already clipped to the panel's rect and
already inside the panel frame, so an implementation draws content and
nothing else.

items.name: on_close
items.doc:
Release what `Drop` never reaches. The host calls this once when it
tears the tool down, so a window that holds a port, a child process, a
pipeline, or a render target can reap it. The default does nothing,
because most windows own only what `Drop` already frees.

This is the registered-tool twin of the built-in panel stops the editor
runs at quit. A tool reached this way needs no editor code that names it.

items.name: apply
items.doc:
Install the palette on a context. Call once per frame, before drawing.

Outside every panel scope, so the chrome — menu bar, transport, tab strips
— is built at the chrome scale whatever any panel is zoomed to.

items.name: chrome_scale
items.doc:
The scale of the chrome: menu bars, tab strips, dividers, and every panel
that has not been zoomed on its own.

The person's setting, times the factor of the window being drawn. See
`window_factor` for what the second term corrects and why one number
cannot serve two monitors.

items.name: px
items.doc: Turn a design unit into a pixel count.

items.name: ui_scale
items.doc:
The scale in force right now: the chrome's, times the factor of whatever
panel is being drawn.

This is what `px()` reads, and outside a panel body it is `chrome_scale`.

items.name: zoom_keys
items.doc:
Read Command plus `+`, `-` and `0`, and set a scale from them.

Call this once per frame PER WINDOW, before that window's panels. Per
window and not once per process: each window owns an egui context, and a
key press only ever reaches the context of the window that has focus. A
call made in the primary window alone is a key that does nothing in every
torn-off one, which is exactly what it used to do.

The game does not call it: a zoom key inside a running game would resize
the HUD and nothing else, and the game has its own key map.

WHICH THING GROWS
-----------------
`panel` is the panel the window would send a keystroke to — see
`DockState::zoom_target`. It gets the plain keys, so Command and `-` inside
a terminal shrinks that terminal and leaves the window around it alone.
Shift takes the chrome instead, process-wide, which is what the key used to
do for everything.

Command is `command` in egui, which is Cmd on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere, so
the keys are the ones the platform browser already uses.

items.name: DEFAULT_UI_SCALE
items.doc:
Scale used until somebody sets one. Two matches a retina display, which is
what the lock costs the most.

items.name: MIN_UI_SCALE
items.doc: Smallest and largest scale a person may pick.

items.name: Material
items.doc:
A procedural material: game WGSL that returns a `MaterialSample`.

`wgsl` must define
`fn lit2d_material(uv: vec2<f32>, world: vec2<f32>, inst: Lit2dInstance) -> MaterialSample`.
`uv` is 0..1 across the sprite, y down. `world` is the world position.
The normal is in sprite space: +x is the sprite right, +y is the sprite
up, +z points to the camera. `wgsl` can hold more functions.

items.name: SpriteSheet
items.doc:
A textured material: RGBA8 images, all `width` x `height`.

`albedo` is sRGB colour and coverage. `normal` is a tangent-space normal
map, encoded `n * 0.5 + 0.5`. `surface` holds roughness (r), metallic (g),
height (b) and an emissive mask (a). A `None` map gets a neutral value:
a flat normal, roughness 0.8, metallic 0, height 0, no emission.

items.doc:

items.name: palette_distance
items.sig: pub fn palette_distance(p_bg: Rgb, p_ink: &[Rgb], q_bg: Rgb, q_ink: &[Rgb]) -> f32
items.doc:
How far apart two palettes look; 0 is the same colours. Each ink set is
sorted by OKLab L. With the same ink count, the inks pair up in that
order. Else each ink takes its nearest ink in the other set (both ways).
The paper counts as much as one ink pair.

The lowest WCAG contrast of the first `n` inks (ink k is ink[k % len])

items.name: harmony
items.sig: pub fn harmony(seed: Rgb, kind: Harmony, n: usize, dark: Option<bool>, rng: &mut Rng) -> Swatch
items.doc:
A palette from one seed colour, with `n` inks (2..5). `dark` sets the
paper; `None` chooses from the seed (a light seed gets dark paper). The
inks take the harmony hues at a spread of lightness. The first ink then
moves in lightness until its contrast on the paper is 3.2 or more.

items.doc: The taste rules a table palette breaks. Empty means it passes.

items.name: check_swatch
items.doc: The taste rules a swatch breaks. Empty means it passes.

items.name: suited

The palettes that suit a mood phrase: the palettes with the most tags
that the words of the phrase name. With no known word, every palette.

items.name: vary
items.sig: pub fn vary(p: &Palette, rng: &mut Rng) -> Swatch
items.doc:
A seeded change of a palette that keeps its character: a hue turn of up
to 12 degrees, a chroma scale of 0.9..1.1, and a new ink order (a first
ink with contrast 3 or more is preferred). A contrast repair of the
first ink follows. If the result breaks a taste rule, the inks keep
their table colours in the new order.

items.name: pick
items.sig: pub fn pick(mood: &str, seed: u64) -> Swatch
items.doc:
A distinct, tasteful swatch for a mood phrase (for example "ocean calm"
or "spooky neon") and a seed. The same phrase and seed always give the
same swatch. The pick favours palettes with a high contrast score.
[`vary`] then makes the colours of this seed its own.

The sixty-odd `crt_*` fields of the tube, kept as one block.

A game that wants to tune the tube reads and writes them by their
`DisplaySettings` names through [`CrtTuning::fields_mut`]. Only the
`crt_*` fields of that value are kept; `crt_enabled` is `Crt::enabled`.

The look of the boot splash. Build it, then call `install` before `run`.

```ignore
use warp_sdk::boot::{Layout, Progress, Splash, Status};
Splash::new("REEF")
.palette([4, 18, 28], [80, 220, 200], [220, 240, 240])
.layout(Layout::Centered)
.progress(Progress::Dots)
.status(Status::IconOnly)
.install();
warp_sdk::run::<MyGame>(config);
```

items.name: get
items.doc:
A copy of the newest display mode. Callable from any thread, and from
inside `Renderer::gui`.

```ignore
let vsync_on = warp_sdk::display_mode::get().vsync;
```

items.name: set
items.sig: pub fn set(f: impl FnOnce(&mut DisplayMode))
items.doc:
Change the display mode. The engine applies the change at its next frame.

The store is locked while `f` runs, so `f` must not call another function
of this module.

```ignore
warp_sdk::display_mode::set(|m| { m.window = WindowMode::Windowed; m.resolution = Some([1600, 900]); });
```

items.name: replace
items.doc:
Replace the display mode whole.

```ignore

```

items.name: revision
items.doc:
How many `set` and `replace` calls the process has made. A different
number since the last read means the display mode changed.

```ignore
let rev = warp_sdk::display_mode::revision();
```

items.name: monitors
items.doc:
All monitors. The engine reads them on the main thread at the first frame
and after each change. Empty before the first frame, and in a headless
test.

```ignore

```

items.name: resolutions
present_mode_for
items.sig: pub fn present_mode_for(vsync: bool, supported: &[crate::wgpu::PresentMode]) -> crate::wgpu::PresentMode
items.doc:
The present mode the engine uses for `vsync` on a surface that supports
`supported`. Vsync on is Fifo. Vsync off is Mailbox, else Immediate, else
a mode the surface has.

```ignore
use warp_sdk::wgpu::PresentMode as P;
assert_eq!(present_mode_for(false, &[P::Fifo, P::Immediate]), P::Immediate);
```

items.name: DisplayMode

The display state a game asks for. All fields apply together, at the
next frame.

items.name: DEFAULT

The state of a window that `run` opened with no change: windowed, no

items.name: Ocean
items.body:
/// The particle system. Add kinds and emitters to it directly.
pub particles: Particles,

items.name: new
items.doc:
An ocean with no terrain. It registers its two `perf` budgets.

```ignore
let ocean = Ocean::new(OceanConfig::new([-8.0, -4.5, 8.0, 4.5]));
```

items.name: with_terrain
items.sig: pub fn with_terrain(mut self, terrain: Terrain) -> Self
items.doc:
Give the ocean a terrain. Its SDF becomes the solver obstacle field
and the particle collision field.

```ignore
let ocean = Ocean::new(cfg).with_terrain(Terrain::generate(TerrainConfig::side(7)));
```

items.name: config
items.doc:
The config.

```ignore
let rect = ocean.config().world_rect;
```

items.name: terrain
items.doc:
The terrain, if any.

```ignore
if let Some(t) = ocean.terrain() { let solid = t.is_solid(p.into()); }
```

items.name: terrain_mut
items.sig: pub fn terrain_mut(&mut self) -> Option<&mut Terrain>
items.doc:
The terrain, to dig or fill. The next `step` bakes the changed
chunks, and the water and the particles see the change.

```ignore
if let Some(t) = ocean.terrain_mut() { t.dig(p.into(), 1.5); }
```

items.name: solver
items.doc:
The solver, after the first `step`. Use it for the velocity view, the
dye views and the stats.

```ignore
if let Some(s) = ocean.solver() { let v = s.velocity_view(); }
```

items.name: solver_error
items.doc:
The error from the solver creation, for example a device with no
compute. With an error the particles still run, with no water.

```ignore
if let Some(e) = ocean.solver_error() { eprintln!("{e}"); }
```

items.name: splat
items.sig: pub fn splat(&mut self, pos: [f32; 2], velocity: [f32; 2], radius: f32)
items.doc:
Push the water: add `velocity` around world point `pos`, with a
Gaussian of world `radius`. Call it each frame while a body moves.

```ignore
ocean.splat(sub.pos, sub.vel, 0.6);
```

items.name: splat_dye
items.sig: pub fn splat_dye(&mut self, channel: u32, pos: [f32; 2], amount: f32, radius: f32)
items.doc:
Add dye to one solver channel. The default config has no dye
channels; set `solver_config().dye_channels` to use dye.

```ignore
ocean.splat_dye(0, vent, 1.0, 0.3);
```

items.name: emit
items.sig: pub fn emit(&mut self, kind: KindId, pos: [f32; 2], count: u32, speed: f32)
items.doc:
Spray `count` particles of `kind` from `pos`, up to `speed`.

```ignore
ocean.emit(silt, hit_pos, 300, 0.5);
```

items.name: step
items.sig: pub fn step(&mut self, device: &Arc<wgpu::Device>, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, dt: f32)
items.doc:
Record one frame of simulation: bake the terrain, step the solver,
then step the particles in the new water. It draws nothing.

```ignore
ocean.step(&device, &queue, &mut encoder, dt);
```

items.name: draw
items.sig: pub fn draw( &mut self, device: &wgpu::Device, queue: &wgpu::Queue, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, target: &wgpu::TextureView, format: wgpu::TextureFormat, cam: Camera, )
items.doc:
Record the particle draw into `target`. Call `step` before.

```ignore
ocean.draw(&device, &queue, &mut encoder, &hdr_view, warp_sdk::gpu::HDR_FORMAT, Camera::from_view(view));
```

items.sig: pub fn encode( &mut self, shared: &SharedGpu, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder, hdr_view: &wgpu::TextureView, view: &crate::types::View, dt: f32, )
items.doc:
The one call for a game: `step`, then `draw` into the engine HDR
target with the camera of `view`. Call it from
`Renderer::scene_underlay`.

```ignore
self.ocean.encode(shared, encoder, hdr_view, view, self.dt);
```

items.name: over_budget
items.doc:
True when the solver GPU time is over its half of the budget.
Always false with no timestamps. A game then makes a new ocean
with a lower `quality`.

```ignore
if ocean.over_budget() { /* rebuild with Quality::Low */ }
```

items.name: OceanConfig
new
items.doc:
Medium water over `world_rect`, 100k particles, a GPU budget of
2 ms (1 ms solver, 1 ms particles) and a CPU budget of 0.5 ms.

```ignore
let cfg = OceanConfig::new([-8.0, -4.5, 8.0, 4.5]);
```

items.name: solver_config
items.doc:
The solver config that this ocean config makes. The solver gets
half of the GPU budget.

```ignore
let s = OceanConfig::new(rect).solver_config();
```

items.name: PERF_GPU
items.doc: The `perf` channel of the GPU time of the solver step.

items.name: PERF_CPU
items.doc: The `perf` channel of the CPU time that `encode` takes to record.

items.name: size_rect_to_bounds
texel_of
items.sig: pub fn texel_of(p: [f32; 2], bounds: [f32; 4], dims: [u32; 2]) -> Option<[u32; 2]>
items.doc:
The texel that contains world point `p` in a texture of `dims` texels
that covers `bounds` `[min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y]`. Row 0 is the min y
row. A point outside `bounds` gives `None`. The solver and the particle
shaders use the same mapping: `uv = (p - min) / (max - min)`.

```ignore
let t = texel_of([1.0, 2.0], [0.0, 0.0, 64.0, 32.0], [128, 64]); // Some([2, 4])
```

items.doc: The WGSL that both passes include. The update and draw shaders follow it.

items.name: compose_update_wgsl
compose_draw_wgsl
Fields
items.doc:
The two optional input fields of one step. Each is a texture view and
the world rect `[min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y]` that it covers.

`velocity`: Rgba16Float, `.xy` = world units per second. Outside its
rect the fluid is still.
`sdf`: R16Float or R32Float signed distance in world units, negative
inside solid. Outside its rect there is no solid.

```ignore
let f = Fields::none().velocity(&vel.view, vel.rect).sdf(&rock.view, rock.rect);
```

new

items.doc:

items.name: set_obstacles
items.sig: pub fn set_obstacles(&mut self, sdf: &wgpu::TextureView, sdf_rect: [f32; 4])
items.doc:
Use a signed distance texture as the obstacles. The texture is
R16Float or R32Float, in world units, NEGATIVE inside a solid. It
can have any resolution, and `sdf_rect` is its own world rect
[min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y]. Cells outside `sdf_rect` are open water.

The solver reads the texture again at each `step`, so a game can
draw moving obstacles into the same texture each frame. The
obstacles have free-slip walls: water slides along them but does
not go in.

```ignore

```

items.name: install
items.sig: pub fn install(ctx: &egui::Context, pair: &Pair) -> Result<(), FontError>
items.doc:
Registers the families "display", "text" and "mono" from the pair's
regular files, read at run time. See the module header for the search
order. A face that does not load gives a `FontError`, and its family uses
egui's stock fonts. The other two families still install.

egui applies new fonts from the NEXT frame. Do not draw with
`fonts::display`, `text` or `mono` in the frame that calls `install`:
the family is not bound yet and egui panics. Install once in `new` or
in the first `gui`, then return and draw from the next frame.

```ignore
if let Err(e) = fonts::install(ctx, &fonts::pair(Mood::Warm, 9)) {
eprintln!("{e}");
}
```

```ignore

fonts::use_in_style(ctx);
```

items.doc:
The reason for a cue. The standard kinds set the icon, the role colour
and the priority. `Custom` sets them yourself.

```ignore

```

items.name: action
items.doc:
The standard action of this kind. A `Custom` kind has one only when
its sym is a [`Sym::Action`].

Towed shows LowEnergy, the reason for the tow. Stunned and Damaged
show Danger: the standard makes them Warning, and its stun glyph is
a verb of the player (class Action), so a stun cue puts that glyph
first, as the cause.

```ignore
assert_eq!(Kind::Respawn.action(), Some(semiotics::Action::Respawn));
```

items.doc:

the role of the action class, so the colour and the icon frame agree.
A `Custom` kind with no action uses its cue role.

items.doc:
Consecutive frames below [`LEAVE_FRACTION`] of the budget before a

state does not flicker.

```

```

items.name: duration
Bus
items.doc:
The lanes the game plays into.

Holds only the controller half of each lane. The mixer half went to rodio
inside a `Tap` when the bus was built, and lives on the audio thread from
then on.

items.name: new
items.doc:
Build every lane and hand each one's tap to the output stream.

Every lane is registered in one pass, before any of them can carry
sound. rodio defers a pending source until its channel count divides
the samples it has produced, so lanes offered together are accepted
together and begin at one offset. Offering them at different times
would risk starting one a sample later than the other, and the scope
sums the lanes by index on the promise that this does not happen.

items.name: sink
items.sig: pub fn sink(&self, lane: Lane) -> Sink
items.doc:
A sink on one lane.

Replaces `Sink::try_new(&stream_handle)` at a call site and changes
nothing else about it. The returned sink is stopped by dropping it,
reports `empty` when its queue drains, and takes volume and pause the
way it always did.

items.name: play_raw
items.sig: pub fn play_raw<S>(&self, lane: Lane, source: S) where S: Source<Item = f32> + Send + 'static,
items.doc:
Play a source on one lane with no handle to control it.

For sound that is over before anything could want to stop it, and for
the silent primer a device wants at open. Everything else should take
a sink, because a sound with no handle cannot be silenced when the
transport stops.

items.name: Lane
items.doc:
Which of the game's two kinds of sound a block of samples belongs to.

The two are separated at the bus and stay separated all the way to the
display, because the question the monitor exists to answer is usually
about one of them: whether the music is ducking, or whether a sound effect
fired. A single mixed lane can be summed out of these two, and two lanes
cannot be recovered from one mixed one.

A third kind — ambient beds, dialogue — is one variant here, one row in
`ALL`, and one arm in `label`. Nothing else counts lanes.

items.name: ALL
items.doc: Every lane, in display order.

items.name: index
items.doc: Its index into the ring array.

items.name: label
items.doc: The name the panel puts on it.

items.name: from_index

items.doc:
One biome: gameplay first, then looks, then placement.

Make one with [`Biome::new`] and [`BiomeBuilder::build`], or the default
biome with [`Biome::base`] and [`BiomeBuilder::build_base`].

```
use warp_sdk::world::biome::{Biome, Hazard, Reward};
let trench = Biome::new("trench")
.reward(Reward::discovery("abyssal_eel"))
.cost(Hazard::Pressure, 1.0)
.light(0.05)
.band(120.0, 400.0)
.build()
.unwrap();
assert_eq!(trench.costs[0].hazard, Hazard::Pressure);
```

items.name: DeadZone
items.doc:
A radial dead zone with scaled output.

Inside `inner` the output is zero. From `inner` to `outer` the length
goes from 0 to 1, so the smallest move past the dead zone is a small
output, not a jump. Past `outer` the length is 1. The direction stays.

```ignore
let dz = DeadZone::default(); // inner 0.15, outer 0.95
let v = dz.apply(pad.stick(Stick::Left));
```

items.doc:

```ignore

```

items.name: motion
items.doc:

```ignore

```

items.name: tick
items.sig: pub fn tick(&mut self, dt: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
Move every effect forward by the real frame time `dt`, in seconds.
Return the game time for this frame: less than `dt`, or zero, while a
hit-stop holds.

```ignore
let game_dt = juice.tick(dt);
world.step(game_dt);
```

items.name: active
items.doc:
True while anything still moves. A `gui` can stop repaints when false.

```ignore
if juice.active() { ctx.request_repaint(); }
```

items.name: hit_stop
items.sig: pub fn hit_stop(&mut self, impact: f32)
items.doc:
Freeze the game for a time that grows with `impact`. 1.0 is a normal
hit: [`HIT_STOP_PER_IMPACT`] seconds. No freeze is longer than
[`HIT_STOP_MAX`]. A second hit during a freeze does not add to it.

```ignore
juice.hit_stop(damage as f32 / 10.0);
```

items.name: frozen
items.doc:
True while a hit-stop holds the game.

```ignore
if juice.frozen() { /* skip the input buffer */ }
```

items.name: pop
items.sig: pub fn pop(&mut self, at: World, value: i64, color: Color32)
items.doc:
Show `value` at `at` as a number that rises, grows and fades.

A pop merges into a live pop of the same colour and sign that is
nearer than [`POP_MERGE_DIST`] and got a value less than
[`POP_MERGE_SECS`] ago. The values add, and the pop grows again, so
fast hits read as one big number.

```ignore
juice.pop(enemy.pos, -damage, Color32::from_rgb(255, 90, 80));
juice.pop(chest.pos, 25, Color32::GOLD);
```

items.name: SAVE_VERSION
items.doc:
The save format version that [`Meta::save`] writes.

The layout is the 4 bytes `WMP\0`, a little-endian `u16` version, then
each section in order: wallet, counters, unlocked, upgrades, milestones,
stages, codex, runs. A count is a `u32`, a number is a `u64`, and a
string is a `u32` length and UTF-8 bytes.

```
assert_eq!(warp_sdk::metaprog::SAVE_VERSION, 1);
```
