items.name: dropdown
items.sig: pub fn dropdown<R>( ui: &Ui, id: egui::Id, trigger: &Response, width: f32, add: impl FnOnce(&mut Ui) -> R, ) -> Option<R>
items.doc:
A panel that hangs below a button, at a width the caller picks.

The click on `trigger` opens and closes it, Escape closes it, and a click
anywhere else closes it. Returns None while it is shut, so the body costs
nothing when nobody looks at it.

Not `egui::popup::popup_below_widget`. That helper sets the panel width to
the width of the button that opened it, so a form behind a narrow button
would be a narrow column.

items.name: foldout
items.sig: pub fn foldout<R>( ui: &mut Ui, id: &str, title: &str, open_default: bool, body: impl FnOnce(&mut Ui) -> R, ) -> Option<R>
items.doc:
A collapsing section with a triangle, the main grouping device.

The open state lives in egui memory under `id`, so the section keeps its
state across frames and across a rebuild of the panel. `id` must be
unique inside the parent Ui.

The body runs only while the section is open, so the return is an Option.

items.name: header
items.doc:
A section title on a filled bar, with a rule along its bottom edge.

The bar spans the full width and the rule sits on the bottom edge of that
bar. The first version drew its rule at the top of the space that was
still free, which put the line below the title and below the gap, so the
line floated away from the text it belonged to.

items.name: hint
items.sig: pub fn hint(ui: &mut Ui, text: &str) -> Response
items.doc: Dim helper text, for a default value or a derived name.

items.name: icon_button
items.sig: pub fn icon_button(ui: &mut Ui, glyph: &str, tooltip: &str, enabled: bool) -> Response
items.doc:
A square button that carries one glyph, for a `-` or `+` control.

The tooltip is not optional here. A glyph alone cannot say what the button
changes, so the caller must give the words.

items.name: label_text
items.sig: pub fn label_text(ui: &mut Ui, text: &str) -> Response
items.doc:
Plain body text that does nothing when the pointer touches it.

Use this for a value a toolbar shows, such as a count or a mode name. A
caller that reached for a button to show a value made the value look
clickable, which is the confusion this widget removes.

items.name: row
items.sig: pub fn row<R>(ui: &mut Ui, label: &str, add: impl FnOnce(&mut Ui) -> R) -> R
items.doc:
One inspector row: a fixed-width label, then whatever the caller adds.

The label column has one width for every row, so a column of fields lines
up down the panel even when the labels differ in length. The row lays out
left to right with vertical centering, so a field shorter than the row
sits on the middle line and not on the top edge.

items.name: separator_h
items.doc: A single-pixel rule across the panel, with a little air each side.

items.name: set_foldout
items.sig: pub fn set_foldout(ui: &Ui, id: &str, open: bool)
items.doc:
Force one foldout open or shut, before or after it draws.

`foldout` reads its own state from egui memory and a caller cannot reach
that state through the return value, so a panel that wants to open its
groups from a control ABOVE them has no other way in.

`id` is the same string the `foldout` call uses, and the same `Ui` must
make both — `make_persistent_id` hashes the parent, so an id built in a
different `Ui` names a different foldout and the call does nothing.

The write lands on the next frame, which is what makes the order safe: a
caller can set the state before the group draws, or after it.

items.name: slider
items.sig: pub fn slider(ui: &mut Ui, value: &mut f32, range: std::ops::RangeInclusive<f32>) -> Response
items.doc:
A slider that spans the row, with the number in a fixed column at its end.

The gestures, in the order somebody discovers them:

drag the handle      the value follows the pointer, no jump at the press
press the rail       the handle jumps to the pointer and the drag begins
Shift while dragging a tenth of the distance, taken or dropped mid-drag
Cmd while dragging   snap to a step read from the span of the range
arrows, when focused one step; Shift for a tenth of one
Page Up, Page Down   ten steps
Home, End            the ends of the range
the value box        drag it for fine work, click it to type a number

The response is the union of the rail and the box, so `.changed()` is true
for a move made either way.

items.name: toggle_button
items.sig: pub fn toggle_button(ui: &mut Ui, text: &str, active: bool, enabled: bool) -> Response
items.doc:
A button that holds an on state, for a view switcher or a mode switch.

The on state paints theme::bg_selected(), the one saturated value in the
palette, so the choice that is showing is obvious across the toolbar. The
earlier chrome had no such widget, and callers wrote the state into the
label as `[Grid]`, which reads as text and not as a state.

items.name: tool_button
items.sig: pub fn tool_button(ui: &mut Ui, text: &str, enabled: bool) -> Response
items.doc:
A toolbar button with a raised face, a border and a centered label.

The face is btn_face(), which is much lighter than the BG_HEADER strip a
toolbar paints, so the button carries a visible edge before the pointer
arrives. Hover lifts the value and lights the border. A press drops the
value to theme::bg_active(). A disabled button senses hover only, so a
caller never reads a click from it.

items.name: set_motion
items.doc:
Set the motion preference for one egui context, for example from a
settings toggle. The saved process preference applies when none is set.

items.name: Deck
items.doc:
A corner cluster of squircle keys, each owning a panel that unfolds out of
it. Build it every frame and call `show`.

```ignore
let r = squircle::Deck::new("hud")
.corner(squircle::Corner::TopRight)
.panel("Data", |ui| { ui.label("..."); })
.add(squircle::Panel::new("View", |ui| { ui.label("..."); })
.glyph(squircle::Icon::Eye))
.add(squircle::Panel::action("Reset").glyph(squircle::Icon::Refresh))
.show(ctx);
if r.clicked("Reset") { /* ... */ }
```

items.sig: pub fn paint_key( painter: &Painter, look: &Look, rect: Rect, glyph: &Glyph, label: &str, hover: f32, open: f32, pulse: f32, dot: Option<Color32>, )
items.doc:
Paint one key face in its resting slot `rect`.

`hover`, `open` and `pulse` are eased 0..1 values. `hover` grows the key
about its centre and lifts its fill. `open` runs the fill to the accent.
`pulse` is a short accent flash after an action key fires. `dot` is a small
status mark in the top-right corner.

before you ship it.

items.sig: pub fn mix(a: Color32, b: Color32, t: f32) -> Color32
items.doc: Blend two colours in straight RGBA. `t` is clamped to 0..1.

items.name: set_look
items.doc:
Set the default look for one egui context. Every key, readout, toast,
hover-card and deck without its own `look` reads it.

items.name: Corner
items.doc: A corner of the screen. A deck, a toast stack and a tray each sit in one.
items.body:
TopLeft,
TopRight,
BottomLeft,
BottomRight,

items.name: is_top
items.doc: True for the two top corners. A top deck unfolds its panels downward.

items.name: is_left
items.doc: True for the two left corners.

items.name: align
items.doc: The egui alignment of this corner, for an anchored `Area`.

items.name: Look
items.doc:
The token set every squircle surface paints with.

Colours are straight (unmultiplied) RGBA. Sizes are design points at
scale 1; read them through `s`, never raw.

items.name: dark
items.doc:
The default: dark glass over a dark viewport, with a cool accent.

It is tuned for scientific visualisation. The surfaces stay below the
luminance of a plotted point, so the data stays the brightest thing on
the screen, and the accent is a sky cyan that does not read as a status.

items.name: light
items.doc: Light paper, for a tool that is drawn over a light plot.

items.name: from_palette
items.doc:
The project palette, mapped onto the tokens. A `[settings.theme]` edit
then reaches the squircle kit too. Sizes stay at the dark defaults.

Not on Android: the project palette lives in `panels`, which an
Android build does not compile.

items.name: with_accent
items.sig: pub fn with_accent(mut self, accent: Color32) -> Self
items.doc: The same look with another accent.

items.name: with_scale
items.sig: pub fn with_scale(mut self, scale: f32) -> Self
items.doc: The same look at a pinned interface scale.

items.name: with_pace
items.sig: pub fn with_pace(mut self, pace: f32) -> Self
items.doc: The same look with another motion pace. See `pace`.

items.name: with_toast_corner
items.sig: pub fn with_toast_corner(mut self, corner: Corner) -> Self
items.doc: The same look with the toast stack in another corner.

items.name: scale
items.doc: The interface scale this look draws at.

items.name: s
items.sig: pub fn s(&self, v: f32) -> f32
items.doc: A design size in points, at this look's scale.

items.name: tone
items.sig: pub fn tone(&self, t: Tone) -> Color32
items.doc: The hue of a tone.

items.name: get
items.doc: The context default. A context that never had one set gets `dark`.

items.name: Tone
items.doc: The meaning of a toast or a readout, which selects its hue.

items.name: format_value
items.sig: pub fn format_value(v: f64, sig: usize) -> String
items.doc:
Format `v` at `sig` significant digits. Exponent form at or above 1e5 and
under 1e-3; fixed form between. `NaN` prints as `nan`.

items.name: Readout
items.doc:
A telemetry chip: caption, value, unit, and an optional sparkline.

```ignore
ui.add(squircle::Readout::new("Energy", e).unit("J").digits(5).spark(&history));
```

items.name: new

items.name: digits

items.name: spark

items.doc:
A sparkline of recent samples, oldest first. Fewer than two samples
draw no line.

items.name: tone
items.sig: pub fn tone(mut self, tone: Tone) -> Self
items.doc: Colour the value and the line by a tone, for a value out of range.

items.name: vertical
items.sig: pub fn vertical(mut self, on: bool) -> Self
items.doc: True stacks the contents in a column. The default is a row.

items.name: look

items.doc: The look for the spacing. The default is the context look.

items.name: within
items.sig: pub fn within(mut self, rect: Rect) -> Self
items.doc: Anchor inside `rect`. The default is the whole screen.

items.name: show
items.sig: pub fn show<R>(self, ctx: &Context, add: impl FnOnce(&mut Ui) -> R) -> InnerResponse<R>
items.doc: Draw the tray and its contents.

items.name: show_toasts
items.doc:
Draw the toast stack at the context look. Call it once per frame in an app
with no deck; a deck calls it for you.

items.name: toast
items.sig: pub fn toast(ctx: &Context, text: impl Into<String>)
items.doc: Push an information toast. It holds for `DWELL` seconds.

items.name: toast_count
items.doc:
The number of toasts not yet expired at the last draw, plus any pushed
since.

items.name: toast_for
items.sig: pub fn toast_for(ctx: &Context, text: impl Into<String>, tone: Tone, secs: f32)
items.doc: Push a toast that holds for `secs` seconds before it fades.

items.name: toast_tone
items.sig: pub fn toast_tone(ctx: &Context, text: impl Into<String>, tone: Tone)
items.doc: Push a toast with a tone: `Ok`, `Warn`, `Bad`, `Info` or `Neutral`.

items.name: TOAST_DWELL
items.doc: Seconds a toast holds at full before it fades.

items.name: Icon
items.doc: The toolbar glyphs.

items.name: MotionPref
items.doc: The viewer's motion preference for one egui context. `Full` is the default.

items.name: ALL
items.doc:
Every preference, in the order a menu lists them and the index the
atomic stores.

items.name: title
items.doc: The name a person reads in the menu.

items.name: token
items.doc:
The word written to the store. Stable across builds, or a rename resets
the choice of everybody who already made one.

items.name: from_token
items.doc:
Read a token back. An unknown word gives `Full`, so a store written by a
later build still opens.

items.name: Curve
items.doc:
The named easing curves the shell shares. One definition, so every reveal
and every move reads the same.

items.name: apply
items.sig: pub fn apply(self, t: f32) -> f32
items.doc: Reshape a linear `t` in 0..1 by this curve. `t` is clamped first.

items.name: Motion
items.doc: The five shell motion tokens. A caller names one instead of a raw duration.

items.name: base_secs
items.doc: The base duration of this token at full motion, in seconds.

items.name: curve
items.doc: The curve this token moves along.

items.name: secs_for
items.sig: pub fn secs_for(self, pref: Pref) -> f32
items.doc:
Resolve the duration against a preference. Pure, so a test needs no
context.

items.name: secs
items.doc: Resolve the duration against the context's preference.

items.name: dt
items.doc:
The frame step to advance an animation by, in seconds.

egui's `stable_dt` is the measured step while frames run back to back, and
the predicted step after an idle gap. An idle app therefore does not snap
its first animation frame.

items.name: snaps
items.doc: True when the viewer asked for less motion, so every squircle move snaps.

items.name: secs
items.sig: pub fn secs(ctx: &Context, token: Motion, pace: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
The duration of `token` for this context, times `pace`. Zero when motion is
reduced or off.

items.name: tween_pref
items.doc:
The preference a `motion::RectTween` steps under for a squircle surface:
full, or off. See "REDUCED MOTION SNAPS".

items.name: Progress
items.doc:
A linear 0..1 clock that runs toward a boolean target.

Store it in egui memory between frames. Read it through `eased`.
items.body:
/// The linear value, 0 shut and 1 open.
pub u: f32,

items.name: at
items.doc: A clock already at rest at one end.

items.name: step
items.sig: pub fn step(&mut self, on: bool, secs: f32, dt: f32)
items.doc:
Advance toward `on` by `dt` over a run of `secs`. A zero run lands at
once.

items.name: eased
items.sig: pub fn eased(self, curve: Curve) -> f32
items.doc: The value shaped by `curve`.

items.name: settled
items.doc: True at either end. A settled clock asks for no repaint.

items.name: is_open
items.doc: True only at the open end. A panel takes clicks only then.

items.name: is_shut
items.doc: True at the shut end. A shut panel is not drawn.

items.name: approach
items.sig: pub fn approach(cur: f32, target: f32, secs: f32, dt: f32, snap: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
Move `cur` toward `target`, independent of the frame rate.

The step is exponential decay with a time constant of a quarter of `secs`,
so the value is within two percent of the target after `secs`. The tail
snaps onto the target inside `snap`. Without the snap a value stays just
short of its target, and the surface asks for a repaint forever.

items.name: MIN_TOUCH
items.doc: The smallest hit target for a finger, in design units.

items.name: NARROW
items.doc: A safe area narrower than this, in design units, gets the dock.

items.name: SHEET_MAX_W
items.doc:
The widest a bottom sheet grows, in design units, so a sheet on a tablet
in portrait stays one a hand can cross.

items.name: LONG_PRESS_S
items.doc: Seconds a finger must rest, without a drag, to make a long press.

items.name: COAST_S
items.doc: Seconds of coast a released drag projects forward, before it snaps.

items.name: FLING
items.doc: Speed, in design units per second, past which a release is a fling.

items.name: DRAG_FADE
items.doc: Opacity of an unpinned panel while the viewport is dragged.

items.name: PRESS_SHRINK
items.doc: How far a key shrinks under a finger, as a fraction of its size.

items.name: Metrics
items.doc:
The design-unit sizes the layout needs. A deck fills it from its own look,
so this file holds no colour and reads no skin.

items.name: Insets
items.doc:
Safe-area insets in points: the strips a notch, a home indicator or a
system bar covers.
items.body:
pub top: f32,
pub right: f32,
pub bottom: f32,
pub left: f32,

items.name: from_content_rect
items.sig: pub fn from_content_rect(window_px: [u32; 2], content_px: [i32; 4], pixels_per_point: f32) -> Insets
items.doc:
The insets that a host content rect leaves inside its window, in
points. `window_px` is the window size and `content_px` is
`[left, top, right, bottom]`, both in physical pixels. An empty content
rect means that the host has not reported one, so the result is zero.
The Android host calls this function each frame.

items.name: PointerKind
items.doc: What the person points with.

items.name: Arrangement
items.doc: How the keys and panels are arranged.

items.name: Detent
items.doc: The rest heights of a bottom sheet.

items.name: Form
items.doc: The input to `layout`.

items.name: Layout
items.doc: The output of `layout`. Every length is in points.

items.name: detent_h
items.sig: pub fn detent_h(&self, d: Detent) -> f32
items.doc: The height of one detent.

items.name: nearest_detent
items.sig: pub fn nearest_detent(&self, h: f32) -> Detent
items.doc: The detent whose height is nearest `h`.

items.name: sheet_rect
items.sig: pub fn sheet_rect(&self, h: f32) -> Rect
items.doc: The rect of a sheet at height `h`: bottom-anchored in `sheet`.

items.name: layout
items.doc:
Lay out a form. Pure: the same form gives the same layout.

The dock is chosen for a safe area narrower than `NARROW` design units, or
for a finger on a portrait screen. Everything else gets corners.

items.name: dock_keys
items.sig: pub fn dock_keys(l: &Layout, widths: &[f32], gap: f32) -> Vec<Rect>
items.doc:
The key rects of a dock, for key `widths` in points: centred in the dock
strip, `gap` apart. A row wider than the dock keeps its left edge at the
dock's left edge, so the first key is always reachable.

items.name: Room
items.doc: Where an open panel goes so it does not cover what the user acts on.

items.name: rect
items.doc: The rect the panel goals to.

items.name: make_room
items.sig: pub fn make_room(panel: Rect, focus: &[Rect], region: Rect, gap: f32, header_h: f32, pinned: bool) -> Room
items.doc:
The make-room rule for a floating panel (Corners).

`panel` is where the panel wants to be. `focus` are the rects the user
acts on, `region` is where panels may go, and `header_h` is the header
height in points. The rule, in order: a pinned panel or a clear panel
stays; else the nearest clear place one step past a side of a focus rect;
else the header at the wanted place, if that is clear; else the header at
the nearest clear step.

items.name: make_room_sheet
items.sig: pub fn make_room_sheet(l: &Layout, height: f32, focus: &[Rect], gap: f32, pinned: bool) -> Room
items.doc:
The make-room rule for a bottom sheet (Dock): a sheet over a focus rect
drops to peek. A pinned sheet stays.

items.name: step_off
items.sig: pub fn step_off(slot: Pos2, size: Vec2, occluders: &[Rect], bounds: Rect, gap: f32) -> Pos2
items.doc:
The dodge rule for a surface with no header to fold to: `slot` when it is
clear of `occluders`, else the nearest clear place one step past a side of
an occluder, inside `bounds`, else `slot`. `make_room` is the same rule
with the header fold after it.

items.name: anchored_at
items.sig: pub fn anchored_at(anchor: Pos2, size: Vec2, occluders: &[Rect], bounds: Rect, gap: f32) -> Pos2
items.doc:
The follow rule: place a surface of `size` beside `anchor`, clear of
`occluders`, inside `bounds`. It tries right-below, then left-below, then
right-above. Then it tries the same three pulled back inside `bounds`, then
one step past an occluder. Up-left covers the subject, so it is not tried.

items.name: chrome_fade
items.sig: pub fn chrome_fade(viewport_drag: bool, pinned: bool) -> f32
items.doc:
The opacity target of a panel while the viewport is dragged: unpinned
panels fade back so the picture under them shows, and pinned ones stay.
Ease toward it on `Motion::Standard`; it is a fade, so reduced motion
keeps it short and `Off` snaps it.

items.name: coast_to_anchor
items.sig: pub fn coast_to_anchor(drop: Pos2, velocity: Vec2, size: Vec2, anchors: &[Pos2], region: Rect) -> Pos2
items.doc:
Where a released drag lands: the drop point projected `COAST_S` seconds
along the release `velocity`, then snapped to the nearest of `anchors`.
With no anchors it lands on the projection, pulled inside `region`.
Under reduced motion the caller draws the landing at once.

items.name: flung_home
items.sig: pub fn flung_home(velocity: Vec2, toward: Vec2, scale: f32) -> bool
items.doc:
Is a release a fling toward the deck's corner, which retracts the panel?
`toward` points from the panel at its corner (any length). `scale` is
points per design unit, so the threshold does not change with the zoom.

items.name: sheet_release
items.sig: pub fn sheet_release(l: &Layout, height: f32, vy: f32, scale: f32) -> Option<Detent>
items.doc:
Where a released sheet goes: the detent nearest its projected height, or
`None` to close it. `vy` is the release velocity, positive downward. A
fast downward fling closes from any height; a slow release closes only
below half the peek height.

items.name: press_scale
items.sig: pub fn press_scale(kind: PointerKind, hover: f32, press: f32, hover_grow: f32) -> f32
items.doc:
The draw scale of a key: a mouse hover grows it by `hover_grow`, and a
finger press shrinks it by `PRESS_SHRINK`, because a finger has no hover
and covers a grown key anyway. `hover` and `press` are eased 0..1.

items.name: press_secs
items.doc:
The duration a key's press feedback runs on: quick, and none at all
under `Off`.

items.name: set_insets
items.doc: Report the safe-area insets for this context. Zero until called.

items.name: insets
items.doc: The insets reported for this context.

items.name: set_pointer
items.doc: Fix the pointer kind for this context. `None` returns to detection.

items.name: pointer_kind
items.doc:
The pointer kind: the one set, else `Coarse` on Android or once a touch
event has arrived, else `Fine`.

items.name: form_of
items.sig: pub fn form_of(ctx: &Context, screen: Rect, scale: f32) -> Form
items.doc: The form of this context over `screen`, at `scale` points per design unit.

items.name: report_focus
items.doc:
Report a rect the user is acting on this frame: the selection on screen, a
brush or a drag in progress, the point under a finger. Call it each frame
the focus holds. A frame with no report clears the focus.

items.name: focus_rects
items.doc: The focus rects reported this frame.

items.name: report_viewport_drag
items.doc:
Report that a pointer or touch drag is in progress on the viewport this
frame. Call it each frame the drag holds.

items.name: viewport_drag
items.doc: Is a viewport drag reported this frame?

items.name: probe
items.sig: pub fn probe(ctx: &Context, over_chrome: bool) -> Option<Pos2>
items.doc:
The point a hover-card describes. A mouse probes where it hovers. A finger
probes where it rests in a long press, and a tap leaves a sticky probe
until the next tap or Esc. `over_chrome` is true when the pointer is on a
key or a panel, so a tap there probes nothing.

items.name: N
items.doc:
The superellipse exponent. 4.0 is the canonical squircle. A higher value
moves toward a rectangle; a lower value rounds toward an ellipse.

items.name: points
items.sig: pub fn points(rect: Rect, radius: f32) -> Vec<Pos2>
items.doc:
The outline of `rect` with one corner radius, at the canonical exponent.

The points come back in clockwise screen order (y grows down). The radius
is clamped to half the shorter side, so a large radius gives the fully
rounded shape and never a self-intersection.

items.name: points_corners
items.sig: pub fn points_corners(rect: Rect, radii: [f32; 4]) -> Vec<Pos2>
items.doc: The outline with one radius per corner, ordered `[tl, tr, br, bl]`.

items.name: points_with
items.sig: pub fn points_with(rect: Rect, radii: [f32; 4], n: f32) -> Vec<Pos2>
items.doc: The outline with one radius per corner and an explicit exponent `n`.

items.name: fill
items.sig: pub fn fill(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radius: f32, color: Color32)
items.doc: Fill a squircle. The outline is convex, so `convex_polygon` is safe.

items.name: fill_corners
items.sig: pub fn fill_corners(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radii: [f32; 4], color: Color32)
items.doc: Fill a squircle with one radius per corner, ordered `[tl, tr, br, bl]`.

items.name: stroke
items.sig: pub fn stroke(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radius: f32, stroke: Stroke)
items.doc: Stroke a squircle outline.

items.name: paint
items.sig: pub fn paint(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radius: f32, fill: Color32, stroke: Stroke)
items.doc: Fill and stroke in one shape, with one generated path.

items.name: shadow
items.sig: pub fn shadow(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radius: f32, color: Color32, blur: f32)
items.doc:
A soft drop shadow under a squircle: three widening layers, offset down.

`color` carries the strength in its alpha. `blur` is the widest spread in
points. The layers paint widest first, so the darkest band hugs the shape.

items.name: shadow_shapes
items.sig: pub fn shadow_shapes(rect: Rect, radius: f32, color: Color32, blur: f32) -> Vec<Shape>
items.doc:
The shadow layers as shapes, for a caller that places them after it has
measured its content (`Painter::add(Shape::Noop)` then `Painter::set`).

items.name: shape
items.sig: pub fn shape(rect: Rect, radius: f32, fill: Color32, stroke: Stroke) -> Shape
items.doc: A filled and stroked squircle as one shape, unpainted.

items.name: fill_textured
items.sig: pub fn fill_textured(p: &Painter, rect: Rect, radius: f32, tex: TextureId, uv: Rect, tint: Color32)
items.doc:
Draw a texture clipped to a squircle, as a triangle fan.

`Painter::image` emits an axis-aligned quad, so a portrait drawn with it
keeps square corners. This mesh clips the pixels to the curve. `uv` is the
sub-rect to sample; pass `Rect::from_min_max(pos2(0,0), pos2(1,1))` for the
whole texture.

items.name: x_span
items.sig: pub fn x_span(rect: Rect, radius: f32, y: f32) -> Option<(f32, f32)>
items.doc:
The left and right edge of the squircle interior on the scanline at `y`.

The span is solved from the implicit form `dx = r * (1 - (dy/r)^n)^(1/n)`.
The result is `None` when `y` is off `rect`.

items.name: contains
items.sig: pub fn contains(rect: Rect, radius: f32, pos: Pos2) -> bool
items.doc:
The hit test: true when `pos` is inside the squircle of `rect`.

A key is mostly its rect, but its corners are not. A press in a cut-away
corner falls through to the scene under it.

items.name: Domain
items.doc:
The application name in the handshake transcript, and the hooks for
peers from before the handshake.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(app: impl Into<String>) -> Domain
items.doc: The domain of application `app`, with no old-peer hooks.

items.name: FrameIo
items.doc: One transport, in its three parts.
items.body:
pub tx: Box<dyn FrameTx>,
pub rx: Box<dyn FrameRx>,
pub ctl: Arc<dyn FrameCtl>,

items.name: tcp
items.doc:
A TCP stream as a transport: a u32 little-endian length, then the
frame. Sets nodelay and blocking reads.

items.name: backoff
items.sig: pub fn backoff(base: Duration, n: u32) -> Duration
items.doc:
The reconnect wait before attempt `n` (1-based): 1, 2, 4, 8, 8, ... x
`base`.

items.name: host_invite
items.sig: pub fn host_invite(fmt: &InviteFormat, port: u16, node: Option<[u8; 32]>, code: &str, public: Option<&PublicAddress>) -> Result<String, invite::InviteError>
items.doc:
The invite of a host: the LAN address of this machine, the public
address from `public` when it found one and it differs, the TCP
`port`, the P2P `node` id when the host has an endpoint, and the join
`code`. The application gives the InviteFormat.

items.name: timers_from
items.sig: pub fn timers_from(get: impl Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> Timers
items.doc:
The timers from `get` (an env lookup): WARP_NET_INTERRUPT_S,
WARP_NET_HOLD_S and WARP_NET_GIVE_UP_S, in seconds. A missing, bad or
non-positive value keeps the default.

items.name: Admit
items.doc: What the guest filter decided for one message.

items.name: ChannelLimit
items.doc:
The rate of one class of guest message: `burst` messages, then `rate`
a second.
items.body:
pub rate: f64,
pub burst: f64,

items.name: DEFAULT
items.doc: 60 a second, burst 240: room for a 60 Hz input stream.

items.name: ChatKind
items.doc: What kind of chat line this is. A GUI picks the color from it.

items.name: ChatLine
items.doc: One line in the relay.

items.name: Connected
items.doc: A connected transport that a Dial worker gives to the Guest.

items.name: DialHandle
items.doc: A handle on one Dial, to watch it (the P2P fallback).

items.name: failed
items.doc: The connect error, once the worker failed.

items.name: label
items.doc: What the Dial connects to.

items.name: Dialer
items.sig: pub type Dialer = Arc<dyn Fn() -> Result<FrameIo, String> + Send + Sync>
items.doc:
Opens a new transport to the same host, for a reconnect. For TCP,
transport::tcp::dialer gives one.

items.name: EndReason
items.doc: Why a session ended for this guest.

items.name: Event
items.doc: One thing that happened in the session.

items.name: Guest
items.doc:
A handle on a guest link. Clones share one link. The worker threads
hold weak handles, so a dropped guest closes its link.

items.name: start
items.sig: pub fn start(io: FrameIo, dialer: Option<Dialer>, spec: JoinSpec) -> Guest
items.doc:
Start the handshake on a connected transport `io`. `dialer` opens a
new transport to the same host for a reconnect: with None, a lost
link ends the session. The handshake runs on a thread, so this
returns at once. A refusal sets the status to "Refused: ..." and
ends the guest.

items.name: leave
items.doc:
Leave: send Bye(Leaving), then close. The session ends with Left and
no reconnect. The host frees the seat at once.

items.name: status
items.doc: One status line for a lobby or a banner.

items.name: counters
items.doc:
The wire bytes that the links of this guest wrote, per class
(JoinSpec::counting).

items.name: local_id
items.doc: The seat of this guest, after Welcome.

items.name: roster
items.doc: Every person in the session, host first, as the host sent it.

items.name: closed
items.doc:
True when the session ended (Ended). An Interrupted guest is not
closed: it reconnects.

items.name: interrupted
items.doc: True while the link is Interrupted and a reconnect runs.

items.name: token
items.doc: The seat token, after Welcome.

items.name: host_name
items.doc: The host name from Welcome.

items.name: poll_events
items.doc: Every event since the last call, oldest first.

items.name: history
items.doc: The newest link events (no messages), oldest first. No drain.

items.name: events_dropped

The blob in transfer: its name, the bytes received and the packed

items.doc:
Send `data` on `channel` to the host, reliably and in order. False
before Welcome, while Interrupted (the send is dropped and counted),
after the end, or for data over GUEST_APP_MAX bytes (the host would
close the link).

over the guest frame cap.

Ask the host for blob `name`. The host answers with the blob
(Event::BlobProgress, then Event::BlobDone or Event::BlobFailed), or
with a status Notice when it cannot build it. A new request replaces
a request that got no answer. False when not linked.

Send one chat line to the host. The line shows when the host relays
it back. Err is a sentence for the player: no link, or the local
rate check refused it.

items.name: GuestConfig
items.doc: The guest timers. Tests make them short, so they need no env.

items.name: Host
items.doc:
A handle on a running host. Clones share one host. Call `stop` to end
it: the housekeeping thread and the links hold the host until then.

items.name: new
items.sig: pub fn new(domain: Domain, name: &str, build: &str, code: &str, cfg: HostConfig) -> std::io::Result<Host>
items.doc:
Start a host. `name` is the host's own name in the roster. Only a
guest that runs the handshake in the same `domain` (the application
name), with `code` and the same `build`, joins. The host has no transport of its own: give it each accepted
transport with `accept_io`. Err when the housekeeping thread does
not start.

items.name: set_filter
items.sig: pub fn set_filter(&self, f: impl Fn(&Inbound) -> Admit + Send + Sync + 'static)
items.doc:
Set the guest filter: the application check on each guest message
that passed the rate limits. It runs on the reader thread of the
guest, with no host lock held, so it may call the Host. With no
filter, every message is accepted.

items.name: accept_io
items.sig: pub fn accept_io(&self, io: FrameIo, from: &str)
items.doc:
Start the handshake on a transport that the application accepted:
a TCP stream, a P2P connection, a platform connection. `from` names
the transport in the log, and its `source_key` is the source for the
lockout and the ban (for example "ip:port" for TCP).

items.name: name
items.doc: The host's own name, cleaned.

items.name: join_code
items.doc: The join code that guests must type.

items.name: stopped
items.doc: True after `stop`.

items.name: stop
items.doc:
Close every guest and every transport in the handshake. Every guest
gets Bye(HostEnding) first, so it ends at once and does not try to
reconnect.

items.name: kick
items.sig: pub fn kick(&self, peer: u8) -> bool
items.doc:
Remove guest `peer` from the session. The guest gets Bye(Kicked),
and the link closes. Its token is refused for the rest of the
session. A held seat is freed at once. False when the seat is empty,
or for peer 0 (the host). The source of the guest gets no fresh seat
for the rest of the session, so the guest cannot join again with the
code as a new guest. Other guests behind the same IP keep their
seats, also across a redial with their own token. A loopback source
is not banned when `trust_loopback` is set.

(`channel`, `key`): an unsent older message with the same channel
and key is replaced. For state that only its newest value matters,
for example a cursor or a paddle. False when the seat is empty.

every guest that waits for that name, and end the encode. The call
returns at once.

Tell every guest that waits for blob `name` that it could not be
built, and end the encode.

items.name: join_dialed
items.sig: pub fn join_dialed<F>(&self, label: &str, spec: JoinSpec, connect: F) -> Result<DialHandle, String> where F: FnOnce() -> Result<Connected, String> + Send + 'static
items.doc:
Start a guest join with `connect` on the "net-dial" worker. The role
before ends, and a Dial for `label` takes its place at once, so the
call returns before the connect. When `connect` gives a transport
and the Dial is still the role, the Guest replaces it. A failure
stays on the Dial as its status.

items.name: join_dialed_after
items.sig: pub fn join_dialed_after<F>(&self, watched: &DialHandle, label: &str, spec: JoinSpec, connect: F) -> Result<DialHandle, String> where F: FnOnce() -> Result<Connected, String> + Send + 'static
items.doc:
Start a join in place of the Dial `watched` (a fallback). The check
that `watched` is still the role and the change to the new Dial
occur under one lock. Thus a leave or a newer join that comes after
the check of the caller wins, and this call returns DIAL_SUPERSEDED
and does not connect. No leave runs: a Dial has no link.

items.name: join_tcp
items.sig: pub fn join_tcp(&self, addr: &str, default_port: u16, spec: JoinSpec) -> Result<DialHandle, String>
items.doc:

missing port is `default_port`. Returns at once (join_dialed).

items.name: join_invite
items.sig: pub fn join_invite(&self, fmt: &InviteFormat, text: &str, mut spec: JoinSpec, p2p: Option<P2p>) -> Result<(), String>
items.doc:
Join from a pasted invite. The invite gives the join code, so
`spec.code` is replaced. A version 2 invite dials the host over P2P
first when `p2p` is Some, and the LAN addresses over TCP only after
that dial failed. Err on return only for a bad invite or a failed
worker start.

candidate. The first candidate that decodes with a good check wins.

the clock and the process id. The code is the SPAKE2 password
(crypto.rs), so each guess costs one handshake, and the host lockout
limits the guesses per source.

items.name: Script
items.doc:
A timeline of input, one entry for each frame.

Each step adds frames. The events of a step arrive at the start of its
first frame, before `input` and `gui` run:

| step | frames | what `input` sees |
|---|---|---|
| `wait(f)` | f | no new events |
| `press(k)` | 1 | `key_pressed(k)`; `k` stays held |
| `release(k)` | 1 | `key_released(k)` |
| `hold(k, f)` | f + 1 | `k` held on f frames, released on the last |
| `mouse_to(xy)` | 1 | `mouse()` is `xy` |
| `click(b)` | 2 | `b` pressed, then released |
| `hold_mouse(b, f)` | f + 1 | `b` held on f frames, released on the last |

```ignore
let script = Script::new()
.wait(30)                       // the title fades in
.press(Key::Return)             // start a run
.hold(Key::Right, 60)           // move for one second
.mouse_to([640.0, 360.0])
.click(Button::Left)
.wait(30);
```

items.name: DisplaySettings
items.doc:
Serialisable because the game is a second process now. The Post-processing
section edits the copy in the EDITOR, and the picture is composed by the
child — so the struct has to cross a socket or the panel writes a global
nobody with a framebuffer is reading.

`PartialEq` for the same reason: the editor sends this on the change and
not on the frame, so something has to answer whether it changed.
`serde(default)` is the contract with `project_settings`. The table on disk
holds ONLY the keys that differ from `DEFAULT`, so every absent field must
fall back to it rather than fail the whole block for being incomplete.

items.name: DEFAULT
items.doc:
What a game gets before it asks for anything, as a const so a
`static Mutex` can hold it.

`Default::default()` is not callable in a const initializer, and the
settings are one global now — so the values live here and `Default`
returns this rather than the other way round.

EVERY EFFECT IS OFF, AND THE VALUES BESIDE THE SWITCHES ARE NOT
---------------------------------------------------------------
A new project draws what it drew: the rects and lines its `render`
method submits, at the colours it chose. It used to draw those through
an HDR chain and a barrel-distorted CRT filter, because this const held
the look of one game — so the first picture anybody made in this engine
came out bloomed, saturated and bent, and nothing in the project said
where that came from.

The tuned numbers stay. They are the look those two passes had, and a
game that wants it sets `pp_enabled` and `crt_enabled` and gets it back
whole; a game that wants its own moves the fields beside them. What
changed is which of the two states costs a line of code.

AND THE TUBE GREW THIRTY-ONE MORE FIELDS WITHOUT MOVING THE PICTURE
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The CRT filter gained a phosphor mask, a parallax model, a per-channel
convergence block and a set of visualisation modes. A project that sets
only `crt_enabled = true` today must get exactly the picture it got
before them, so every one of those features is off in this const:
`crt_mask_type` 0, `crt_mask_strength` 0, `crt_parallax_strength` 0,
all six `crt_conv_*` 0, `crt_viz_mode` 0, and `crt_phosphor_on` false.
`crt_curve_aspect` is 1.0, which makes the two-axis barrel equal to the
single scalar it replaced.

The fields those switches multiply keep real values rather than zero —
`crt_mask_triad_px`, `crt_slot_height_px`, `crt_eye_dist`, `crt_glass_ior`
and `crt_mask_boost` are divisors, periods or a gain of one, where zero
is a divide or a black screen and not a no-op.

`crt_phosphor_gui_exempt` defaults to 1.0 and is dormant. The default
is left where it was because the field is only carried, never read;
changing it would rewrite every saved project for no visible effect.

items.name: copy_crt_tuning_from
items.doc:
Copy every `crt_*` field except `crt_enabled` from `src`.

The tube's tuning is sixty-odd fields that a game sets as one block,
so `warp_sdk::post::CrtTuning` carries them in a `DisplaySettings`
and moves them with this. The list is in ONE place: a field added to
the struct and not here is a field the SDK drops, and the test below
fails on it: it changes every `crt_*` key the struct serialises.

items.sig: pub fn draw_structure_prop( &mut self, position: Vec2, size: f32, rotation: f32, type_id: u32, variant: u32, tint: [u8; 4], extra_flags: u32, )
items.doc:
Draw a structure prop using the Structures mega-atlas by an arbitrary
type id. Unlike `draw_station_module`, this is not gated to the module
index range, so a group the application declares past the module type
ids (a research bench, say) can draw a lit sprite. The type id must name
a group the structures atlas registered, or the mapping answers layer 0.

# Arguments
* `type_id` - Structures-atlas type id of the prop group
* `variant` - Texture variant, wrapped to the group's loaded count
* `tint` - Color tint [R,G,B,A]. Use [255,255,255,255] for no tint.

items.name: draw_mega_atlas_image
items.sig: pub fn draw_mega_atlas_image( &mut self, slot: usize, global_index: i32, position: Vec2, size: f32, rotation: f32, tint: [u8; 4], flags: u32, )
items.doc: Draw a textured sprite using the unified mega-atlas system (low-level).

items.name: draw_scene
items.sig: pub fn draw_scene(&mut self, scene: &Scene) -> usize
items.doc:
Draw every visible object in `scene`, each at its world transform.

Objects with no `Visual` are skipped and still compose for their
children — a group is a transform with a name, and that is a thing
worth having in a scene.

Returns how many instances were pushed, which is what a panel shows
when a person asks why they are looking at an empty viewport.

items.name: mega_atlas_index
items.sig: pub fn mega_atlas_index(&self, slot: usize, type_id: u32, variant: u32) -> Option<i32>
items.doc:
The global texture index for one atlas entry, or `None` when the slot
does not exist.

This is the neutral resolver under the game-shaped `draw_*` helpers. It
names no game noun: a caller gives a slot, a type id and a variant, and
gets back the index `draw_mega_atlas_image` takes. `None` says the slot
is not there, so the scene loop skips the object and a fixed-slot helper
falls back to layer 0. It is `pub` because a game writing its own
`draw_resource`-style helper resolves through this, not through an
engine method that knows the game's nouns.

items.name: atlas_has
items.sig: pub fn atlas_has(&self, slot: usize, type_id: u32) -> bool
items.doc:
Whether an object's picture is actually registered.

For a panel that has to answer "why is my scene invisible". An
unregistered pair does not fail: `get_index` returns 0, so the object
draws SOME texture rather than none, which is worse to diagnose than a
blank — it looks like the store put the wrong art on the object.

A slot past the end of the mapping list answers false, which is the
case `draw_scene` skips outright.

items.name: frame_fingerprint
items.doc:
A stable per-bucket count of one submitted frame, in `FRAME_BUCKETS`
order. The last entry is the sum of the first thirteen. The counts are
`u32`, so a golden value is a plain array literal with no engine type to
import.

items.name: draw_circle
items.sig: pub fn draw_circle(&mut self, position: Vec2, radius: f32, color: [u8; 4])

items.name: draw_flat_circle
items.sig: pub fn draw_flat_circle(&mut self, position: Vec2, radius: f32, color: [u8; 4])
items.doc:
A disc in the instance colour, flat from the middle to the edge.

`draw_circle` pushes `texture_index: -1`, and the fragment shader
answers that with the planet path: it builds a unit-sphere normal
out of the fragment position and shades the fill against it. A
bullet, a spark and a pickup all come out as little balls, and
`lighting_wrap` only flattens the diffuse half of it — the Blinn
lobe stays. This one takes the sentinel the shader reads as FLAT,
so no normal is built and no light term is added at all.

The same overlay rect, with per-instance render flags.

`RECT_FLAG_RECEIVE_SHADOW` makes the rect darken under a station shadow.
The overlay row shares one buffer and one pipeline, so the flag is how
the shader tells a shadow-receiving rect from a plain one. The plain
verb above passes zero, which reproduces every overlay rect written
before the flag.

Receive platform-neutral multitouch contacts. The default keeps
existing projects source-compatible; projects interpret contacts.

items.name: render
items.sig: fn render(&mut self, viewport: ViewportId, ctx: &mut RenderContext)

items.name: gui
items.sig: fn gui(&mut self, viewport: ViewportId, ctx: &egui::Context, display: &mut crate::types::DisplaySettings)

items.name: auto_style
items.doc:
Whether the engine styles this game's chrome GUI for it.

True by default. Before `gui`, the engine installs the editor Style and
the zoom keys, so a game that writes no styling draws at the editor
sizes and answers Command with +, - and 0. The pixels-per-point lock
leaves egui default sizes at half scale on a retina panel, so a bare
context looks too small and its zoom keys do nothing; this default
answers both.

Return false to keep a raw egui context, or to install a style of your
own. A host that runs its own zoom keys, like the shell, returns false
so the engine does not step the scale a second time on one press.

items.name: game_gui
items.doc:
The GUI that belongs INSIDE the game image, on a second egui context.

`gui` above draws in window space and lands on the surface. This one
draws in game-image space and lands on the LDR image, before the CRT
pass, so a HUD drawn here sits inside the game view panel and carries
the same filter the scene does.

Two contexts, because one cannot serve both. A single context lays out
at one screen rect, so a chrome panel and a HUD would share coordinates
and the HUD would paint over the toolbar.

Called only while embedded mode is on. A host that draws no chrome puts
everything in `gui` and leaves this alone, which is the shipped game.

items.name: set_crt_params
items.doc:
Receive CRT distortion parameters for mouse coordinate correction.
Called each frame before input() so game-side mouse transforms match
the barrel distortion applied by the CRT post-process shader.

items.name: set_active_viewport
items.doc:
Notify the renderer which viewport currently has input focus.
Called on CursorEntered / Focused events so camera controls
route to the correct viewport.

items.name: set_secondary_camera
items.doc:
Initialize the secondary viewport camera position and scale.
Called when the secondary window is first created.

items.name: scroll_secondary_camera
items.doc: Apply scroll-zoom to the secondary viewport camera.

items.name: pan_secondary_camera
items.doc: Apply pan offset to the secondary viewport camera.

items.name: set_mouse_scale
items.doc: Set mouse coordinate remap factors (render_size / window_size).

items.name: scene_underlay
items.doc:
Draw an optional UNDERLAY into the HDR scene. The engine encodes it
after the HDR clear and BEFORE the scene pass. The scene layers
(planets, ships, stations, stars) then draw over it. Use it for a
background: sky, terrain, a far field. Default: no-op.
For a pass that draws AFTER the scene layers, use `scene_overlay`.

```ignore
fn scene_underlay(&mut self, shared: &SharedGpu, encoder: &mut wgpu::CommandEncoder,
hdr: &wgpu::TextureView, _z: &wgpu::TextureView, _cov: &wgpu::TextureView,
view: &View, _px: [u32; 2]) {
self.sky.draw(shared, encoder, hdr, view.width(), view.height());
}
```

`surface_px` is the window size in physical pixels. It is NOT the size
of `hdr_view`: the HDR chain runs at a fixed internal resolution and
the final blit scales it to the window. A pass that needs the target
size reads `view.width()` and `view.height()` (packed in
`view.xy`); a pass that needs the window reads this.

`coverage_view` is the shadow coverage buffer, a single-channel target
the application draws shadow quads into with a Max blend. A composite
scene layer reads it after the scene pass. A pass that casts no shadow
ignores it.

items.name: scene_overlay
frame_reset
items.sig: fn frame_reset(&mut self, _viewport: ViewportId, ctx: &mut RenderContext)
items.doc:
Reset the draw buffers for a new frame.

Every buffer RenderContext holds is filled by the application, so what
a new frame resets is the application's decision. The default clears
all of them, which is what every frame loop did by hand.

items.name: on_close_requested
items.doc:
Called once, when this process is about to end.
Implement to trigger save-and-exit before process termination.

Every quit gesture reaches it — the X button, Alt+F4, and the menu or
Cmd+Q, which sends no close event to any window. `reclaim` is what
calls it, and `reclaim` runs its body once.

items.name: on_transport_stop
items.doc:
Called once, on the edge where the transport moves to Stopped.

A host stops the game by no longer calling `render`, `input` and
`game_gui`. That suppresses the frame, and it releases nothing: an
audio sink plays on its own thread and keeps playing, and every
render-side mirror of the dropped world stays in memory. So a host
cannot tear down through the hooks it just stopped calling, and the
application gets this edge instead.

Called before the host clears its running flag, so the implementation
still owns everything it did while playing.
